heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
What it is
text:
`age` ("actually good encryption") is a small file-encryption tool with
deliberately few knobs: no cipher suites to choose, no key servers, no web of
trust. An identity is one line (`AGE-SECRET-KEY-1...`), a recipient is one
line (`age1...`), and the recipient is derived from the identity by X25519.
Encrypting to a recipient needs nothing but that string.

We almost never invoke `age` directly. It is the **backend sops delegates
to** — see [topic-sops](topic-sops.md), which is the other half of this page.
This page exists because the *key* is the part of the system with no undo, and
because it is the part that behaves differently on Windows.

heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
Why we use it as sops' backend
text:
The alternatives sops supports are PGP (a tool whose failure modes are a
career) and the cloud KMSes (AWS/GCP/Azure — a hard dependency on a
hyperscaler, which is the opposite of the point of a sovereign mini-cloud).
age is offline, has no dependencies, and its entire key management is "a file
with one line in it".

Asymmetry is what earns its place: the workstation encrypts with a public
recipient that is committed to git, and the recipient cannot decrypt anything.

heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
Why two topics rather than one
text:
sops and age are separate tools with separate versions, separate failure modes
and separate install ids, and they fail independently — sops' traps are about
path matching and stdin, age's are about key custody and a false Windows
warning. A reader debugging `no matching creation rules found` and a reader
asking "where does the private key live and who can read it" want different
pages. They are cross-linked in both directions; neither is complete alone.

heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
Where it lives in our repos
text:
age is not configured in-repo — it has nothing to configure. What the repos
contain is its *inputs and outputs*:

`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

- `.sops.yaml` — the public recipient, in git, deliberately.
- `scripts/verify-sops-decrypt.sh` — falls back to the key's known home on the
  workstation, so the check is runnable (and therefore testable) by hand.
- `scripts/argocd-deploy-token.sh` — encrypts with it via sops.

Not in any repo, and never:

- `~/.soevereinlab/mini-cloud-age.txt` — the private identity, on the
  workstation.
- The GitLab **protected file variable** `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` — the same
  identity, for CI.

heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
The key regime
text:
The private key exists in **exactly two places**, both deliberate, and that
number is the design:

| Where | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `~/.soevereinlab/mini-cloud-age.txt` on the workstation | minting and encrypting the deploy token |
| GitLab protected file variable `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` | decrypting in the pipeline |

Anything else — a backup in a note, a copy in a second repo, a paste in a chat
— is a third place, and a third place is the one nobody remembers to rotate.

### `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` — the name is load-bearing, not cosmetic

`SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` is the environment variable **sops itself reads** to find
an age identity, and it expects a *path*. GitLab's `--type file` writes the
variable's content to a temp file and sets the variable to **that file's
path**. So the two halves fit exactly: GitLab produces a path, sops wants a
path. Rename the variable and nothing finds the key.

This is the same shape as `ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY` (also `--type file`), and
verified on the project as shipping that way — metadata only, values never
rendered:

```
$ glab api "projects/<group>%2F<project>/variables" \
    | jq -r '.[] | "\(.key)  protected=\(.protected)  type=\(.variable_type)  raw=\(.raw)"'
ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY  protected=true  type=file  raw=true
SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE   protected=true  type=file  raw=true
```

Note the invocation: `jq` selects the fields **before** anything is printed, so
the value never reaches a terminal or a scrollback buffer. Listing variables to
see their shape is a routine thing to want; doing it by printing them is how a
key ends up in a screenshot.

Set it from **stdin**, so the key never enters argv or shell history — see
[topic-glab](topic-glab.md):

```bash
glab variable set SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE --type file --protected --raw < <keyfile>
```

### `--protected` and the coverage gap it buys

Protected variables exist **only** in pipelines on protected branches.
Consequence, worth stating plainly because it is a real gap and not an
oversight: **merge-request pipelines on feature branches cannot decrypt at
all.** A branch nobody has reviewed never receives the identity, which is the
whole point — but it also means no MR pipeline can verify anything about
decryption. That proof lives on `main` (`verify:sops`). See
[topic-gitlab-ci](topic-gitlab-ci.md).

### The public recipient belongs in git; the private key never does

A recipient encrypts and cannot decrypt. That is not a claim to take on trust,
and there is a one-line check for it: **`age-keygen -y <keyfile>` re-derives
the public recipient from the private identity.** The derivation is one-way, so
this is how you confirm that the recipient committed to `.sops.yaml` is the one
you actually hold — before discovering otherwise during an incident.

Verified 2026-07-15 (public values only):

```
$ age-keygen -y ~/.soevereinlab/mini-cloud-age.txt
age1...                           # compare against the recipient in .sops.yaml
```

The check that matters is the comparison, not the output: if `-y` prints
something that is *not* in `.sops.yaml`, then either the file is encrypted to
a key nobody holds, or you are holding a key for a file that no longer exists.

heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
Flags & settings we use
text:
### `age-keygen -o <path>`

Generate an identity and write it to a file. Without `-o` it writes to stdout,
which on this workstation means the key lands in a scrollback buffer — so `-o`
is not a convenience, it is the leak-avoidance rule applied to key generation.
`age-keygen` prints the public key to stderr as it goes, which is safe and
useful (stderr is not the key).

### `age-keygen -y <keyfile>`

Re-derive the public recipient from a private identity. Reads a private key,
writes a public one; the reverse is not possible. Documented above because it
is the only way to answer "is the recipient in git mine?".

heading_path: age — the encryption backend and the key regime
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### age warns "writing secret key to a world-readable file" on Windows — and the warning is a false alarm

```
$ age-keygen -o "$W/id.txt"
age-keygen: warning: writing secret key to a world-readable file
Public key: age1...
$ stat -c '%a' "$W/id.txt"
644
```

age is reading the POSIX mode, and on Git Bash the POSIX mode is a **fiction**:
everything is mounted `noacl` and reports 644 forever. See
[topic-workstation-toolchain](topic-workstation-toolchain.md) for the full
mechanism — `chmod` there exits 0 and changes nothing, verified again while
writing this page:

```
$ chmod 600 "$W/id.txt"; echo $?; stat -c '%a' "$W/id.txt"
0
644
```

What actually governs access is the **NTFS ACL**, and it says something quite
different (verified 2026-07-15 against the real key):

```
$ icacls C:\Users\<user>\.soevereinlab\mini-cloud-age.txt
    NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
    BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)
    <DOMAIN>\<user>:(I)(F)
```

Every entry is `(I)` — **inherited**. SYSTEM, Administrators, the user. No
`Everyone`, no `Users`. The key is not world-readable and age has no way to
know that.

**This is written down because someone will otherwise "fix" it with a `chmod`
that does nothing** — and then believe the key is protected *because they ran
the chmod*, which is strictly worse than believing nothing. A `chmod 0600` here
exits 0, changes nothing, and silences no warning.

The honest version, and the part that is not comfortable: **the key's
protection rests entirely on profile-directory ACL inheritance.** Every entry
being `(I)` is exactly what that means. `~/.soevereinlab/` is safe because of
where it is, not because of anything age, sops, or any script in this
programme did. Move the key somewhere with different inheritance — a repo
directory on a second drive, a synced folder, `C:\temp` — and the protection is
gone **silently**: no warning changes, no mode changes, `chmod` still exits 0.
The mode was never the control.

### The leak-avoidance rules for anything that touches key material

These are the rules `scripts/argocd-deploy-token.sh` and
`scripts/viewer-kubeconfig.sh` follow; they are the reference implementations
and worth reading before writing a third one.

- **Never in argv.** `sops --set ... "$token"` puts the secret in the process
  table, where any local process can read it. Pipe it instead.
- **Never in a shell variable.** `bash -x` prints every expansion; a debug flag
  someone adds while troubleshooting turns the whole log into a disclosure.
  The value goes from one process' stdout to the next one's stdin and is never
  named.
- **Nothing echoed.** The success message names the *file* and the token's id —
  never the value.
- **Temp files outside the repo**, and ignored anyway. A `mktemp` file holding
  the encrypted output is not a plaintext risk, but a credential written to the
  repo root is a credential `git add -A` stages, and patterns like `*.key` match
  none of the names we actually use.
- **stderr is left alone.** It carries the tools' own diagnostics and not the
  secret; muting it to be safe just means failures become silent.

The one that generalises: the secret should be a value that only ever exists
**in flight between two processes**. If you can name it, you can leak it.

heading_path: Ansible — agentless configuration management over SSH
What it is
text:
Ansible configures machines over plain SSH: no agent on the nodes, no server
component. You describe the desired state in YAML ("playbooks" containing
"tasks", grouped into reusable "roles"), and Ansible makes the machine match
it. Tasks are **idempotent**: they report `changed` when they had to alter
something and `ok` when the state was already correct, so running the same
playbook twice is safe — the second run should report `changed=0`.

Key vocabulary: **inventory** (which hosts, in which groups), **module** (the
unit that does one kind of work: `apt`, `template`, `ufw`, …), **handler** (a
task that runs only when notified by a changed task, typically a service
restart), **facts** (data gathered about a host at play start).

heading_path: Ansible — agentless configuration management over SSH
Why we use it
text:
Chosen over bash (not idempotent), pyinfra/Salt (less common at client
sites — Ansible knowledge transfers), and Terraform (provisions
infrastructure, does not configure OSes). See the bootstrap design spec in
the marketplace repo, §5.

heading_path: Ansible — agentless configuration management over SSH
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`: `ansible/ansible.cfg` (behaviour), `ansible/
inventory/hosts.yml` (the two nodes, in the `k3s_server`/`k3s_agent` child
groups), `ansible/bootstrap.yml` (one-off root run), `ansible/site.yml` (the
real playbook: baseline everywhere, then server, then agents),
`ansible/roles/baseline/` (hardening role), `ansible/roles/k3s/` (the cluster,
see [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md)). Version pins for ansible and ansible-lint live
in `ci/ansible.yml`. Executed from GitLab CI (`.gitlab-ci.yml`), never by hand.

heading_path: Ansible — agentless configuration management over SSH
Flags & settings we use
text:
### `ansible.cfg` — `[defaults]`

- **`host_key_checking = True`** — refuse to connect to a host whose SSH key
  is not in the known-hosts file. Other option: `False` (accept anything —
  convenient and MITM-able). We pin host keys in a committed
  `ansible/known_hosts`, so strict checking costs nothing.
- **`interpreter_python = /usr/bin/python3`** — skip interpreter discovery
  and use the system python3. Default `auto` probes per host; being explicit
  removes a warning and a failure mode on minimal Debian images.
- **`retry_files_enabled = False`** — do not write `*.retry` files next to
  playbooks on failure. Default `True` litters the repo; CI retries by
  re-running the job anyway.
- **`force_handlers = True`** — run pending handlers **even when the play
  fails**. Default `False` means: a play that writes a config file and dies
  before the notified restart leaves the daemon on the old config — and the
  next run reports `ok` (file already correct) so the restart never happens.
  This exact failure hit us in phase A (see Pitfalls).

### `ansible.cfg` — `[ssh_connection]`

- **`ssh_args = -C -o ControlMaster=auto -o ControlPersist=60s -o
  UserKnownHostsFile=ansible/known_hosts -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`** —
  **setting `ssh_args` replaces Ansible's defaults wholesale**, it does not
  extend them. `ControlMaster`/`ControlPersist` (connection reuse) are
  Ansible defaults and must be repeated here, or every task opens a fresh SSH
  connection — which trips ufw's rate-limit on 22/tcp and kills the play
  mid-run. `-C` enables compression. The two `-o` options pin host-key
  verification to the committed file. See [topic-ssh-client](topic-ssh-client.md)
  for what each SSH option does.
- **`pipelining = True`** — send module code over the existing SSH session
  instead of copying files first: fewer round-trips, faster plays. Requires
  that `requiretty` is not set in sudoers (Debian default: it is not).

### Playbook/task keywords we rely on

- **`become: true`** — run tasks with privilege escalation (sudo). We connect
  as the unprivileged `deploy` user; `become` is how tasks get root.
- **`notify:` + `handlers/`** — restart a service only when its config
  actually changed. Beware the stale-daemon pitfall below.
- **`validate:` on `template`/`copy`** — run a syntax check against the new
  file *before* it replaces the old one (`visudo -cf %s` for sudoers,
  `sshd -t -f %s` for sshd config). A typo then fails the task instead of
  locking us out.
- **`gather_facts: false` + explicit `setup:`** — in `bootstrap.yml`, fact
  gathering needs python, which a minimal image may lack; we install python
  first with `raw:` (executes over SSH without module machinery), then gather.
- **`changed_when: false`** — mark a read-only command as never "changed" so
  idempotency reporting stays honest.
- **`failed_when: false`** — treat a task that may legitimately fail (e.g.
  querying a unit that does not exist) as informational.
- **`check_mode: false`** — run this task even in dry-run mode (used for
  state queries whose results later tasks need).
- **`no_log: true`** — suppress a task's output in logs; mandatory on any
  task that touches secret material (join tokens, API tokens).
- **`loop:`** — run one task once per element of a list, the element exposed
  as `item`. Other option: `with_items` and the rest of the `with_*` family,
  the pre-2.5 form you will still meet in older code and most tutorials —
  they are not deprecated but `loop` is the current spelling and the one we
  write. One behavioural difference if you port old code: `with_items`
  flattens one level of nested lists, `loop` does not (use
  `| flatten(levels=1)` if you relied on that). Why ours: the ufw rules for
  80/443 and for the k3s ports are one task each, not five copy-pasted ones
  (80, 443, and 6443/51820/10250 per peer).
- **`loop_control: label:`** — choose what Ansible prints for each iteration.
  Default is the whole `item`, which for our `{port, proto}` dict crossed
  with an IP is an unreadable blob per line; a label reduces it to
  `6443/tcp from <peer-ip>`. This is **output cosmetics only** — it is not a
  secrets measure: the value still goes to the module and still shows up
  under `-vvv` or in an error. `no_log: true` (above) is the tool for that.
  Other `loop_control` options: `loop_var` (rename `item` — required when
  nesting loops via `include_tasks`), `index_var`, `pause`.
- **task-level `vars:`** — variables scoped to the single task they sit on.
  Other options: role `defaults/main.yml` (lowest precedence, meant to be
  overridden), `group_vars`/`host_vars` (per inventory group or host),
  `set_fact` (computed once, then persists for the rest of the play on that
  host). Why ours: the firewall task's port table means nothing to any other
  task, so scoping it there keeps the role's namespace clean and puts the
  value next to its only use. The peer list beside it is a `set_fact`
  instead — the assert guarding it needs the same value, and a duplicated
  expression could drift out of sync with the rule it guards. Note task vars
  sit at 17 of 22 in the precedence chain: `defaults/`, `group_vars` and
  `host_vars` all rank *lower*, so this is still *not* where anything an
  operator should be able to override belongs — that is what `defaults/` is
  for. Of the five entries that outrank task vars, only `-e` extra vars (22,
  documented as "always win") is one an operator would reach for; the rest —
  `include_vars`, `set_fact`/registered vars, role params, include params —
  are authoring constructs, not knobs.
- **`lookup('file', ...)`** — read a workstation/CI-side file into a value;
  resolves relative to the playbook's `files/` search path.
- **`serial: 1`** (play keyword) — run the play over one host at a time
  instead of all hosts in parallel. Default is all at once; `serial` also
  takes a list (`[1, 5, "30%"]`) for canary batches. Why ours: on the k3s
  agents play, a config change that breaks an agent stops at the first one
  instead of taking every agent out at once. Note what it is *not* for any
  more — it used to carry the server-before-agent ordering as well, and that
  job now belongs to separate plays (see the dispatch section below).
- **`environment:`** — set environment variables for the task's process on
  the *remote* host. Scopeable at task, block or play level. This is how the
  k3s installer gets `INSTALL_K3S_VERSION`, `K3S_URL` and `K3S_TOKEN`: they
  are inputs to a shell script, not Ansible variables, and `environment:`
  passes them without them ever appearing in an argument list (where `ps`
  would show them to every user on the box).
- **`delegate_to: <host>`** — run this task on a different host than the one
  the play is iterating over, while all its variables still resolve for the
  original host. The k3s role uses it twice: to slurp the join token from the
  server, and to ask the server whether *this* agent is a Ready member —
  questions only the server can answer. Two things worth knowing before you
  use it. First, **`become` applies to the host the task is delegated to**,
  so a delegated task gets root there; that is what makes reading the
  root-only `node-token` work. Second, delegation resolves through the
  inventory and does not care which hosts the play targets — the alternative,
  reading a fact off `hostvars[server]`, only works while the server is part
  of the same run, so `--limit <agent-name>` (the obvious way to re-join one
  rebuilt agent) would die on an undefined variable.

### `command:` with a string will shlex-split and eat your quotes

Worth its own heading because it cost a review round and would have been
invisible in production.

`ansible.builtin.command` accepts either a string (`cmd:`) or a list
(`argv:`). A string is **`shlex.split()`** — the same parsing a shell does for
word-splitting and quote removal, minus the shell. So the quotes are consumed
by Ansible and never reach the program.

A review suggested this membership check:

```yaml
cmd: k3s kubectl get node X -o jsonpath={.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}
```

`shlex` strips the quotes around `"Ready"`, so kubectl receives
`jsonpath={.status.conditions[?(@.type==Ready)].status}` — not valid jsonpath.
kubectl exits non-zero, and since the task's failure was being read as "this
node is not a member", the check would have been **permanently true**: every
apply would re-join the agent and report `changed` forever. A green pipeline
doing pointless work on every run, which is the noise that hides the run that
matters.

`argv:` takes a list and passes it to `execve` unchanged — no splitting, no
quote removal:

```yaml
argv:
  - k3s
  - kubectl
  - get
  - node
  - "{{ inventory_hostname }}"
  - -o
  - jsonpath={.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}
```

Rule of thumb: the moment an argument contains quotes, spaces or anything a
shell would touch, reach for `argv:`. (And if you genuinely need shell
features — pipes, redirection, `&&` — that is `shell:`, not `command:`.)

### Play dispatch: inventory child-groups, not a templated `hosts:`

`site.yml` runs one play against the `k3s_server` group and one against
`k3s_agent`. Those are **inventory child-groups** of `nodes` in
`inventory/hosts.yml`, each setting `k3s_role` once as a group var, so a
node's group and its role are the same statement and cannot disagree. `nodes`
still contains every host — a child group's hosts are part of its parent — so
the baseline play and `bootstrap-if-needed.sh` are unaffected.

The obvious-looking alternative does not work and fails **silently**:

```yaml
hosts: "{{ groups['nodes'] | selectattr('k3s_role', 'eq', 'server') }}"   # no
```

A play's `hosts:` is resolved at play-parse time, **before `groups` and
`hostvars` exist**. The pattern renders empty, matches zero hosts, and the
playbook reports a flawless green run that installed nothing at all. Nothing
errors, because selecting no hosts is not an error in Ansible — it is Tuesday.
`ansible-playbook --list-hosts` is what catches it, and it is worth running
whenever you touch a `hosts:` line.

Two plays also give the ordering for free: the server's play runs to
completion before the agents' play starts, because that is simply what
separate plays mean. The previous version leaned on one play with `serial: 1`
and `order: inventory` — which worked only because the server happened to be
listed above the agent. Reordering the inventory, an edit that looks like
formatting and would pass any review as such, ran the agent first and slurped
a node-token that did not exist yet. `order:` is gone from the repo now; the
correctness of the cluster is not something to leave resting on line order.

### Jinja filters we use

One thing to get straight before the list: of the four filters below only
`map` is Jinja's own. `extract`, `difference` and `product` are **Ansible
additions** (`ansible/plugins/filter/core.py` and `mathstuff.py`) — they
exist in playbooks and in templates Ansible renders, and nowhere else. Do not
go looking for them in the Jinja manual.

The firewall role derives the peer node's address from the inventory instead
of writing it down. The inventory already knows both node IPs; hardcoding the
peer would mean two places to edit when a node is replaced. The price is one
dense expression:

```yaml
{{ groups['nodes'] | map('extract', hostvars, 'ansible_host')
   | difference([hostvars[inventory_hostname].ansible_host]) | list }}
```

- **`map('extract', hostvars, 'ansible_host')`** — `groups['nodes']` holds
  host *names* as the inventory writes them, not addresses. `extract` uses
  each name as a key into `hostvars` and pulls one attribute out of it, here
  `ansible_host`. Result: the list of node IPs. (`difference` already hands
  back a list, so the trailing `| list` on our expression is belt-and-braces,
  not load-bearing — leave it, but do not read meaning into it.)
- **`difference([...])`** — set subtraction: everything in the left list that
  is not in the right one. The right list is the host's own `ansible_host`,
  so what survives is the peer(s). Siblings: `union`, `intersect`,
  `symmetric_difference`. It is literally `list(set(a) - set(b))`, which has
  two consequences worth knowing before you reach for it elsewhere:
  duplicates collapse and **order is not guaranteed**. Both are harmless for
  an allowlist, where the rules are order-independent anyway.
- **`product(...)`** — cartesian product: every element on the left paired
  with every element on the right. Ansible exposes Python's
  `itertools.product` directly under this name, so its semantics are exactly
  that. Peers × k3s ports yields one `(ip, port)` tuple per rule, so a single
  task emits all of them — `item.0` is the IP, `item.1` the port dict.

Derived beats hardcoded, but only if the expression is actually right, so it
was run against the real inventory rather than eyeballed. The concrete
addresses are deliberately not reproduced here — spec §7 puts concrete IPs and
hostnames in the config repo, and `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` is where they
live.

What is worth checking anyway is the **shape**, not the octets: on a two-node
inventory the expression must yield **exactly one** address per node, and it
must be the *other* node's — never the host's own. That is not a tautology,
because the two ways to get it wrong break the shape rather than the syntax.
Lose the `difference` and the list keeps the host's own address, so each node
opens the k3s ports to itself and the rule count doubles. Run it on an
inventory with a single node and `difference` removes that node's own address
to leave **nothing** — `loop` then skips every rule and the play reports green
with no k3s port opened at all, which is exactly why an `assert` sits beside
it in `firewall.yml`.

Check the end state rather than the expression: `sudo ufw status verbose` on a
node lists the k3s ports allowed from exactly one source address, and it is
the peer's.

One honest note, since this page is about knowing rather than believing. The
version of this paragraph that named the two observed addresses was evidence
that somebody had actually run the thing; the shape argument above is only
reasoning. It is sound, but it is not the same currency. Nor can you check
"it was run against the real inventory" from where you are sitting: that
output was never recorded anywhere durable — not in a commit message, not in
a kept job log — so with the addresses gone there is nothing left to point
at. Take that as the lesson rather than the caveat: **an observation worth
citing is worth committing somewhere.** If you change this expression, run it
and read the real output — do not trust the shape because it is written down
confidently.

### Modules in our roles (one line each)

`ansible.builtin.apt` (packages; `upgrade: safe` = upgrade without removing
anything, `cache_valid_time: 3600` = skip `apt update` if cache is fresh),
`ansible.builtin.user` (create `deploy`), `ansible.posix.authorized_key`
(install a public key), `ansible.builtin.copy`/`template` (files, the
latter with Jinja2 variables), `ansible.builtin.file` (here only
`state: directory`, to create `/etc/rancher/k3s` mode 0700 before the config
lands in it), `ansible.builtin.systemd_service` (query or restart units —
passing only a name *queries* state; with `state: started` + `enabled: true`
it asserts the end state, which is the task the k3s role was missing entirely),
`community.general.ufw`
(firewall rules, see [topic-ufw](topic-ufw.md)), `community.general.timezone`,
`ansible.builtin.stat` (file/dir metadata, also `/proc/<pid>` for process
start time), `ansible.builtin.set_fact` (computed variables),
`ansible.builtin.assert` (fail the play when a `that:` expression is false —
our guard against a `loop` over an empty list skipping silently and reporting
green), `ansible.builtin.raw` (plain SSH command, pre-python),
`ansible.builtin.slurp` (read a remote file into a variable).

### ansible-lint (`.ansible-lint`)

- **`profile: production`** — rule set strictness. The ladder is `min` →
  `basic` → `moderate` → `safety` → `shared` → `production`, each including
  the ones before it. Raised from `basic` alongside the k3s role, on lint's
  own evidence: running at `basic` it reported *"Profile 'basic' was
  required, but 'production' profile passed."* The tree already met the
  higher bar, and a floor set below where the code already stands holds
  nothing up — it just lets the first regression through unremarked. This is
  a policy change rather than a cleanup: future work has to meet
  `production` too, and rules that were advisory before now fail the
  pipeline.
- **`skip_list: [package-latest]`** — that rule forbids `upgrade: safe`-style
  unpinned upgrades; our baseline deliberately applies security updates, so
  the rule is switched off with this comment trail.
- **`exclude_paths: [.git/]`** — paths lint never walks. Housekeeping, not
  policy.

heading_path: Ansible — agentless configuration management over SSH
Pitfalls we hit
text:
- **Green ≠ in effect** (phase A): a failed run had written the sshd drop-in;
  the next run saw the file unchanged, never fired the restart handler, and
  reported green while the daemon ran the old config. Fixes: `force_handlers`,
  a drift-heal task comparing the daemon's start time against the config's
  mtime, and behaviour-level verify jobs. Runbook:
  `rb-2026-07-14-debian-hardening`; practice:
  `dec-2026-07-15-issues-become-guarded-automation`.
- **`ssh_args` replaces defaults**: losing `ControlMaster` re-introduced one
  SSH connection per task and got CI banned by ufw's rate limit
  ("Connection refused" mid-play).
- **Both k3s dispatch bugs above were introduced by review suggestions** —
  the `cmd:` string that lost its quotes to `shlex`, and the templated
  `hosts:` that would have selected zero hosts. Neither reviewer was
  careless; both suggestions read better than what they replaced, which is
  exactly the problem. A fix arriving as a review comment carries the
  reviewer's authority and none of the author's testing, and it is the one
  change nobody re-checks. **A reviewer's fix is not exempt from the
  standard.** Apply the same question to it as to the original: what would
  this look like if it were wrong? Here, both would have looked green.
- **Ansible's failure mode of choice is silence, not error.** A `loop` over
  an empty list, a `hosts:` matching nothing, a `when:` that is never true —
  all of them skip, report `ok`, and colour the run green. That is why the
  roles are full of `assert:` tasks guarding the *inputs* rather than
  trusting the tasks to complain: an empty peer list, an inventory with no
  server, a node in no dispatch group. If a mistake would show up as "did
  nothing, quietly", it needs a guard that says so out loud.

heading_path: Argo CD — the GitOps controller that syncs the cluster from this repo
What it is
text:
Argo CD is a controller that runs inside the cluster and continuously compares
what Kubernetes is running against what a git repository says it should be
running. When the two differ, it either reports the drift or corrects it,
depending on how the `Application` object is configured.

The unit it works in is the `Application`: a custom resource naming a repo, a
revision, a path inside that repo, and a destination cluster/namespace. Argo CD
renders whatever it finds at that path (plain manifests, Helm charts,
Kustomize) and applies it. An `Application` may itself point at a path
containing more `Application` objects — the "app-of-apps" pattern, which is how
one bootstrapped entry point grows into a whole platform without anything
being applied by hand.

heading_path: Argo CD — the GitOps controller that syncs the cluster from this repo
Why we use it
text:
It is the mechanism that makes "the cluster contains nothing that is not in
git" a checkable statement instead of an intention. Before Argo CD, the k3s
role wrote manifests to the node and the honest summary was that nothing
stopped anyone creating objects next to them by hand
(`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`, `ansible/roles/k3s/tasks/manifests.yml` says so
outright). With `selfHeal` on, an out-of-band edit is reverted; with `prune`
on, deleting a file deletes the objects it created.

It also moves the deploy loop off the workstation. After the bootstrap, a
platform change is a commit — no `ansible-playbook` run, no `kubectl apply`,
and no operator with cluster-admin in their shell.

heading_path: Argo CD — the GitOps controller that syncs the cluster from this repo
Where it lives in our repos
text:
All paths in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/tasks/main.yml` | Loads the SOPS secrets, writes the three manifests, waits on the cluster |
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/defaults/main.yml` | The chart pin and the repo URL |
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/templates/argocd-helmchart.yaml.j2` | The `HelmChart` that installs Argo CD |
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/templates/repo-secret.yaml.j2` | The repository credential |
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/templates/root-app.yaml.j2` | The root `Application` |
| `ansible/site.yml` | The `Argo CD bootstrap` play (server node only) |
| `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml` | The deploy token, SOPS-encrypted |
| `gitops/` | What the root `Application` watches |

Argo CD is installed **through k3s' manifests directory**, not by Helm on the
workstation: the role drops a `HelmChart` object into
`/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` and k3s' helm-controller does the
install. See [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md), which documents that directory.

heading_path: Argo CD — the GitOps controller that syncs the cluster from this repo
Flags & settings we use
text:
### `HelmChart` (`helm.cattle.io/v1`)

This is k3s' CRD, not Argo CD's. Every field below was checked against
helm-controller's `pkg/apis/helm.cattle.io/v1/types.go`.

#### `metadata.name` = `argo-cd`

The Helm release name, and it is load-bearing beyond aesthetics: it prefixes
every resource the chart creates, so the server Deployment becomes
`argo-cd-argocd-server` (release name + chart's own `argocd` prefix). The wait
in `tasks/main.yml` names that Deployment literally. Renaming the release
without renaming the wait gives a role that hangs for five minutes and then
fails on a resource that was healthy the whole time.

#### `metadata.namespace` = `kube-system`

Where the helm-controller looks for the job it runs. The chart's own resources
land in `targetNamespace`, not here.

#### `spec.version` = `"10.1.3"` (via `gitops_bootstrap_chart_version`)

Pinned, like every version in these repos. A floating chart means the platform
changes without a commit — the exact property Argo CD is here to prevent, so
leaving the chart itself unpinned would be self-defeating. 10.1.3 was the
newest `argo-cd` chart in `argoproj.github.io/argo-helm`'s index on
2026-07-15 (appVersion v3.4.5), checked against the index rather than
remembered.

Other options: omitting it installs whatever is newest at first install and
then never upgrades (the release is only reinstalled if the object changes) —
"latest, once, on a date determined by when the VPS was built".

#### `spec.repo` = `https://argoproj.github.io/argo-helm`, `spec.chart` = `argo-cd`

The upstream chart repository. `spec.chart` may also be a complete HTTPS URL to
a `.tgz`, and `spec.chartContent` takes a base64 archive inline — the latter is
how you pin a chart against the repository disappearing, which we have not
needed.

#### `spec.targetNamespace` = `argocd`, `spec.createNamespace` = `true`

Helm's `--namespace` and `--create-namespace`. `createNamespace` matters here
for ordering rather than convenience: the repo-secret and the root
`Application` are addressed to namespace `argocd`, and they are written to the
manifests directory at the same moment as the `HelmChart`. Without it the
namespace would only exist if something else created it first, and nothing
does.

#### `spec.valuesContent` — the chart's own values

Inline YAML, passed as Helm's `--values`. Note it is a *string* containing
YAML: an indentation mistake inside it is not a YAML error in the manifest, it
is a different set of values than intended.

- **`dex.enabled: false`** — Dex is the bundled OIDC provider, for logging into
  the UI with an external identity provider. We have no IdP and one operator.
  Other option: `true` adds a Deployment for an SSO flow nobody uses.
- **`notifications.enabled: false`** — the controller that sends sync
  notifications to Slack/e-mail/webhooks. Nothing is wired to receive them.
- **`applicationSet.enabled: false`** — a controller that generates
  `Application` objects from templates (per cluster, per directory, per PR).
  Useful for many clusters or many environments; we have one of each, and the
  app-of-apps root covers it.
- **`redis-ha.enabled: false`** — the highly-available Redis (three replicas
  plus HAProxy) instead of the single Redis the chart runs by default. This is
  a two-node cluster; the chart's default single Redis is already the right
  shape, and `redis-ha` would not fit.

Each of these is a Deployment that would otherwise run forever for no caller.
On a two-node mini-cloud that is memory, not tidiness.

- **`controller.resources.limits.memory: 512Mi`**,
  **`repoServer.resources.limits.memory: 256Mi`**,
  **`server.resources.limits.memory: 256Mi`** — limits only, no requests. The
  application controller does the reconciling and holds cluster state, so it
  gets the larger limit; the repo-server (clones and renders) and the API
  server/UI get less.

**No ingress and no SSO.** The UI is reached with `kubectl port-forward`, which
means the Argo CD web interface is not exposed to the internet at all. Other
option: an ingress plus SSO, which is a public login page and a certificate for
a UI that one person opens occasionally.

### `Secret` — the repository credential

#### `metadata.labels."argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type"` = `repository`

How Argo CD finds it. Argo CD does not read a config file listing repositories;
it watches its own namespace for Secrets carrying this label. Without the
label the Secret is inert and the symptom is an `Application` that cannot
authenticate while its credential sits in the same namespace.

#### `stringData.url` = the repo URL, and why it lives in `defaults/`

Argo CD matches a credential to an `Application` by repository URL. The
`Secret`'s `url` and the `Application`'s `repoURL` must therefore agree, which
is why both render from one variable (`gitops_bootstrap_repo_url`) rather than
being typed twice. A mismatch does not fail loudly — it surfaces as
"authentication required" on a repo whose credential is sitting right there.

Both role variables carry the `gitops_bootstrap_` prefix because ansible-lint's
`var-naming[no-role-prefix]` requires it at `profile: production` — see
[topic-ansible](topic-ansible.md). The two names that do *not* carry it,
`argocd_repo_username` and `argocd_repo_token`, are not role variables: they
arrive from the SOPS file through `load_vars`.

#### `stringData.username` / `stringData.password` — the deploy token

A GitLab deploy token with scope `read_repository`, minted by
`scripts/argocd-deploy-token.sh` and stored SOPS-encrypted in
`ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml`. See [topic-sops](topic-sops.md).

**Where the encryption stops:** this Secret is rendered to the node as
plaintext in `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` (mode 0600, root-owned —
the directory offers nothing else), and Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not
encryption. The SOPS envelope protects the token *in git*, which is where it
would otherwise be world-readable. It does not protect it on the server. What
limits the damage there is the scope: the token can clone this repo and do
nothing else.

### `Application` — the root

#### `metadata.name` = `root`, `metadata.namespace` = `argocd`

`Application` objects live in Argo CD's own namespace, not in the namespace
they deploy into.

#### `spec.source.path` = `gitops`, `spec.source.directory.recurse` = `true`

The directory watched, and whether subdirectories are included. With `recurse`
on, `gitops/` can grow subdirectories per app without another `Application` per
directory. Argo CD's directory source only picks up `.yaml`/`.yml`/`.json`, so
`gitops/README.md` is ignored rather than being a parse error.

#### `spec.source.targetRevision` = `main`

The branch Argo CD follows. Not a tag or a commit: on this platform `main` is
the deployed state by definition, and protected-main plus MR review is what
gates it.

#### `spec.syncPolicy.automated.prune` = `true`

Removing a manifest from `main` removes the objects it created. Other option:
`false`, where deleting a file leaves its objects running forever and the
cluster accumulates things no file describes — which is the drift this whole
layer exists to prevent.

#### `spec.syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal` = `true`

An edit made directly against the API server is reverted on the next sync.
Other option: `false`, where Argo CD reports the drift and waits. We want the
repo to be the truth, not a suggestion.

Both are worth understanding before working on this cluster: **`kubectl edit`
against anything under `gitops/` is temporary**, and deleting a file is a
production change.

#### `spec.destination.server` = `https://kubernetes.default.svc`

The cluster Argo CD itself runs in, addressed from inside. Argo CD can drive
remote clusters; this one only manages its own.

### The waits in `tasks/main.yml`

Not settings, but the part that makes the role mean something. Writing a
manifest is not the controller applying it — the same gap
[topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md) documents for the manifests directory, where a green
Ansible run proves only that bytes are on disk.

- **`kubectl wait --for=condition=available deploy/argo-cd-argocd-server
  --timeout=300s`, wrapped in `retries: 20` / `delay: 15`.** The retries are
  not belt-and-braces. `--for=condition` waits for a **condition on an object**,
  not for the object: kubectl documents a separate `--for=create` for waiting on
  creation, which is the tell. While the helm job runs, this Deployment does not
  exist, so a longer `--timeout` is not the missing ingredient — the retry loop
  is what covers the window between "manifest written" and "Deployment created".

  What exactly kubectl does with a missing object here — error text, exit code —
  is **not recorded as observed**, because nothing has run against this cluster
  yet (see the first pitfall). The design deliberately does not depend on it: it
  retries on any non-zero exit rather than matching a message.
- **`until:` the root `Application` reports `Synced:Healthy`.** Both halves,
  because they answer different questions: `Synced` means Argo CD read the repo
  and applied what it found; `Healthy` means what it applied is actually
  running. `Synced` alone is the state that passes when the repo is fine and
  the cluster cannot run it.

heading_path: Argo CD — the GitOps controller that syncs the cluster from this repo
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### Nothing here has run against the cluster yet

Stated plainly because the rest of this topic reads like it has: at
`last_verified` the role was written, its templates were rendered and parsed,
and its versions and CRD fields were checked against upstream sources — but
`apply` is manual and gated, so **no Argo CD has been installed by it**. The
claims about what the flags *do* come from the chart's values, helm-controller's
`types.go` and Argo CD's CRD; the claims about what *our cluster* does are not
yet observations. The first `apply` after the bootstrap MRs merge either proves
the wait right or fails at it.

When that run happens, this section should be replaced by what it found.

### `load_vars` decrypts on the controller, not on the node

`community.sops.load_vars` is an action plugin: it runs where `ansible-playbook`
runs. So sops and the age identity are needed **on the CI runner** and never on
vps1 — which is why `ci/ansible.yml` installs sops in `.ansible-run` and why
`SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` is a protected CI variable. Reading it as "the node needs
the key" leads to putting a private key on a public-facing VPS for no reason.
See [topic-sops](topic-sops.md) and [topic-ansible](topic-ansible.md).

### A relative `file:` in a role does not mean what it looks like

`community.sops.load_vars`' `file:` resolves a relative path against the
**role's** `vars/` directory first, and only then relative to the playbook. The
secrets file is at `ansible/vars/`, not `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/vars/`,
so the role addresses it absolutely via `{{ playbook_dir }}`.

heading_path: cert-manager — issues and renews the cluster's TLS certificates
What it is
text:
cert-manager is a controller that runs inside the cluster and obtains X.509
certificates for it, then renews them before they expire. It adds a set of
custom resources — `Certificate`, `ClusterIssuer`/`Issuer`, `CertificateRequest`,
`Challenge` — and reconciles them the same way Kubernetes reconciles its own
objects: you declare the certificate you want, cert-manager talks to a
certificate authority, and the signed certificate lands in a Kubernetes
`Secret` that an Ingress can serve.

Its most common mode is ACME (the protocol Let's Encrypt speaks): the CA hands
out a challenge to prove you control the domain, cert-manager satisfies it, and
the CA signs. It never puts a private key in git — the key is generated in the
cluster and stays there.

heading_path: cert-manager — issues and renews the cluster's TLS certificates
Why we use it
text:
The platform exposes apps over HTTPS on public hostnames, and a browser will
not accept them without a certificate a public CA vouches for. Buying and
rotating those by hand is exactly the manual loop this cluster exists to
avoid. cert-manager makes a certificate a declared resource: an annotation on
an Ingress produces and renews it, and there is no operator step to forget.

It also fits the GitOps rule — everything the cluster runs is in git. The
issuers and the app's Ingress are manifests under `gitops/`; Argo CD syncs
them and cert-manager acts on them. See [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md).

heading_path: cert-manager — issues and renews the cluster's TLS certificates
Where it lives in our repos
text:
All paths in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gitops/platform/cert-manager/app.yaml` | The Argo CD `Application` that installs the chart (sync-wave -1) |
| `gitops/platform/cert-manager/issuers.yaml` | The two `ClusterIssuer` objects (staging + prod), sync-wave 0 |
| `gitops/apps/demo/manifests/ingress.yaml` | The demo app's Ingress that requests a certificate via annotation |

cert-manager is installed as a Helm chart *by Argo CD*, not by Ansible: its
`Application` points at `charts.jetstack.io`. The issuers and the consuming
Ingress are ordered after it with sync-waves (see below).

heading_path: cert-manager — issues and renews the cluster's TLS certificates
Flags & settings we use
text:
### `Application` — installing the chart

#### `source.chart` = `cert-manager`, `source.targetRevision` = `v1.21.0`

The upstream chart from `charts.jetstack.io`, version-pinned like everything in
these repos: a floating chart changes the platform without a commit. v1.21.0
was the current release (2026-07-09) checked against `charts.jetstack.io`'s
`index.yaml` on `last_verified`, not remembered. cert-manager ships the app and
its chart under one version, so this pins both.

#### `helm.valuesObject.crds.enabled` = `true`

Installs cert-manager's custom resource definitions (`Certificate`,
`ClusterIssuer`, …) as part of the chart. Other option: `false`, the default,
which assumes the CRDs were applied separately first — the split-install path
for teams that manage CRDs on their own cadence. With one chart owned by Argo
CD, letting the chart carry its CRDs keeps install and upgrade in one object.
Per the chart's docs this replaces the old `installCRDs` flag.

#### `resources` limits on the three Deployments

The controller, `webhook`, and `cainjector` each get a small memory limit
(and the controller a tiny CPU/memory request). These are an 8 GB two-node
cluster's footprint discipline, not a cert-manager requirement; the numbers
are ours, not upstream defaults.

### `ClusterIssuer` vs `Issuer`

We use `ClusterIssuer`. The two are the same object with one difference of
scope: an `Issuer` is namespaced and can only sign for `Certificate` objects in
its own namespace; a `ClusterIssuer` is cluster-wide and any namespace can
reference it. The demo app lives in namespace `demo` while the issuer is
defined alongside cert-manager, so a namespaced `Issuer` would not be reachable
from it. One cluster-wide ACME account, referenced everywhere, is the shape
that matches a single-operator platform.

#### `spec.acme.solvers[].http01.ingress.ingressClassName` = `traefik`

The HTTP-01 challenge: the CA gives cert-manager a token, cert-manager serves
it at `http://<host>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>`, and the CA fetches
it over plain HTTP to prove the domain points at this cluster. cert-manager
provisions a temporary Ingress for that path, and `ingressClassName: traefik`
routes it through k3s' bundled Traefik (see [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md)). The
alternative solver is DNS-01 (prove control by writing a TXT record), which is
what you need for wildcard certificates or when port 80 is not reachable; we
have neither constraint, and HTTP-01 needs no DNS API credential.

### Staging vs prod issuer

Two `ClusterIssuer` objects, identical but for their ACME `server` URL:
`letsencrypt-staging` points at `acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`,
`letsencrypt-prod` at `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`.

The reason both exist is Let's Encrypt's **rate limits**: staging enforces
*significantly higher* limits than production (not the absence of limits), so
it absorbs the repeated issuance of bring-up without spending the tight
production budget. Two distinct limits are worth keeping apart — an earlier
version of this passage conflated them (per `letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits`,
checked 2026-07-17):

- **5 certificates per exact set of identifiers, per 7 days** — historically
  called the "duplicate certificate" limit (the current page names it "New
  Certificates per Exact Set of Identifiers"), keyed on the exact set of
  hostnames (order/case ignored). This is the one that bites during bring-up: re-issuing for the
  *same* name is a duplicate, so a misconfiguration retried a handful of times
  against prod exhausts it and locks you out of new certificates for that exact
  name for the rest of the week.
- **50 certificates per registered domain, per 7 days** — the broader
  "certificates per registered domain" limit, counting all distinct names under
  the domain. Far harder to hit with a single-hostname app.

Staging issues from an untrusted root — a browser rejects it — but proves the
whole challenge path works. The rule that follows: bring a new hostname up on
`letsencrypt-staging`, confirm the chain end to end, and only then switch the
annotation to `letsencrypt-prod`.

#### `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer` annotation on the Ingress

Instead of writing a `Certificate` object, we annotate the Ingress:
`cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-staging`. cert-manager watches
Ingresses, and this annotation (ingress-shim) makes it create the `Certificate`
for the hosts in the Ingress' `tls:` block automatically, storing the result
in the named `secretName`. The sibling annotation `cert-manager.io/issuer`
selects a namespaced `Issuer` instead; we use the `cluster-issuer` form because
our issuers are `ClusterIssuer`s. Switching environments is then a one-line
change to this annotation's value.

heading_path: cert-manager — issues and renews the cluster's TLS certificates
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### This now runs live — what the first sync found

Earlier this section warned that nothing here had run against the cluster yet.
That is no longer true: cert-manager is installed and has issued a real,
browser-trusted Let's Encrypt **production** certificate for the demo app's
host, `demo.<your-domain>` (observed 2026-07-16; issuer `C=US, O=Let's
Encrypt, CN=YR2`, no `STAGING`). The concrete hostname lives in the config repo
(`soevereinlab-mini-cloud/gitops/apps/demo/manifests/ingress.yaml`). The staging-then-prod path, the automatic
renewal on an issuer switch (no secret deletion needed), and the HTTP-01
challenge flow are all documented as a runbook with the clocked observations:
see [rb-2026-07-17-ingress-tls-cert-manager](../runbooks/rb-2026-07-17-ingress-tls-cert-manager.md).
The claims below about what each flag *does* still come from cert-manager's
documentation and the chart values; the claims about what *our cluster* does are
now observations, sourced in that runbook.

### The issuer CRD does not exist until the chart syncs

`ClusterIssuer` is a cert-manager CRD, so `issuers.yaml` cannot be validated —
let alone applied — until the cert-manager chart has installed. Two annotations
handle the ordering, and both are reasoned from Argo CD's behaviour, not yet
observed here:

- `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"` on the chart and `"0"` on the issuers,
  so cert-manager installs before the issuers apply. Waves order resources
  *within* the root-app's sync.
- `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true` on the
  issuers, so Argo CD's server-side dry-run does not fail them for referencing
  a CRD that does not exist during the first pass.

If the first sync still trips on the missing CRD, Argo CD's automated sync
retries; the expectation is that the retry lands once cert-manager is up. On
this cluster the race did not manifest: the `ClusterIssuer` objects came up
`Ready` and the ordering annotations held (observed task 5, 2026-07-16) — so
the retry path is the documented fallback, not something this cluster was seen
to need.

### An old AAAA record sends the HTTP-01 challenge to the wrong host

Let's Encrypt prefers IPv6 when a name has an AAAA record. If a stale AAAA
points at a parking server, the challenge fetch lands there instead of the
cluster and issuance fails while the A record looks fine. The DNS precondition
for this platform is therefore an A record to the node and **no** AAAA on the
app host or the apex.

heading_path: dig — asking DNS the exact question you mean
What it is
text:
`dig` is the standard DNS query tool: ask a specific server for a specific
record type and see exactly what it answers. Unlike a browser or `ping`, it
does not mix in caches, hosts files or happy-eyeballs behaviour — which is
the point: verification needs the raw answer.

Windows note: `dig` is not present in Git Bash; `nslookup` (built into
Windows) covers interactive use (`nslookup -type=AAAA <name> 1.1.1.1`), and
WSL has real `dig`. CI installs `dnsutils`.

heading_path: dig — asking DNS the exact question you mean
Why we use it
text:
`scripts/verify-dns.sh` must prove what *public resolvers* serve — the
records Let's Encrypt and visitors will actually see — not what a local
cache remembers.

heading_path: dig — asking DNS the exact question you mean
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`: `scripts/verify-dns.sh` (the `verify:dns` job).
Policy and incident: runbook `rb-2026-07-15-dns-ipv4-only`.

heading_path: dig — asking DNS the exact question you mean
Flags & settings we use
text:
- **`@1.1.1.1` / `@8.8.8.8`** — query *this* server directly, bypassing the
  system resolver. We ask two independent public resolvers so one stale
  cache cannot produce a false pass (or false alarm).
- **`-t A` / `-t AAAA`** — record type: IPv4 address vs IPv6 address. The
  AAAA query is the core of the IPv4-only guard — it must come back empty.
  Other types worth knowing: `CNAME` (alias), `TXT` (ACME challenges use
  these), `MX` (mail), `NS` (which nameservers are authoritative).
- **`+short`** — print only the answer values, one per line, instead of the
  full response — the machine-readable mode scripts want. Caveat: for a
  CNAME'd name it prints the alias target *and* the address, so
  `verify-dns.sh` filters for address-shaped lines.
- **`+time=5 +tries=2`** — per-query timeout and retry count, so a wobbly
  resolver fails the check in seconds instead of hanging a pipeline.

Reading a full (non-`+short`) reply: the **ANSWER** section holds the
records; **status: NXDOMAIN** means the name does not exist at all, while
**NOERROR** with an empty answer means the name exists but has no record of
the asked type — the state the AAAA check wants.

heading_path: dig — asking DNS the exact question you mean
Pitfalls we hit
text:
- Testing DNS through anything with a cache (browser, `ping`, the OS
  resolver) shows history, not truth — always `@` a public resolver
  directly. TTL still applies at that resolver: after deleting a record,
  cached answers can linger up to the record's TTL.
- Wildcard records only reveal themselves on names you never created —
  `verify-dns.sh` queries a random label for exactly that reason (hoster
  parking defaults live on the wildcard).

heading_path: fail2ban — ban IPs that keep failing authentication
What it is
text:
fail2ban watches authentication logs and temporarily bans (via firewall
rules) IP addresses that keep failing. A **jail** couples a log source and a
failure pattern to a ban action. Where ufw's rate limit counts *connections*,
fail2ban counts *failed logins* — slower brute force that stays under the
connection limit still gets caught here.

heading_path: fail2ban — ban IPs that keep failing authentication
Why we use it
text:
Port 22 is public (no VPN in scope yet, spec §7); two independent,
mechanically different brakes on brute force cost nothing and cover each
other's blind spots.

heading_path: fail2ban — ban IPs that keep failing authentication
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`: `ansible/roles/baseline/tasks/fail2ban.yml` +
`ansible/roles/baseline/templates/jail.local.j2` (rendered to
`/etc/fail2ban/jail.local`). Verified by `scripts/verify-hardening.sh`
(`fail2ban-client status sshd`).

heading_path: fail2ban — ban IPs that keep failing authentication
Flags & settings we use
text:
All in the `[sshd]` section of `jail.local` (a drop-in that overrides the
package's `jail.conf`, which upgrades would overwrite):

- **`enabled = true`** — activate the sshd jail. Debian ships jails defined
  but disabled by default.
- **`backend = systemd`** — read failures from the systemd journal. The
  default (`auto`, effectively file-based) tails `/var/log/auth.log`, which
  **does not exist on minimal Debian without rsyslog** — the jail would
  silently watch nothing. This is the one non-obvious, load-bearing line.
- **`maxretry = 5`** — failures before a ban. Lower = stricter but more
  false positives (a typo-prone human with several keys can burn attempts
  fast).
- **`findtime = 10m`** — the sliding window in which those failures must
  fall. Failures older than this no longer count toward a ban.
- **`bantime = 1h`** — how long the ban lasts. Options range from minutes to
  `-1` (permanent); 1h deters bots without permanently locking out a
  colleague behind a shared NAT IP.

Inspection on a node: `sudo fail2ban-client status sshd` (currently banned
IPs, totals), `sudo fail2ban-client unban <ip>` (undo).

heading_path: Git conventions — commits, branches and line endings in this programme
What it is
text:
The house rules for how changes move through the programme's repos: commit
message format, branch flow, and the line-ending pinning that keeps a
Windows workstation from breaking Linux consumers.

heading_path: Git conventions — commits, branches and line endings in this programme
Why we use it
text:
Small conventions, consistently applied, are what make history greppable
and reviews cheap — and they are enforceable (protected branches, CI)
instead of remembered.

heading_path: Git conventions — commits, branches and line endings in this programme
Where it lives in our repos
text:
Every repo in the programme; `.gitattributes` in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`
is the reference implementation for the line-ending rules.

heading_path: Git conventions — commits, branches and line endings in this programme
Flags & settings we use
text:
### Conventional commits

Format: `type(scope): imperative summary`. Types in use: **`feat`** (new
capability), **`fix`** (repair), **`docs`** (documentation only), **`ci`**
(pipeline/config). Scope is optional and small (`ci`, `plans`, `runbooks`,
`decisions`, `lint`). One logical change per commit; the summary should
still make sense in `git log --oneline` a year later.

### Branch flow

`main` is protected everywhere (push: no one, merge: maintainers) — every
change is a branch + MR, including agent work. Branch names carry the same
types (`feat/…`, `fix/…`, `docs/…`, `feature/…` for larger arcs). Merged
branches are deleted; long-lived branches are a smell.

### `.gitattributes` — line endings

- **`* text=auto eol=lf`** — treat files git detects as text as text, store
  them with LF in the repo **and check them out with LF**. This overrides
  each contributor's `core.autocrlf`, which is the point: per-machine
  settings do not survive new machines.
- **`*.sh text eol=lf`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.j2`, `*.cfg`, `known_hosts`,
  `*.pub`** — explicit pins for the file types consumed by Linux,
  belt-and-suspenders on top of the wildcard: a CRLF that sneaks into a shell
  script produces `bad interpreter: /usr/bin/env bash^M`, and YAML/SSH parsers
  fail in stranger ways. `*.j2` is pinned for the same reason one step
  removed: a Jinja template is not consumed directly, it is *rendered*, and
  the CRLFs come out the other side into whatever the template produces — a
  unit file, a config, a script — where they break the same way. Two `.j2`
  files already existed when the pin landed, so this is not a case of pinning
  an extension before its first file: `* text=auto eol=lf` had already
  normalised them, which makes the explicit pin a no-op for them and safe to
  add — it cannot conflict with anyone's working tree. It lands before phase
  B's k3s templates arrive, and it matches how the rest of the file names its
  extensions rather than leaning on the wildcard.
- The local warning `LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches
  it` on a Windows checkout is git *normalizing* — the repository content
  stays LF; with `eol=lf` pinned the working copy stays LF too.

### Hygiene rules

- `.gitignore` blocks private key material patterns (`*.pem`, `*_key`,
  `*.key`, `id_*`, `.env`) — defense in depth; the real rule is that
  private keys never enter a repo directory at all.
- Executable bit for scripts is set explicitly on Windows:
  `git update-index --chmod=+x <script>` (NTFS has no exec bit for git to
  pick up).

heading_path: Git conventions — commits, branches and line endings in this programme
Pitfalls we hit
text:
- None beyond the CRLF class the `.gitattributes` exists to prevent — it
  was pinned during phase A *because* Windows-authored files were headed at
  Linux runners, before an incident occurred.

heading_path: GitLab CI — pipelines as the only route to the infrastructure
What it is
text:
GitLab CI runs jobs (shell scripts in containers) in reaction to git events:
a push, a merge request, a schedule. Jobs are declared in `.gitlab-ci.yml`
in the repo itself, grouped into **stages** that run in order; jobs within a
stage run in parallel. A **pipeline** is one run of the applicable jobs for
one event.

In this programme the pipeline is not a convenience but the **primary
route**: nothing reaches the nodes except through a pipeline job on a
protected branch. "Hooks advise locally, the server enforces."

heading_path: GitLab CI — pipelines as the only route to the infrastructure
Why we use it
text:
The repos live on gitlab.com; CI is built in, free at this scale, and the
protected-branch + protected-variable model gives exactly the "server
enforces" property the programme wants (spec §5, bootstrap route).

heading_path: GitLab CI — pipelines as the only route to the infrastructure
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`: `.gitlab-ci.yml` (the jobs) plus reusable pieces
in `ci/ansible.yml` (pinned tooling, base jobs) and `ci/pipeline-name.yml`
(pipeline naming and gating), pulled in with `include:`.

heading_path: GitLab CI — pipelines as the only route to the infrastructure
Flags & settings we use
text:
### Structure

- **`stages: [lint, bootstrap, apply, verify]`** — execution order. A stage
  starts when the previous one finished (except where `needs` overrides).
- **`include: - local: ci/ansible.yml`** — splice another YAML file from
  this repo into the config. Other options: `project:` (another repo),
  `remote:` (URL), `template:` (GitLab-provided). `local` keeps everything
  reviewable in one MR.
- **`extends: .ansible-run`** — inherit the keys of a hidden job (name
  starts with `.`; hidden jobs never run themselves). Our pattern: hidden
  jobs carry images and `before_script`, real jobs carry `script` and rules.
- **`variables:`** — pinned versions (`ANSIBLE_VERSION: "10.7.0"`) live in
  `ci/ansible.yml` so one bump updates every job. A floating version turns
  an unrelated MR red the day upstream releases.
- **`!reference [.sops-install, script]`** — splice the `script:` of another
  (usually hidden) job in here, as a list of commands. Unlike `extends:`, which
  merges whole keys and only once per job, `!reference` pulls **one key** into
  an arbitrary position and can be used from several `before_script`s at once —
  which is why the sops install is a hidden job's `script:` rather than a YAML
  anchor: it is consumed by jobs that do not run Ansible at all.
- **`before_script:` / `script:` / `after_script:`** — setup, work,
  always-runs-afterwards. `after_script` sees `$CI_JOB_STATUS`; our `apply`
  job uses that to print known failure causes only when the job failed.

### Rules — when does a job run

Rules are evaluated top-down; the **first match wins**.

- **`if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"`** — the pipeline was
  created for an MR. Used for `lint`.
- **`if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"`** — a push/merge to main. **Also true
  on scheduled pipelines**, which is why schedule exclusions must come first.
- **`if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"` + `when: never`** — exclude a
  job from scheduled pipelines. Our schedules run only drift checks; code
  jobs prove nothing when no code changed.
- **`when: manual`** — the job appears in the pipeline but waits for a human
  click. Used for `apply` (reconfigures live nodes; a human picks the moment
  as long as there is no tested restore).
- **`allow_failure: true`** — the pipeline does not block/redden on this
  job. Paired with `when: manual` so an unplayed `apply` cannot jam the
  pipeline. Deliberately **not** set on `verify`: a broken platform must
  turn the pipeline red.
- **`needs: ["apply"]`** — run as soon as *that job* finishes instead of
  waiting for the whole previous stage; and if `apply` was never played, the
  needing job is simply not created. `needs: []` = start immediately.

### Protection model

- **Protected branch `main`** — push: no one, merge: maintainers. Every
  change is an MR; nothing lands without review.
- **Protected variables** — CI variables marked *protected* exist **only**
  in pipelines on protected branches: a feature-branch pipeline cannot
  exfiltrate the deploy key. Type **File** writes the value to a temp file
  and puts its path in the variable — right shape for SSH keys
  (`--private-key "$ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY"`). Two gotchas: the file lands with
  permissive modes (`chmod 600` first, OpenSSH refuses readable keys), and
  the value must keep its trailing newline or OpenSSH rejects it.
  *Mask variable* stays off — multi-line values cannot be masked.
  The same shape carries the age identity as `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE`, where the
  name is load-bearing: sops reads that variable expecting a *path*, which is
  exactly what a file-type variable produces (see [topic-age](topic-age.md)).
- **The consequence of *protected*, stated as a gap rather than a feature:**
  protected variables are **absent** on unprotected branches, so **MR
  pipelines on feature branches cannot decrypt anything at all**. That is
  deliberate — `lint` runs on every MR, including from branches nobody has
  reviewed, and handing those the age key would defeat the point — but it
  leaves real coverage missing: no MR pipeline can prove decryption works.
  That proof necessarily lives on `main` (`verify:sops`), which means it lands
  *after* review, not during it. Worth knowing when a secrets change looks
  green in an MR.

### Pinned tooling and the supply chain (`ci/ansible.yml`)

- **`SOPS_VERSION` + `SOPS_SHA256`** — the sops binary is fetched from a
  GitHub release and its SHA-256 checked with `sha256sum -c` **before it is
  executed**. Not optional and not decoration: the job downloads an executable
  and runs it as root, in a pipeline that on protected refs holds the age
  private key. `curl -f` proves the request succeeded, which is a different
  question from what arrived — release assets are mutable in ways a tag is
  not. The check must be able to fail, so the job runs without `|| true`. The
  two variables are one fact written twice; bump them together.
- **`COMMUNITY_SOPS_VERSION: "2.1.0"`** — the Ansible side of sops, providing
  `community.sops.load_vars`. **This is not what makes `load_vars` work**, and
  it is worth being exact because the line looks redundant and the tempting
  comment on it is false. Verified 2026-07-15 in the CI image
  (`python:3.12-slim`) with nothing but the pinned ansible installed:

  ```
  $ pip install "ansible==10.7.0"
  $ ansible-doc community.sops.load_vars     # resolves -> already bundled
  $ ansible-galaxy collection list community.sops
  community.sops 1.9.1
  ```

  `ansible==10.7.0` already bundles community.sops 1.9.1. The honest reason to
  pin it: the playbooks name `community.sops.load_vars` directly, which makes
  it a **direct dependency of our code**, and letting it arrive inside the
  `ansible` package means the next `ANSIBLE_VERSION` bump silently changes it.
  Pinning makes the version a decision instead of a side effect.
- **Expected consequence of that pin, so nobody hunts it:** with both copies
  present, **`ansible-lint` warns** — and only when it actually lints:

  ```
  $ ansible-lint <playbook>.yml
  WARNING  Another version of 'community.sops' 1.9.1 was found installed in
  /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/ansible_collections, only the first
  one will be used, 2.1.0 (/root/.ansible/collections/ansible_collections).
  ```

  Two copies exist, the pinned one wins, deterministically. Benign. Note the
  precise attribution, because the obvious guess is wrong: `ansible-galaxy
  collection install` and `ansible-galaxy collection list` print **no** such
  warning (`list` simply shows both versions), and `ansible-lint --version`
  does not either. Only a real lint run emits it.

### Workflow & schedules

- **`workflow:name` + `workflow:rules`** (in `ci/pipeline-name.yml`) — a
  readable label per pipeline ("main · abc1234 · fix: …"); the rules double
  as gating so only MRs, main and schedules create pipelines at all (a
  branch push otherwise creates an empty pipeline). Rule order matters:
  the schedule rule must precede the main rule because schedules also have
  `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"`.
- **Pipeline schedules** — cron-triggered pipelines
  (`0 6 * * *`, timezone Europe/Amsterdam, ref `main`). Ours exists to run
  `verify:dns` daily: DNS drifts without commits, so a push-triggered check
  would miss exactly the interesting case.

heading_path: GitLab CI — pipelines as the only route to the infrastructure
Pitfalls we hit
text:
- A permanently failing job is wallpaper: the original always-on `bootstrap`
  job could only succeed before hardening closed root login. It now checks
  for work first and exits green when there is none
  (`scripts/bootstrap-if-needed.sh`).
- `verify` runs automatically after `apply` (`needs`), not manually: a
  verification you must remember is skipped on the day it matters. Runbook:
  `rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline`.
- Scheduled pipelines match `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"` rules — without
  explicit `when: never` exclusions every code job would rerun each night.

heading_path: glab — GitLab from the terminal
What it is
text:
`glab` is GitLab's official CLI: merge requests, pipelines, variables and
the raw REST API from the terminal, authenticated once via `glab auth
login`. Everything it does can also be done in the web UI — the CLI makes
it scriptable and reviewable.

heading_path: glab — GitLab from the terminal
Why we use it
text:
The execution model has agents doing repo chores end-to-end (create MR,
watch pipeline, set variables); the CLI keeps those steps reproducible and
copy-pasteable into runbooks. The web UI remains the documented fallback in
every runbook.

heading_path: glab — GitLab from the terminal
Where it lives in our repos
text:
Not configured in-repo; used from the workstation. Its commands appear
throughout the runbooks and plans.

heading_path: glab — GitLab from the terminal
Flags & settings we use
text:
- **`glab auth status`** — is this terminal authenticated, and as whom.
  First check in every runbook that touches GitLab.
- **`glab repo create <name> --group <group-path> --private --description`**
  — new project inside a group. `--private` because infrastructure repos
  hold IPs and host keys (deliberate, but not public).
- **`glab mr create --title --description`** (optionally `--repo`,
  `--source-branch`, `--target-branch`) — open a merge request; the only
  route to `main` under branch protection.
- **`glab mr list [--merged]`**, **`glab ci list`** — state of MRs and
  pipelines without opening a browser.
- **`glab api [--method POST|DELETE] "<endpoint>" -f key=value`** — the
  escape hatch: raw REST calls for anything without a subcommand. `-f`
  sends a **string** parameter. We use it for **branch protection**
  (`protected_branches` with `push_access_level=0` = no one,
  `merge_access_level=40` = maintainers) and **pipeline schedules**
  (`pipeline_schedules` with `cron`, `cron_timezone`, `ref`). For anything
  needing a **JSON array** — such as `deploy_tokens` — `-f` cannot express
  it; see the pitfall below.
- **`glab variable set <KEY> < <file>`** — reads the value from **stdin**,
  which is how a secret is set without entering argv (visible in the process
  table) or shell history. `glab`'s own help documents the form. Flags we
  use: **`--type file`** (GitLab writes the content to a temp file and sets
  the variable to that *path* — the shape `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` and
  `ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY` both need), **`--protected`** (the variable exists
  only in pipelines on protected branches), **`--raw`** (`EXPANDED=false`:
  the value is a literal string, no `$VAR` expansion — matching the existing
  `ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY` regime):

  ```bash
  glab variable set SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE --type file --protected --raw < <keyfile>
  ```

  To inspect variables without printing their values, let `jq` select the
  metadata *before* anything renders:

  ```bash
  glab api "projects/<group>%2F<project>/variables" \
    | jq -r '.[] | "\(.key)  protected=\(.protected)  type=\(.variable_type)"'
  ```
- **Project paths in API URLs are URL-encoded**: every `/` in
  `group/subgroup/project` becomes `%2F`. Forgetting this is the most
  common `404 Not Found` cause.

Access levels used in the API (GitLab convention): `0` no one, `30`
developers, `40` maintainers.

heading_path: glab — GitLab from the terminal
Pitfalls we hit
text:
- `glab api` errors are terse (`404` for a wrong path *or* missing rights); check the URL-encoding and your role on the project before debugging anything else. ### `glab api` cannot send a JSON array with `-f` / `--raw-field` This page previously said array parameters use `"scopes[]=..."` syntax. That is false, and it was corrected on 2026-07-15 after the deploy-token call failed on it. glab's own help says so plainly: *"Neither `--field` nor `--raw-field` parses JSON arrays or objects; those values are sent as strings. To pass a JSON body literally, use `--input`."* What `-f "scopes[]=read_repository"` actually puts on the wire — `scopes[]` becomes a **literal JSON key** with a string value, not an array: ``` $ GLAB_DEBUG_HTTP=1 glab api --method POST "projects/

/deploy_tokens" \ -f "name=test" -f "scopes[]=read_repository" POST /api/v4/projects/

/deploy_tokens HTTP/1.1 {"name":"test","scopes[]":"read_repository"} <- not an array {"error":"scopes is missing"}glab: HTTP 400 ``` `--input -` alone does not fix it either — glab sets no Content-Type, and GitLab refuses the body: ``` $ echo '{"name":"test","scopes":["read_repository"]}' \ | glab api --method POST "projects/

/deploy_tokens" --input - {"error":"The provided content-type '' is not supported."}glab: HTTP 415 ``` **The working form is `--input -` plus an explicit Content-Type:** ```bash echo '{"name":"","scopes":["read_repository"]}' \ | glab api --method POST "projects/%2F/deploy_tokens" \ --input - -H "Content-Type: application/json" ``` All three were verified against a **nonexistent** project, which is what makes the experiment safe to repeat: GitLab validates the body *before* it looks the project up, so the two broken forms fail at validation (400/415) and create nothing. The working form is the one that gets far enough to return `404 Project Not Found` — reaching the project lookup is precisely the proof that the body parsed. The deploy token's value is shown **exactly once**; capture it in the same pipe that creates it (`scripts/argocd-deploy-token.sh` in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` pipes it straight into sops) rather than printing it and copying it by hand. ### `GLAB_DEBUG_HTTP=1` — how to see what glab actually sends The debugging tool for all of the above. It prints the full request and response, including the request body and headers, which turns "GitLab says `scopes is missing` and I clearly sent scopes" into a two-second answer. Reach for it before theorising about an API. Note that it prints **everything**, so never use it on a command carrying a real secret — a `glab variable set` with the age key would dump the key to the terminal.
