heading_path: Haven Compliancy Checker (Haven CLI) — running VNG's compliancy checks
What it is
text:
The **Haven CLI** is VNG Realisatie / Common Ground's official tool for checking
whether a Kubernetes cluster is *Haven compliant* — Haven being the Dutch
government standard for platform-independent cloud hosting. The one subcommand
that matters is `haven check`, which runs a fixed set of **15 required
compliancy checks** (plus optional external suggestions). A cluster is Haven
compliant when all required checks pass, including the CNCF Kubernetes
Conformance check. The canonical check list lives in `checks.yaml` in the Haven
repo; `haven check --rationale` prints it locally without touching a cluster.

heading_path: Haven Compliancy Checker (Haven CLI) — running VNG's compliancy checks
Why we use it
text:
It is the objective, external yardstick for the mini-cloud: instead of asserting
the platform is "cloud-native enough", we run the standard's own checker and read
the score. Plan C uses it as a **baseline** (before observability/backup) and an
**end measurement** (after) — see `haven-nulmeting-2026-07`.

heading_path: Haven Compliancy Checker (Haven CLI) — running VNG's compliancy checks
Where it lives / how to pin it
text:
Not a package-manager install — download a pinned release from the GitLab generic
package registry `commonground/haven/haven`, package name `cli`:

```
# List versions (read-only API):
curl -s "https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/commonground%2Fhaven%2Fhaven/packages?per_page=100"
# Download a pinned artifact (example: 12.10.0, windows-amd64):
curl -sSL -o haven-v12.10.0-windows-amd64.zip \
  "https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/commonground%2Fhaven%2Fhaven/packages/generic/cli/12.10.0/haven-v12.10.0-windows-amd64.zip"
```

Verify the SHA-256 against the registry's `file_sha256` before trusting the
binary (the registry API exposes it per file). Artifacts exist for
`darwin-amd64`, `darwin-arm64`, `linux-amd64`, `linux-arm64`, `windows-amd64`;
the zip unpacks to `_dist/<os-arch>/haven[.exe]`. On the workstation it is pinned
under `~/.soevereinlab/tools/haven/` — **never installed on the nodes**.

The checker also has one self-check (#15, "SHA has been validated") that it is a
genuine release; and check #1 requires the CLI itself to be the latest major or
within a 3-month upgrade window, so a stale pinned binary eventually fails its
own version check.

heading_path: Haven Compliancy Checker (Haven CLI) — running VNG's compliancy checks
Flags & settings we use
text:
```
haven check                 # runs all required checks; --cncf defaults to TRUE
haven check --cncf=false    # skip the CNCF/Sonobuoy conformance check (reported skipped)
haven check -o json         # machine-readable output (default: text)
haven check --rationale     # print the check list + reasoning; does NOT run anything
haven check --cis <file>    # optional external CIS benchmark (suggestion)
haven check --kubescape <file>  # optional external Kubescape scan (suggestion)
haven check --help          # authoritative flag list
haven version               # prints the CLI version (note: `--version` is NOT a flag)
```

`--cncf=true` (the default) runs **Sonobuoy** CNCF conformance under the hood —
it deploys a namespace, a ClusterRoleBinding and conformance pods and is
long-running. Use `--cncf=false` for a fast structural run.

heading_path: Haven Compliancy Checker (Haven CLI) — running VNG's compliancy checks
Access route / RBAC — the load-bearing pitfall
text:
**`haven check` requires cluster-admin.** This is documented
(`haven.commonground.nl/techniek/compliancy-checker`: "cluster admin rechten
nodig") and enforced by the tool itself:

- Check #2 is a self-test: *"does HCC have cluster-admin"*.
- Before running any check, at preflight, it **deploys a Haven CRD and a
  ClusterRole** — i.e. it *writes* cluster-scoped RBAC and API-extension
  objects.

So the mini-cloud's read-only `viewer` route (built-in `view` ClusterRole) is
**not enough**: `view` cannot create CRDs/ClusterRoles and cannot even list
`nodes` (cluster-scoped, excluded from `view`). Observed verbatim on the viewer
route:

```
[F] Error occured while detecting or deploying Haven CRD: clusterroles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:soevereinlab-access:viewer" cannot create resource "clusterroles" in API group "rbac.authorization.k8s.io" at the cluster scope
```

Note the checker exited `0` despite that `[F]` fatal — **trust the `[F]` line,
not the exit code**. Because every write was RBAC-rejected, nothing was created;
running it read-only mutates nothing, but it also cannot complete. A real run
needs a cluster-admin kubeconfig (or a temporary cluster-admin binding, torn
down after) reached over the SSH tunnel that the k3s runbook (step 8) describes —
6443 is peer-only, so the kubeconfig points at `127.0.0.1:6443` and needs
`ssh -N -L 6443:127.0.0.1:6443 deploy@<server-ip>` first.

heading_path: Haven Compliancy Checker (Haven CLI) — running VNG's compliancy checks
Pitfalls (summary)
text:
- **Needs cluster-admin** — the viewer route only proves the shortfall, it can't
  score the cluster.
- **Exit code lies** — a fatal `[F]` preflight error still exited `0`; parse the
  log, not `$?`.
- **`--version` is not a flag** — use `haven version`.
- **CNCF = Sonobuoy** — the default run is long and writes to the cluster; use
  `--cncf=false` when you only want the structural checks fast.
- **Not on the nodes** — pin the binary on the workstation only.

heading_path: Helm — how charts enter our cluster: k3s' helm-controller and Argo CD
What it is
text:
Helm is the Kubernetes package manager: a **chart** is a parametrised bundle of
manifests, and Helm renders it against a set of **values** into concrete
objects. The thing worth internalising for this platform is that **we never run
the `helm` CLI against the cluster.** There is no `helm install`, no
`~/.config/helm`, no Tiller-style component we operate. Helm lives here as a
*rendering step* that two other controllers drive for us — k3s' helm-controller
and Argo CD — each turning a chart reference plus values into applied objects
without a workstation ever holding a release.

heading_path: Helm — how charts enter our cluster: k3s' helm-controller and Argo CD
Why we use it
text:
Every third-party component in the cluster (Argo CD, cert-manager,
kube-prometheus-stack, Loki, and the k3s-packaged Traefik) ships as a chart, so
the choice is not "Helm or not" but "which route renders the chart, and how do
we keep it from drifting". Our answer is: pin every chart to an exact version,
and let a controller render it — never a person. A floating chart changes the
platform without a commit, which is the exact property the GitOps layer exists
to prevent (see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)).

The non-Helm alternatives were considered and not chosen for third-party
components: **raw manifests** (copy the upstream YAML into `gitops/`) means
tracking every upstream change by hand and losing the maintainer's tested
defaults; **Kustomize** (overlays over a base) fits our *own* small manifests
but not a large upstream component like kube-prometheus-stack, whose CRDs and
templating live in the chart. We do use plain manifests for the things we
author (the demo app, the issuers) — Helm is specifically for the vendored
components. Adjusting a vendored chart's values is `HelmChartConfig` (k3s) or
Argo's `valuesObject`, both below — never a fork.

heading_path: Helm — how charts enter our cluster: k3s' helm-controller and Argo CD
Where it lives in our repos
text:
Two routes, and which one a chart takes depends on when it must exist:

**Route 1 — k3s' helm-controller (`HelmChart` / `HelmChartConfig` CRDs).** For
things that must exist before Argo CD does, or that k3s itself packages. A
`HelmChart` object dropped into the server's manifests directory
(`/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/`) is rendered and installed by a
controller inside k3s. Its README describes it as "A simple way to manage helm
charts with Custom Resource Definitions in k8s". In `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | Route | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/templates/argocd-helmchart.yaml.j2` | 1 | The `HelmChart` that installs Argo CD, before there is an Argo CD to install it |
| `gitops/platform/traefik/helmchartconfig.yaml` | 1 | A `HelmChartConfig` overriding the packaged Traefik chart's values |

**Route 2 — Argo CD's Helm source (`chart` / `targetRevision` /
`helm.valuesObject`).** For everything after Argo CD is up. An `Application`
names a chart repo, chart name, version and inline values; Argo CD renders and
reconciles it. In `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | Chart | Pin (`targetRevision`) |
|---|---|---|
| `gitops/platform/cert-manager/app.yaml` | cert-manager | `v1.21.0` |
| `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml` | kube-prometheus-stack | `87.16.1` |
| `gitops/platform/logging/loki-app.yaml` | loki | `7.1.0` |

heading_path: Helm — how charts enter our cluster: k3s' helm-controller and Argo CD
Flags & settings we use
text:
### Route 1: `HelmChart` and `HelmChartConfig` (k3s' `helm.cattle.io/v1`)

These are k3s' CRDs, not Helm's own. The `HelmChart` field set our repos use
(`metadata.name` as release name, `spec.version`, `spec.repo`, `spec.chart`,
`spec.targetNamespace`, `spec.createNamespace`, `spec.valuesContent`) is
documented field by field in [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md#helmchart-helmcattleiov1),
where the Argo CD bootstrap uses it — the same CRD, so it is not repeated here.

`HelmChartConfig` is the second CRD, and the only place we use it is the
Traefik redirect. A `HelmChartConfig` sharing a `HelmChart`'s name and
namespace supplies **additional `valuesContent` that merges over** the chart's
existing values, without redefining the chart — which is exactly how you adjust
a component k3s packages (you do not own the `HelmChart`, so you cannot edit it;
you layer a config beside it). Verified in use: our
`gitops/platform/traefik/helmchartconfig.yaml` (name `traefik`, namespace
`kube-system`) carries the comment "Values merge over k3s' packaged Traefik
chart (traefik-40.1.3+up40.1.0)", and the redirect it adds is live
(2026-07-16). See [topic-traefik](topic-traefik.md).

- **`spec.valuesContent`** — inline YAML as a *string*, passed as Helm's
  `--values`. An indentation slip inside it is not a manifest YAML error, it is
  a different set of values than intended (same trap as the Argo CD
  `valuesContent`).
- **`spec.version` (on `HelmChart`)** — pinned, always. Omitting it installs
  whatever is newest at first install and then never upgrades — "latest, once,
  on the day the VPS was built" (see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)).

### Route 2: Argo CD `Application` Helm source

Per Argo CD's docs, Argo CD does **not** run `helm install`; "Helm is only used
to inflate charts with `helm template`... The lifecycle of the application is
handled by Argo CD instead of Helm" — so there is no Helm release to `helm ls`,
and reconciliation/prune/self-heal are Argo CD's, not Helm's.

- **`source.chart` + `source.repoURL`** — the chart name and the repository
  (an HTTPS Helm repo or an OCI registry) it is pulled from. `repoURL` here
  points at a chart repo, not our git repo.
- **`source.targetRevision`** — the **chart version**, pinned in every one of
  our `Application`s (`v1.21.0`, `87.16.1`, `7.1.0` above). For a git source
  `targetRevision` is a branch/tag/commit; for a Helm source it is the chart
  version — same field, different meaning per source type. Each pin is
  verified against the chart repo's `index.yaml` in the topic that owns it.
- **`source.helm.valuesObject`** — the chart's values as a real inline YAML
  object (not a string). We use `valuesObject` over the alternatives on
  purpose:
  - **`valueFiles`** — value files by path/glob inside the source repo. Fine
    for a git source; for a remote chart there is no repo of ours to read them
    from.
  - **`values`** — the same values but as a YAML **string** (the stringly-typed
    forerunner of `valuesObject`), which reintroduces the indentation-in-a-string
    trap.
  - **`parameters`** — individual `key=value` overrides that, per Argo CD's
    docs, "trump all of them" (highest precedence). Good for one-off overrides,
    not for expressing a component's whole configuration.
  `valuesObject` keeps the values structured and diffable in the one place the
  `Application` already is.

### Chart-pinning, the rule both routes share

Every chart above is pinned to an exact version, and the reasoning is
documented per component rather than restated here:
[topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md) (chart `argo-cd` 10.1.3),
[topic-kube-prometheus-stack](topic-kube-prometheus-stack.md) (`87.16.1`) and
[topic-cert-manager](topic-cert-manager.md) (`v1.21.0`) each carry the pin and
how it was checked against the upstream index.

heading_path: Helm — how charts enter our cluster: k3s' helm-controller and Argo CD
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### The two routes are not interchangeable

Route 1 (k3s manifests directory) is **asynchronous and not GitOps** — deleting
the file does not delete the objects, and a bad manifest retries silently
forever (see [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md)). Route 2 (Argo CD) prunes and
self-heals. We use Route 1 only where Route 2 cannot exist yet — the Argo CD
install itself — or where k3s owns the chart (Traefik). Reaching for a
`HelmChart` CRD to install an ordinary app would opt that app out of the very
convergence Argo CD provides.

### `helm template`, not `helm install` — no release to inspect

Because Argo CD renders with `helm template`, the familiar debugging reflex
`helm ls` / `helm get values` returns nothing: there is no release object. The
rendered state and its drift are read through Argo CD (`kubectl -n argocd get
applications`), not through Helm. Sourced: Argo CD's Helm user guide, this
session.

### A `HelmChartConfig` values key the chart does not read is silent

helm-controller merges whatever `valuesContent` you give it; the chart ignores
keys it does not recognise. So a Traefik chart bump that renames a values key
turns our redirect off without any error — the failure surfaces only in
`verify:platform`. This is the chart-version-dependent-values trap documented
in [topic-traefik](topic-traefik.md); it is a property of the merge, not of
Traefik specifically.

heading_path: jq (and python -c) — building and parsing JSON in our command pipelines
What it is
text:
`jq` is a command-line JSON processor: it reads JSON on stdin and emits
transformed JSON (or plain text) on stdout, driven by a small filter language.
In this programme it earns its place at exactly two jobs — **building** a
request body to send to an API, and **reshaping** an API response — both inside
a shell pipe where the data must never touch disk or a shell variable. Its
frequent companion is `python3 -c`, used where the job is *parsing* a response
to loop over or format it.

Neither tool is version-pinned in our repos; both arrive from the CI job image
or the workstation. `jq` is installed explicitly where a job needs it — the
`test:deploy-token` job in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`'s `.gitlab-ci.yml`
`apt-get install`s `jq` (and `age`, `git`) as real tooling for the script under
test.

heading_path: jq (and python -c) — building and parsing JSON in our command pipelines
Why we use it
text:
Because pasting JSON together with string interpolation is how you ship a
malformed body or leak a value. Two properties matter here:

- **Correct quoting for free.** `jq` builds JSON (and reshapes to YAML via
  `@json`) with proper escaping, so a value that happens to contain a quote,
  backslash or newline does not break the payload.
- **Pipe-friendly, no intermediate variable.** A secret can flow
  `glab → jq → sops` in one pipe without any stage rendering it to a variable
  or a file — which is a security property, not a style choice.

heading_path: jq (and python -c) — building and parsing JSON in our command pipelines
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`, `scripts/argocd-deploy-token.sh` — the fullest
example, minting Argo CD's deploy token:

- **`jq` builds the request body.** `jq -nc --arg name … --arg scope …
  '{name: $name, scopes: [$scope]} + (if $expires == "" then {} else
  {expires_at: $expires} end)'` — a JSON object assembled from shell variables,
  not string-pasted. The script's own comment records why: the `-f
  "scopes[]=…"` form "DOES NOT WORK" (glab sends it as a JSON *string*
  parameter and GitLab answers `400 {"error":"scopes is missing"}`, observed
  2026-07-15), so the array must be sent as a real JSON body via `--input -`.
- **`jq` reshapes the response to YAML**, with a filter that `error()`s if the
  response carried no `username`/`token` — so a tokenless response cannot become
  a valid-looking encrypted file full of nulls — using `@json` to quote each
  value. The whole thing is one pipe: `printf "$REQUEST" | glab api … --input -
  | jq -r "$YAML_FILTER" | sops encrypt …`, no variable holding the token.

The command-cookbook (`reference/command-cookbook.md`) carries the reusable
forms:

- **Recipe 3** — the `glab api` JSON-body rules: URL-encode the project path,
  send arrays as a JSON body (not `-f`) with an explicit `Content-Type`. This is
  the deploy-token body above, recomposed as a standalone one-liner.
- **Recipe 4** — inspecting pipeline jobs: pipe `glab api …/jobs` into
  `python3 -c "import json,sys; [print(...) for j in json.load(sys.stdin)]"`.
- **Recipe 14** — the kubectl service proxy returns JSON (Prometheus,
  Alertmanager, Loki, Grafana health), read the same way.
- **Recipe 16** — verifying a SOPS envelope's keys without printing values:
  `sops decrypt … | python -c "import sys,yaml; print(sorted(...))"`
  (see [topic-sops](topic-sops.md)).

heading_path: jq (and python -c) — building and parsing JSON in our command pipelines
When jq, when python
text:
- **`jq`** when you are **constructing or reshaping JSON in a pipe** and want its
  quoting/escaping and a filter that can fail closed (`error()`) — request
  bodies, response-to-YAML, a single-field extract (`| jq -r .token`).
- **`python3 -c`** when you are **parsing to loop or format** (recipe 4's
  per-job line), or when you need **YAML** (`jq` speaks JSON, not YAML input —
  recipe 16 loads YAML with PyYAML, which the ansible-core image already
  brings). It is also what we reach for when a response needs real logic rather
  than a filter.

heading_path: jq (and python -c) — building and parsing JSON in our command pipelines
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### `python -c`, never a heredoc, when a pipe feeds stdin

`cmd | python3 - <<'PY' … PY` **starves** `json.load(sys.stdin)`: the heredoc
claims python's stdin, so the pipe is lost; and a heredoc inside `$( … )` prints
a spurious `unterminated here-document` warning. Use the `-c` form —
`cmd | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); …"` — which every
cookbook recipe here uses. Both failure modes observed 2026-07-17 (cookbook
recipe 15).

### Guard the parse, don't trust the response

The deploy-token filter `error()`s on a missing `username`/`token` on purpose:
an API response is not guaranteed to contain what you asked for, and a silent
`null` written through `sops encrypt` is a plausible-looking file that fails
much later. Whether jq (`error()`) or python (raise / check), the parse stage is
where a bad response should fail loudly, before it is stored.

heading_path: jq (and python -c) — building and parsing JSON in our command pipelines

text:

  whose JSON responses `jq`/python parse
- [topic-sops](topic-sops.md) — the encrypt stage at the end of the

heading_path: k3s — the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
What it is
text:
k3s is a single-binary Kubernetes distribution from Rancher/SUSE. One
executable contains the API server, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet
and a container runtime, plus batteries that upstream Kubernetes leaves to
you: a CNI (flannel), an ingress controller (Traefik), a service load
balancer (ServiceLB) and a local-path storage provisioner. It is a conformant
Kubernetes, not a subset — the trimming is in the packaging, not the API.

A cluster is made of **servers** (nodes running the control plane) and
**agents** (nodes that only run workloads). Which one a node becomes is
decided by the subcommand it is started with, `k3s server` or `k3s agent`.
Agents find the control plane over the network and authenticate with a **join
token**; from then on the cluster is one logical machine.

The datastore under the control plane is pluggable — `datastore-endpoint`
takes "etcd, NATS, MySQL, Postgres, or SQLite (default)". **SQLite is the
default** and is what a lone server uses: "SQLite is the default datastore,
and will be used if no other datastore configuration is present, and no
embedded etcd database files are present on disk." Our server passes neither
a datastore endpoint nor `--cluster-init`, so it is SQLite — **not etcd**.
Worth fixing in your head early: most k3s writing you will find online
assumes embedded etcd, and the advice that follows from it (quorum, snapshot
schedules, `etcdctl`) does not apply here. It also matters for the HA gap at
the bottom of this page.

heading_path: k3s — the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Why we use it
text:
The mini-cloud design spec (in the marketplace repo,
`docs/specs/2026-07-14-mini-cloud-bootstrap-design.md`, §4) picks k3s for two
stated reasons: it is **CNCF-certified**, which is what makes it credible as
Haven-style platform material, and it is **light enough for these VPSs**. The
spec also calls the SQLite datastore out as a feature rather than a
concession — lighter than etcd, and a backup is a simple snapshot. §3 fixes
the shape: both VPSs form one cluster — one node is the server (control plane
*and* worker), the other joins as an agent.

The rest of the stack follows from that choice: Traefik is taken because it
is the k3s default (fewer moving parts than adding ingress-nginx), storage is
k3s' local-path provisioner, and the WireGuard flannel backend is what buys
encrypted node traffic **without depending on a netcup vLAN add-on**. Note
what is not claimed here: there is no decision record weighing k3s against
k0s or plain Kubernetes. The spec chose it; this page documents it.

heading_path: k3s — the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

- `ansible/roles/k3s/defaults/main.yml` — the version pin and the derivation
  of which node is the server.
- `ansible/roles/k3s/tasks/install.yml` — the asserts, the version gate, the
  membership check, the token slurp, both installer invocations and the
  "running and enabled" task.
- `ansible/roles/k3s/tasks/drift.yml` — the restart-when-stale heal.
- `ansible/roles/k3s/tasks/manifests.yml` — the server-only copy into k3s'
  manifests directory.
- `ansible/roles/k3s/files/viewer-rbac.yaml` — the read-only identity, as
  static YAML rather than a template, so what is in git is byte-for-byte what
  lands on the node.
- `scripts/viewer-kubeconfig.sh` — mints the viewer's token and writes a
  kubeconfig. The token is not in git and not in the cluster; the reviewed
  recipe for getting one is.
- `ansible/roles/k3s/templates/config-server.yaml.j2` and
  `config-agent.yaml.j2` — rendered to `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml`.
- `ansible/site.yml` — one play against `k3s_server`, one against `k3s_agent`.
- `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` — the child groups that decide a node's role.
- `ansible/roles/baseline/tasks/firewall.yml` — the ports k3s needs
  (see [topic-ufw](topic-ufw.md)).

On a node: the binary at `/usr/local/bin/k3s`, config at
`/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml` (0600), the admin kubeconfig at
`/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml`, state under `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/`, the
server-only manifests directory at `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/`,
and the unit and its environment file in `/etc/systemd/system/`.

heading_path: k3s — the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Flags & settings we use
text:
Three surfaces set k3s' behaviour and it is worth keeping them apart, because
which one a setting belongs to decides who reads it and when:

| Surface | Written by | Read by | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml` | our templates | the **k3s daemon** | at daemon startup |
| `INSTALL_K3S_*`, `K3S_*` env | our `environment:` on the installer task | the **install script** | during install |
| the systemd unit | `get.k3s.io` | systemd | at boot/restart |

The install script and the daemon do **not** read the same file. See the
first pitfall — this is the single most load-bearing correction on this page.

### `k3s_version` = `"v1.36.2+k3s1"`

The role default, handed to the installer as `INSTALL_K3S_VERSION`. This is
what the `stable` channel pointed at on 2026-07-15.

Leave `INSTALL_K3S_VERSION` unset and the script resolves a channel instead
(`get_release_version`): it requests
`${INSTALL_K3S_CHANNEL_URL}/${INSTALL_K3S_CHANNEL}` — defaulting to
`https://update.k3s.io/v1-release/channels` and `stable` — then follows the
redirect and takes the last path segment as the version. The channel list held
27 entries on 2026-07-15: the three named channels (`stable`, `latest`,
`testing`), one per minor (`v1.16` … `v1.36`), and three legacy
`v1.1x-testing` leftovers. On 2026-07-15 `stable` and `latest` both resolved to
`v1.36.2+k3s1` — which is worth not misreading as "they are the same thing".
They are separate channels that happen to coincide today: `latest` carries an
exclude-regexp that filters pre-releases and a couple of known-bad versions,
and it is the one that moves first. That `testing` was sitting on a stale
`v1.18.2-rc3+k3s1` is a reminder that a channel is only as current as whoever
maintains it.

Why ours: a channel makes the cluster's Kubernetes version a function of the
day someone happened to press apply. Two nodes installed a month apart would
silently run different minors. A pin makes a version bump what it should be —
a reviewed commit. The cost is that nobody gets security patches for free;
bumping the pin is a deliberate chore.

The pin is also the *gate*: `install.yml` runs `k3s --version`, takes the
third field of the first line (the output is `k3s version v1.36.2+k3s1
(<commit>)` followed by a `go version` line) and compares it **whole** against
the pin, so a second apply reports `changed=0` and `v1.36.20+k3s1` cannot pass
as the pinned `v1.36.2+k3s1` by mere containment.

### `flannel-backend: wireguard-native` — server only

How flannel moves pod traffic between nodes. **This is a server flag only**:
it appears in `pkg/cli/cmds/server.go` and not in `agent.go` (which has
`flannel-iface`, `flannel-conf` and `flannel-cni-conf`, but no backend). The
agent takes the backend the server hands it, which is why the agent template
deliberately omits it — the choice is stated once.

Option space (`server.go` usage string: `'none'`, `'vxlan'`, `'host-gw'`,
`'wireguard-native'`; the code in `pkg/agent/flannel/setup.go` also accepts
`tailscale`, which the usage string forgets to mention):

- **`vxlan`** — the default. Encapsulates pod traffic in UDP on port
  **8472**, unencrypted. Fine inside a trusted L2 network; on the public
  internet it is every pod-to-pod packet in cleartext.
- **`host-gw`** — no encapsulation, routes pod CIDRs to peers directly.
  Fastest, but requires the nodes to be on the same L2 segment. Ours are two
  separate VPSs reached over routed internet, so it cannot work here.
- **`wireguard-native`** — **k3s** writes `{"Type": "wireguard",
  "PersistentKeepaliveInterval": 25}` into flannel's `net-conf.json` and
  flannel then uses the kernel's WireGuard, so there is no extra daemon and no
  userspace crypto hop. Mind the attribution, which an earlier version of this
  bullet got wrong: the keepalive is **k3s'** decision (the
  `wireguardNativeBackend` const in `pkg/agent/flannel/setup.go`), not
  flannel's — flannel's own default is `PersistentKeepaliveInterval: 0`
  (`pkg/backend/wireguard/wireguard.go`, v0.28.4) and it merely reads what k3s
  hands it. Note also *how* flannel uses the kernel: it is a netlink client
  (`wgctrl`) and configures the device itself, so the tunnel needs no userland
  WireGuard package and ran without one here for the cluster's first day. We
  install `wireguard-tools` anyway, purely so the tunnel can be *inspected* —
  see [topic-wireguard-tools](topic-wireguard-tools.md), including the `wg show
  all dump` trap that prints the node's private key.
- **`none`** — bring your own CNI (Cilium, Calico). More power, more parts.
- **`tailscale`** — flannel as an extension over a tailnet. Encrypted too,
  but it puts a third-party coordination service in the path of the pod
  network, which is the opposite of the point of a sovereign lab.

Why ours: **the two nodes talk over the public internet.** There is no
private network between them, so the pod network must encrypt itself or
publish itself. This is exactly why the firewall opens **51820/udp** and not
8472/udp — the port follows the backend, and picking the backend without
moving the port would produce a cluster whose pods cannot reach each other.
Per the k3s requirements table: UDP 8472 is "Required only for Flannel
VXLAN", UDP 51820 "Required only for Flannel Wireguard with IPv4", and UDP
**51821** "Required only for Flannel Wireguard with IPv6". We are IPv4-only
(`rb-2026-07-15-dns-ipv4-only`), so 51821 stays shut — open it only if this
lab ever grows an IPv6 pod network.

### `secrets-encryption: true`

Encrypts Kubernetes Secrets at rest in the datastore. The flag is a boolean
with no default value set in `server.go`, so **the default is off**: without
it, every Secret sits in the datastore in plaintext. Since our datastore is
SQLite on the server's disk, and the spec's backup plan for it is "a simple
snapshot", off would mean every backup is a set of credentials in the clear.
The spec asks for this explicitly: its secrets row (§4) pairs SOPS + age for
secrets *in git* with "k3s draait daarnaast met secrets-encryption-at-rest"
for secrets *in the cluster* — the two halves of the same rule.

Companion flag we leave alone: `secrets-encryption-provider`, which defaults
to `aescbc` and is marked experimental; the alternative is `secretbox`. No
reason to move off the default.

Be honest about the threat model this closes: the encryption key lives on the
same node as the database it protects. This defeats "someone walks off with a
snapshot"; it does nothing against "someone has root on the server", who has
both halves. Encryption at rest is a backup-and-disposal control here, not an
intrusion control.

### `write-kubeconfig-mode: "0600"`

The mode of the admin kubeconfig `/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml` — a file holding
**cluster-admin** credentials. Spec §7 wants "geen rondslingerende
cluster-admin-kubeconfig": none of these lying around, with Argo CD deploying
under its own service accounts and day-to-day looking done through a
read-only context.

Read the source before believing this is load-bearing. In
`pkg/server/server.go` the mode is applied as:

```go
if config.ControlConfig.KubeConfigMode != "" {
    mode, err := strconv.ParseInt(config.ControlConfig.KubeConfigMode, 8, 0)
    ...
} else {
    util.SetFileModeForPath(kubeConfig, os.FileMode(0600))
}
```

So **0600 is already what k3s does when the flag is unset** at this version.
Declaring it changes no behaviour today; it pins the intent so a future k3s
default cannot loosen the file without someone editing this repo. That is a
real reason to keep it and a bad reason to feel protected by it — the
protection was already there.

What the option space costs: the mode is parsed **base 8**, and the tutorial
answer to "kubectl says permission denied" is `write-kubeconfig-mode: "0644"`
(or worse, `0777`), which hands cluster-admin to every local user on the node.
Note the quotes are not decoration: the value is parsed as octal, and a value
that is not valid octal is logged as an error and then *skipped entirely* —
the branch above simply does not chmod. A mode that fails to parse is not a
loud failure, it is a silently unapplied setting.

Our agents never get this file at all; `k3s kubectl` on the server is the only
admin path, which is why the membership check in `install.yml` is
`delegate_to` the server.

### `node-name: {{ inventory_hostname }}` — both roles

The name the node registers under. Unset, k3s falls back to the OS hostname —
and then lowercases it. Verified in `pkg/util/net.go` at the pinned tag,
`GetHostnameAndIPs`:

```go
if name == "" {
    hostname, err := os.Hostname()
    ...
    name = hostname
}

// Use lower case hostname to comply with kubernetes constraint:
name = strings.ToLower(name)
```

Two things to take from that, and the second is the one people get wrong:
the fallback is `os.Hostname()`, **and the `ToLower` sits outside the `if`**.
It is applied unconditionally — to a name we declare just as much as to a
hostname it guessed. Declaring `node-name: Node-A` still registers `node-a`.

Why declare it: it makes the node's identity the inventory's business rather
than whatever `hostnamectl` says on the day, and it makes the membership check
in `install.yml` answerable — that task asks the server whether
`{{ inventory_hostname }}` is Ready, and it can only ask about a name we
chose. The role backs this with an assert that `inventory_hostname` is already
lowercase, because the unconditional `ToLower` would otherwise turn a
capitalised inventory entry into a node that registers under a name the check
can never match, and the agent would be re-joined on every apply, forever.

### `node-ip: {{ ansible_host }}` — both roles

The address the node advertises. Unset, `GetHostnameAndIPs` calls
`apinet.ChooseHostInterface()` — the address of the default-route interface.
On our nodes that is the same address today, so this is not a fix; it is a
refusal to depend on a coincidence. Saying it means the firewall rule, the
agent's `server:` URL and the node's advertised address all derive from one
place: `ansible_host` in the inventory. A node with a second interface, or a
provider that reorders them, would otherwise advertise an address the peer
cannot reach and the fault would surface as pod networking that half-works.

### `server: https://<server-ip>:6443` — agent only

Where the agent joins. `k3s_server_ip` resolves to the `ansible_host` of
whichever node the inventory marks `k3s_role: server`, so the server is never
named twice. 6443 is the k3s supervisor and Kubernetes API port, opened by the
firewall from the peer IP only.

### `INSTALL_K3S_VERSION`, `K3S_URL`, `K3S_TOKEN` — installer environment

Passed via Ansible's `environment:` on the two installer tasks, not written
into `config.yaml`, because they are the *install script's* inputs:

- **`INSTALL_K3S_VERSION`** — pins the payload (`get_release_version`).
- **`K3S_URL`** — the server to join. The script verifies it starts with
  `https://` and, notably, **defaults the subcommand to `agent` when it is
  set**; we pass `agent` explicitly anyway rather than lean on that.
- **`K3S_TOKEN`** — the join credential, slurped from the server's
  `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token`. `no_log: true` on every task that
  touches it.

Every variable matching `^(K3S|CONTAINERD|KINE)_` in the installer's
environment is captured verbatim into the unit's environment file, which is
created `touch` + `chmod 0600` before it is written. This is also why the
role's `| trim` on the token is load-bearing rather than tidy: the capture is
a line-per-variable `tee`, so a trailing newline in the value splits the line
and leaves the agent with a truncated token.

### `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` — the declarative front door

Not a flag: a **directory**, and the fourth surface that decides what this
cluster runs. A controller inside the k3s server **re-reads it every 15
seconds** and applies what it finds "in a manner similar to `kubectl apply`",
from startup onwards. (Upstream names the function `WatchFiles`, which is
where the word "watches" keeps coming from — including from an earlier draft
of this very page. It does not watch; see below.) It is how k3s installs its
own batteries — `coredns`,
`traefik`, `local-storage` and `metrics-server` all arrive as files dropped
here — and it is our bootstrap path for anything that must exist in the
cluster before there is anything in the cluster to install it with. Argo CD
lands this way in a later task; the viewer RBAC below is the first thing we
put here ourselves, and the pattern is deliberately the same.

Read the mechanism carefully, because "it applies the directory" hides three
behaviours that matter:

- **It polls; it does not watch.** The loop re-lists the directory every
  **15 seconds** rather than taking a filesystem notification. So there is a
  window, up to 15s wide, in which the file is on disk and the objects do not
  exist. That window sits *after* Ansible has reported success — see the
  pitfall below.
- **It compares checksums.** Each file's SHA256 is recorded on an **`AddOn`
  custom resource in `kube-system`**, and a file whose checksum matches its
  AddOn is skipped. `kubectl -n kube-system get addon` is the list of what
  this directory has actually done, and `kubectl -n kube-system describe
  addon <name>` (or the namespace's events) is where an apply failure is
  visible. Not the Ansible log — the failure happens minutes later, on the
  cluster.
- **It retries, and it retries silently.** A file that fails to apply is
  logged and left; the next pass tries again, 15 seconds later, forever. The
  common way to earn that: the controller resolves an object's GVK against
  the cluster, so a manifest naming a **CRD that does not exist yet** never
  applies and never stops trying. This is a real trap for the Argo CD work
  (its manifests reference their own CRDs) and worth knowing before you meet
  it. It is *not* reachable from the viewer manifest, which is core `v1` and
  `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` objects only — both present before the API
  server finishes starting.

Three more sharp edges:

- **Deleting a file does not delete the objects.** The doc is explicit:
  "Deleting files out of this directory will not delete the corresponding
  resources from the cluster." The directory is a way in, not a source of
  truth. Removing something means `--disable` (which does actively uninstall
  the AddOn and delete the source file) or deleting the objects yourself.
  Do not model this as GitOps: git converges *towards* the cluster here, never
  away from it. Argo CD is what will close that half of the loop.
- **Server-only.** The path is under `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server`; an agent
  has no such directory and nothing on an agent reads one. Our role guards the
  copy with `when: k3s_role == 'server'` for that reason. With more than one
  server it would get worse — "K3s does not sync AddOn content between nodes",
  so keeping the file identical across servers would be our problem. At one
  server, it is a note.
- **The packaged files are k3s'.** It rewrites `traefik.yaml` and friends on
  every start "in order to ensure their integrity", so editing them is a
  change that silently reverts. Add files; do not edit theirs. (A `.skip` file
  makes k3s ignore a manifest — but only before it has been applied; a `.skip`
  added afterwards removes nothing.)

### The viewer ServiceAccount, and how it gets a token

The first thing we put in that directory: a read-only identity, in
`ansible/roles/k3s/files/viewer-rbac.yaml`. Three core objects — a dedicated
namespace, a `viewer` ServiceAccount, and a ClusterRoleBinding to the built-in
**`view`** ClusterRole. Note what is not in that list: **no token**. That is
the interesting part, and it is below.

**Why it is in git at all**, because the plan said to create it by hand with
`k3s kubectl` on the server and that would have worked fine — for a while.
Spec success criterion 1 is "er is niets handmatig aangepast dat niet in git
staat", and this is what that criterion is *for*: a hand-made ServiceAccount
exists in exactly one place, k3s' SQLite datastore on the one server. Rebuild
from the repo after a loss and every other object comes back; this one does
not. Nothing goes red. The kubeconfig on the workstation just starts answering
401, at some remove from the change that caused it. **State that cannot be
rebuilt from git is state nobody is checking** — and a two-node lab whose HA
story is "restore from backup" (see the gap at the bottom of this page) cannot
afford a category of object that the restore silently drops.

Say plainly what that does *not* buy, though, because it is easy to read the
manifest as if it enforced the criterion: it does not. The viewer access is now
in git, but **nothing checks that the cluster contains only what git
declares.** Anyone can still `kubectl create` an object by hand next to it and
no layer in either repo will notice. "Niets handmatig" is currently a rule with
no enforcement; the maintainer has decided it gets a real check in a later task
(`scripts/verify-platform.sh`). Until that exists it is a convention, not a
property.

#### The token is minted, not stored

Kubernetes stopped auto-creating a token Secret per ServiceAccount in **1.24**
(the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` gate, default-on from 1.24,
**removed in 1.27** when it went GA — so on 1.36 there is no gate to switch
back). A bare ServiceAccount therefore hands out no credential at all, and
exactly two things can produce one:

1. A **`Secret` of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`** annotated
   `kubernetes.io/service-account.name: viewer`. The token controller populates
   it. It never expires, and the only revocation is deleting the Secret.
2. **`kubectl create token viewer`** — the TokenRequest subresource. Bound and
   expiring. Upstream recommends it and calls Secret tokens *"not
   recommended... because of the risks associated with static, long-lived
   credentials."*

We do (2), from `scripts/viewer-kubeconfig.sh`.

The first draft of this work did (1), and the argument for it is worth
recording **because it was wrong** and it is the kind of wrong that survives
review. It ran: *a TokenRequest token cannot be declared, only called, so a
short-lived token must be minted by a human running a command, which
reintroduces exactly the hand-made state criterion 1 forbids — every expiry
rather than once.*

The flaw is in the second half. **`kubectl create token` creates no persistent
object.** It is a pure API call that returns a signed JWT; the cluster
afterwards contains precisely what git declares — the SA and the binding.
Nothing drifts and nothing needs reconciling, so criterion 1 is not engaged at
all: the criterion is about *cluster state* that is not in git, and a token is
not cluster state. The premise holds for `kubectl create secret`; it does not
hold for `create token`. And "a human runs a command" is not ad-hoc handwork
when the command is a reviewed script in git — which is what
`viewer-kubeconfig.sh` is for.

What settles it is the firewall, and it is worth following the chain because it
inverts the usual answer. **6443 is open to the peer node only** (see
[topic-ufw](topic-ufw.md); `verify-hardening.sh` proves it from outside on
every run). So the viewer kubeconfig cannot reach the API from a workstation at
all without an SSH tunnel to the server node. **SSH is therefore already a
precondition of looking at the cluster** — which means minting a fresh token
inside that same session costs nothing, and the "it fails closed at 03:00 and
you have to SSH to the control plane to fix it" objection describes a price
that is being paid on every single use anyway. A never-expiring credential
would buy nothing we do not already have. Failing closed is also the *right*
failure here: nothing automated depends on this token, and the human it exists
for is by construction already at an SSH prompt.

#### Nothing enforces the short lifetime except the script

The one genuinely surprising finding, and the reason the recipe is in git.

`kubectl create token --duration` is a *request*: the docs say **"The server
may return a token with a longer or shorter lifetime."** The cap would come
from the apiserver's `--service-account-max-token-expiration`. We do not have
one:

- k3s never sets that flag — it does not appear anywhere in its source at our
  tag; the only service-account arguments it passes the apiserver are
  `service-account-signing-key-file`, `service-account-key-file` and
  `service-account-issuer`.
- The upstream default is the Go zero value, i.e. **unset**.
  `WithServiceAccounts()` assigns `Lookup`, `ExtendExpiration` and
  `MaxExtendedExpiration`, and pointedly never assigns `MaxExpiration`.
- The shortening branch in the TokenRequest handler is `if
  r.maxExpirationSeconds > 0 && req.Spec.ExpirationSeconds >
  r.maxExpirationSeconds`. With 0, **nothing is shortened.**
- The only bounds actually enforced are TokenRequest validation: not less than
  10 minutes, not more than 2^32 seconds.

So `--duration=87600h` would be honoured just as cheerfully as `8h` and hand
out a ten-year credential. **The short lifetime is a property of one line in
one script, not of the cluster.** Anyone who "temporarily" bumps that number to
stop re-minting has silently rebuilt the long-lived token we rejected, with no
Secret to find and delete afterwards.

(`--service-account-extend-token-expiration` defaults to true and extends some
tokens to a year, but only pod-bound ones — *"Only perform the extension when
token is pod-bound"* — so it does not touch ours.)

We ask for **8h**: long enough to outlive an incident, short enough not to
outlive the day. **Not yet observed on a real cluster** — the above is read
from upstream source, not from a token anyone has held. The effective lifetime
must be confirmed after the first apply.

#### `view`, and why it cannot read Secrets

The default `view` ClusterRole grants read on most namespaced objects and
pointedly not on Secrets, roles or rolebindings — upstream's reasoning being
that reading Secrets in a namespace means reading ServiceAccount tokens, which
is privilege escalation. That exclusion is what stops this design being a
**ladder**: a viewer that could read Secrets could read every other
ServiceAccount's token in the cluster, including ones that are not viewers, and
stop being one. The answer to "my viewer can't see Secrets" is *good* — do not
fix it by binding to a role that can.

`view` is also aggregated — it collects rules labelled
`rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view` — so a CRD that ships view rules
extends the binding for free. That is the second reason not to hand-write a
read-only role.

Bound with a **ClusterRoleBinding**, not a RoleBinding: `view`'s rules are
namespaced, and binding them cluster-wide is what turns them into "read
anything, anywhere". A RoleBinding would scope the viewer to its own namespace,
which contains nothing but the viewer — a viewer of nothing.

Not mitigated, out loud: this reads **every ConfigMap in every namespace**, and
ConfigMaps are where people put what belonged in Secrets. `view` protects
Secrets; it cannot protect a password someone typed into a ConfigMap.

#### The kubeconfig points at 127.0.0.1, and the certificate allows it

Because 6443 is peer-only, the kubeconfig `viewer-kubeconfig.sh` writes points
at `https://127.0.0.1:6443` and is used through a tunnel:

```sh
ssh -i <key> -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
    -o UserKnownHostsFile=ansible/known_hosts \
    -N -L 6443:127.0.0.1:6443 deploy@<server-ip>
KUBECONFIG=./viewer.kubeconfig kubectl get nodes
```

The two `-o` options are not decoration: they are the same host-key pinning
`ansible.cfg` and every script in the config repo use (see
[topic-ssh-client](topic-ssh-client.md)). A tunnel that accepts an unknown host
key on first use is a tunnel someone can stand in front of, and it would be an
odd place to start trusting strangers — this one carries a cluster credential.

For that to survive TLS verification, `127.0.0.1` has to be a SAN on the API
server's serving certificate. **It is, by default, and no `tls-san` entry is
needed** — but the place it comes from is not where you would look, which is
why this is written down.

Read the certificate code (`pkg/daemons/control/deps/deps.go`,
`genServerCerts`) and you would conclude the opposite. The altNames literal for
the `serving-kube-apiserver` cert contains only cluster DNS names:

```go
altNames := &certutil.AltNames{
    DNSNames: []string{"kubernetes", "kubernetes.default",
    "kubernetes.default.svc", "kubernetes.default.svc." + config.ClusterDomain},
}
addSANs(altNames, config.SANs)
```

No loopback. The `localhost`/`127.0.0.1`/`::1` block a few lines below it is
real but belongs to the **kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager** serving
certs, not the apiserver's — an easy misread.

The loopback arrives through `config.SANs`, appended a layer up in the CLI
(`pkg/cli/server/server.go`, tag `v1.36.2+k3s1`), unconditionally and behind no
flag:

```go
// Ensure that we add the localhost name/ip and node name/ip to the SAN list.
// This list is shared by the certs for the supervisor, kube-apiserver cert,
// and etcd.
serverConfig.ControlConfig.SANs = append(serverConfig.ControlConfig.SANs,
    "127.0.0.1", "::1", "localhost", nodeName)
```

The proof that it really lands: k3s' own admin kubeconfig
`/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml` points at `https://127.0.0.1:6443` (`deps.go`:
`apiEndpoint := fmt.Sprintf("https://%s:%d", config.Loopback(true),
config.APIServerPort)`), and `k3s kubectl` on the node works every day. If the
SAN were missing, nothing on the server could talk to its own API server.

Our `node-ip` is a SAN too (the same block appends the node IPs), so a
kubeconfig pointing at the public address would also verify — it just could not
connect, because of the firewall.

#### Namespace: a dedicated one, not `kube-system`

`kube-system` is the obvious choice and the wrong one. kube-system holds k3s'
packaged components and their service accounts, so anything that ever gets
namespaced read there — an operator, a monitoring agent, a Role written
slightly too wide — would reach whatever we put in it as a side effect of a
grant that was about something else. A namespace whose only contents are this
ServiceAccount makes that impossible to hand out by accident: there is nothing
in it anyone would want, so nobody will ask. It also keeps our objects out of
the namespace k3s treats as its own.

The cost is one extra object and an ordering question — the Namespace must
exist before the ServiceAccount — which the file answers by declaring it first,
and which the controller's retry would heal anyway.

### The `get.k3s.io` route and the systemd units

`curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -s - server` (or `- agent`). The
subcommand decides the unit name, which is what `k3s_unit` in the role's
defaults reconstructs:

```sh
if [ "${CMD_K3S}" = server ]; then SYSTEM_NAME=k3s
else SYSTEM_NAME=k3s-${CMD_K3S}; fi
```

So `server` → **`k3s.service`**, and anything else → `k3s-<subcommand>`, hence
**`k3s-agent.service`**. The unit the script writes sets:

- **`Type=notify`** — the unit template writes `Type=${SYSTEMD_TYPE}`, which
  defaults to `notify`, and we never set `INSTALL_K3S_TYPE`, so `notify` is
  what we actually get. systemd then holds the start transaction open until
  k3s signals readiness itself. The installer ends in `systemctl restart
  ${SYSTEM_NAME}`, so **the shell command does not return until k3s is
  actually serving.** That is what makes the **play split** in `site.yml`
  enough on its own: the agents' play cannot begin until the server's play has
  finished on every host in it, so by the time an agent runs, 6443 answers and
  the node-token exists. No `wait_for` needed — a rare case where the blocking
  behaviour of someone else's script is the feature.

  This does **not** rest on `serial:`, and it is worth saying because both an
  earlier draft of this page and the role's own comment credited `serial: 1`
  for it. The server's play has no `serial:` at all; `serial: 1` sits on the
  *agents'* play, for blast radius. The claim is a leftover from when one play
  over `nodes` carried the ordering — see the dispatch trap in
  [topic-ansible](topic-ansible.md). A retired mechanism keeps getting credit
  long after it is gone, because the sentence still reads true.
- **`TimeoutStartSec=0`** — no start timeout. The flip side of the above: a
  server that never becomes ready **hangs the apply instead of failing it**.
  The CI job's own timeout is the only backstop. Know this before you spend an
  hour watching a task that will never come back.
- `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=5s`, `KillMode=process`, `Delegate=yes` (cgroup
  management handed to k3s), and generous `LimitNOFILE`/`TasksMax`.

text:
### `get.k3s.io` does not read `config.yaml` — and the plan said it did

The design plan asserted that the install script reads
`/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml`, which made "write the config before
installing" sound like it was feeding the installer. It is not.

Fetch the script and count: **the string `config.yaml` does not occur in it at
all.** What occurs three times is the *directory* `/etc/rancher/k3s`, and all
three sit somewhere that never runs on our nodes — twice inside the OpenRC
branch (`elif [ "${HAS_OPENRC}" = true ]`, which is where the OpenRC
`FILE_K3S_ENV` lives) and once in the generated uninstall script
(`rm -rf /etc/rancher/k3s`).
On systemd the env file is `${SYSTEMD_DIR}/${SERVICE_K3S}.env` —
`/etc/systemd/system/k3s-agent.service.env`, mode 0600. On a systemd host the
script never reads anything under `/etc/rancher` at all; it only ever creates
that directory on OpenRC, and removes it on uninstall.

Config-before-install is still correct, but for a different reason, and the
difference is not academic. It is right because **the installer ends by
starting the unit, and the *daemon* reads `config.yaml` at startup.** A server
that comes up before the file exists comes up on vxlan with no secrets
encryption — and turning either on afterwards is a migration, not a restart.
The ordering requirement is real; the mechanism named in the plan was
invented.

The general lesson: a plausible mechanism, stated confidently, is the most
expensive kind of wrong, because it survives review — everyone nods at it,
and the code built on top happens to work for a reason nobody has written
down. Read the script. It is 1215 lines and `grep` answers in a second.

### Green while not a member

The role's first version gated the agent's join on `k3s --version` matching
the pin. That is a proxy question, and it comes apart from the real one on
ordinary paths: a server restored from a snapshot hands out a **new**
node-token, so the agent's token goes stale and it never rejoins; `kubectl
delete node <agent-name>` removes the membership; a CI job that times out
after the binary lands but before the join completes leaves exactly this
state.

In every one of those cases the binary *is* the pinned version. So the gate
was satisfied, the join was skipped, and **every apply reported green forever
while the cluster had one node in it.** Nothing was broken enough to notice
until you asked the cluster what was in it.

The gate now asks the real question — `k3s kubectl get node <name>`,
delegated to the server, and nothing short of a `Ready` status counts as
membership. `rc != 0` covers both "no such node" and "could not ask at all",
so it fails towards doing the work rather than towards a quiet green.

The lesson is the same one the phase A sshd incident taught and the same one
`scripts/bootstrap-if-needed.sh` is built on: **ask what you actually want to
know.** "Is the right binary installed" is easy to ask and is not the
question. "Is this node a working member of the cluster" is the question, and
only the server can answer it. Practice:
[`dec-2026-07-15-issues-become-guarded-automation`](../decisions/dec-2026-07-15-issues-become-guarded-automation.md).

### Green while not running

The role declared no `state: started` and no `enabled: true` anywhere. An
installed-but-stopped k3s therefore produced a **fully green apply with no
control plane** — and no layer in the role could catch it:

- The drift-heal **structurally cannot**: a dead unit reports `MainPID` 0, so
  the `/proc/<pid>` stat is guarded off, so the restart it guards is skipped
  with it. It compares the daemon's start time to the config's mtime; a
  daemon that does not exist has no start time to be stale.
- Re-running the installer does not heal it either. `get.k3s.io` takes
  `sha256sum` of the binary, the unit file and the env file before and after
  its work, and if they match:

  ```sh
  info 'No change detected so skipping service start'
  return
  ```

  It returns **without starting anything**. On an unchanged node the installer
  is a no-op, including the part you were counting on. (Read the order
  carefully: `systemd_enable` runs *before* this early return, so a re-run
  does re-enable the unit — it just never starts it. Enabled and stopped is
  precisely the shape of this bug.)
- And on a steady-state apply the installer does not run at all: the version
  gate skips it. So there was no layer left.

So the end state is now stated outright, with `systemd_service: state: started,
enabled: true`. It sits last in the file so it cannot run in place of a failed
installer and dress the failure up as success.

To be accurate about what `enabled: true` adds: the installer already enables
the unit on any run that installs, so this is not what stands between us and a
dead reboot on a fresh node. It is convergence — it heals a unit somebody
disabled by hand, on the runs where the installer never executes. Declaring
the end state costs one task and stops depending on a side effect of someone
else's script.

Generalised: **"installed" is not a state anyone wants.** Every layer in the
role reasoned about a *running* daemon, so nothing owned the question of
whether it was running at all. Absent state is invisible to checks that
inspect state.

### Green while the objects do not exist

A new one, and a fair warning rather than an incident — the viewer manifest
has not been applied yet as this is written.

The manifests directory has a property the rest of this role does not: **it is
asynchronous.** Every other task here converges before Ansible moves on — the
installer blocks on `Type=notify`, the drift heal restarts and waits. The
manifest copy does not converge at all. It writes bytes to disk and returns.
The deploy controller picks them up on *its* clock, up to 15 seconds later,
long after the play has printed its recap and CI has gone green.

So `changed=1` on that task means "the file is on disk". It does not mean the
ServiceAccount exists. And if the controller rejects the manifest, it logs the
error, retries in 15 seconds, and fails again forever — while the apply that
placed it stays green, permanently. There is no arrangement of Ansible tasks
that closes this: the question "does the viewer exist" can only be answered by
the API server, after the fact.

Which is the same sentence as the sshd incident, the membership gate and the
`state: started` gap above, arriving from a fourth direction: **writing the
config is not the daemon reading it.** The gap here is not a bug to fix but a
property to check — `scripts/verify-platform.sh` (a later task) has to ask the
cluster whether the viewer can actually list pods, from outside, the way
`verify-hardening.sh` asks sshd whether it really refuses root. Until that
exists, the viewer RBAC is **delivered but unverified**, and should be read
that way rather than trusted because the pipeline was green.

One consolation, and it is a genuine argument for minting over storing: with
the token minted on demand, **the first use is itself the check.**
`viewer-kubeconfig.sh` asks the API server for a token for a named
ServiceAccount in a named namespace, so a manifest that never applied makes it
fail loudly and immediately — `serviceaccounts "viewer" not found` — rather
than hand back a working kubeconfig. A pre-populated Secret would have had to
exist for that to happen at all, so the "did it apply?" question would have
gone unasked until someone needed it. This does not close the gap
(`verify-platform.sh` still has to ask on a schedule rather than when a human
happens to want a kubeconfig), but the failure surfaces at the moment someone
cares, pointed at the right thing.

If you are debugging it before then: `kubectl -n kube-system get addon` and
`kubectl -n kube-system describe addon viewer-rbac`. The answer is on the
cluster, not in the job log.

### The supply chain, stated honestly

This role pipes `https://get.k3s.io` into a **root shell**. We trust Rancher's
host and its TLS certificate for the contents of that shell, on every run that
installs.

The script does verify the binary: it downloads `sha256sum-${ARCH}.txt`,
greps the expected hash, and `fatal`s on a mismatch (`verify_binary`). Read
where both come from, though — `BIN_URL` and `HASH_URL` are both built from
`INSTALL_K3S_ARTIFACT_URL`, defaulting to
`https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/releases/download`. **The binary and the
checksum that vouches for it share an origin.** That catches a corrupted
download; it cannot catch a compromised release. A checksum is only a
signature when the key is yours.

`INSTALL_K3S_VERSION` pins the payload, which is the part we do control: the
script cannot hand us whatever `stable` means this week. What it buys is the
part we would otherwise hand-roll and get wrong — the unit, the env file, the
uninstall and killall scripts.

Mirroring the artifacts ourselves and verifying signatures against a key we
hold is the right answer above two nodes. **It is a named gap, not done.**
Named, because a gap nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a gap nobody
noticed.

### Only one control-plane node

There is one server, and the role asserts exactly that. Note what the assert
is actually for, though — it is not an HA statement. `k3s_server_host` is
`k3s_server_hosts | first`, so an inventory naming two servers would produce
no error at all: the agents would simply join whichever host came first in the
group — `first` takes group/inventory order, not sort order — and an empty
list would fail with an error naming the *filter* rather than the inventory
that caused it. The assert turns both into a sentence about the inventory.

So: if the server is down, workloads on the agent keep running (the kubelet
does not need the API server to keep containers alive), but there is **no
control plane** — nothing schedules, nothing heals, `kubectl` answers nothing,
and a pod that dies stays dead. The server is also the ingress node the public
A-records point at, so in practice the server being down is the lab being
down.

Real HA is not a small step from here. It needs **three or more servers**: k3s'
embedded etcd needs quorum, and "for a cluster with n servers, quorum is
(n/2)+1" — two servers have a quorum of two, so either one failing takes the
cluster down. That is *worse* than one server, not better; an even-sized etcd
cluster buys nothing. It would also mean moving off SQLite onto embedded etcd,
which is a datastore migration.

This is a **known gap, not an accident**: the spec names it in §7 under
"Restrisico's, benoemd" — *één control-plane-node (§3)* — as one of the risks
accepted on purpose. Two nodes is the budget. The point of writing it here is
that a risk you accepted and a risk you forgot look identical at 03:00; only
one of them has a page explaining what it costs.

heading_path: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana as one chart
What it is
text:
kube-prometheus-stack is a Helm chart from the `prometheus-community` project
that installs a whole monitoring stack as one release: the Prometheus Operator
and a Prometheus instance, Alertmanager, Grafana, node-exporter (a DaemonSet of
host-metric exporters) and kube-state-metrics (an exporter of Kubernetes object
state), plus a set of default recording/alerting rules and Grafana dashboards.
The operator turns monitoring into Kubernetes objects — `Prometheus`,
`Alertmanager`, `ServiceMonitor`, `PodMonitor`, `PrometheusRule` — so what gets
scraped and what fires is declared, not hand-configured.

heading_path: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana as one chart
Why we use it
text:
Plan C introduces observability. One chart gives the metrics half of it
(collection, storage, dashboards, and the alerting *plumbing*) with a single
pinned version and one Argo CD `Application`, instead of wiring Prometheus,
Alertmanager, Grafana and the two exporters together by hand. It fits the
GitOps rule — the `Application` and its values live under `gitops/`, Argo CD
syncs them (see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)).

heading_path: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana as one chart
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml` | The Argo CD `Application` that installs the chart (sync-wave `"0"`) |
| `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml` | Holds `grafana_admin_password` (SOPS-encrypted) among the other secrets |
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/templates/grafana-admin-secret.yaml.j2` | Renders the `grafana-admin` Secret onto the node |

The chart is installed **by Argo CD** (its `Application` points at
`https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts`); only Grafana's admin
Secret arrives via Ansible — see the secret route below.

text:
This is written in the build phase: the stack is committed but has not been
synced against the cluster yet. Every claim below about what a value *does*
comes from the chart's `values.yaml` at the pinned version (read 2026-07-17),

heading_path: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana as one chart
Flags & settings we use
text:
### `Application` — installing the chart

#### `source.chart` = `kube-prometheus-stack`, `targetRevision` = `87.16.1`

Version-pinned like everything in these repos: a floating chart changes the
platform without a commit. 87.16.1 was the current release, **verified served by
the repo** — its entry is in `prometheus-community`'s `index.yaml`, with the
release-download `urls`, checked on `last_verified` rather than remembered. Its
`appVersion` is `v0.92.1` (the Prometheus Operator version the chart carries).

#### `syncPolicy.syncOptions` = `CreateNamespace=true`, `ServerSideApply=true`

`ServerSideApply=true` is not optional for this chart. Its CRDs (for example
`prometheuses.monitoring.coreos.com`) are large; under Argo CD's default
client-side apply, kubectl stores the whole object in the
`kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation, which pushes the
CRD past Kubernetes' 262144-byte annotation limit and the sync fails with
`metadata.annotations: Too long: must have at most 262144 bytes`. Server-side
apply writes no such annotation and sidesteps it (Argo CD ≥ 2.5). This is a
well-documented kube-prometheus-stack + Argo CD footgun, not a guess.

#### `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` = `"0"`

One wave after cert-manager (`"-1"`), so the ordering has room for a future
dependency (a `ServiceMonitor` over TLS, say) without a reshuffle. Waves order
resources within the root-app's sync — see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md).

### Prometheus

#### `prometheus.prometheusSpec.retention` = `7d`

The chart default is `10d`. 7 days is a privacy choice (less data retained) and
a disk choice: Prometheus runs on the pod's `emptyDir` in this phase (no PVC),
so its history has to stay bounded on an 8 GB node. Backing up longer history is
a later plan-C task, not this one.

#### `prometheus.prometheusSpec.serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues` = `false`

The chart default is `true`, which builds Prometheus' `serviceMonitorSelector`
from this Helm release's own label — so only the chart's own `ServiceMonitor`s
are scraped. Setting it `false` makes a nil selector match **every**
`ServiceMonitor` in the cluster, so monitors that later apps ship (plan C C3/C4)
are picked up without editing this file again. Sourced: the field's comment in
`values.yaml` at 87.16.1.

#### `resources` limits on every component

Prometheus (limit 1Gi), Grafana (256Mi), Alertmanager (128Mi), node-exporter
(64Mi), kube-state-metrics (128Mi). Memory limits only — a CPU limit throttles
rather than protects — with CPU as a request so the scheduler still reserves
headroom. These numbers are ours (8 GB two-node footprint discipline), not
upstream defaults, the same posture as [topic-cert-manager](topic-cert-manager.md).

**Option space — smaller/larger profiles.** These values are *lower bounds that
protect an 8 GB node*: on a smaller node the stack would not fit at all, and on
a larger node (16/32 GB) they are cramped — Prometheus would still be capped at
1Gi with tens of GB free, so the node is bigger but the stack does not run
roomier. They are correct for their context and wrong outside it, which is why
raising each number by hand is the wrong answer and a node-size-aware
**resource profile** (a limit-set per node-size class, small/medium/large) is
the designed one — see the scaling design
(`soevereinlab-marketplace/docs/plans/2026-07-17-scaling-design.md`, §4.1–4.3).
That these are observed bounds and not guesses is shown by the sibling Argo
application-controller pin, which was bumped 512Mi→1Gi only after an observed
`OOMKilled` crashloop at 6 managed apps (scaling design §4.1). The decision that
records the pin posture is
[dec-2026-07-17-two-node-topology-resource-pins](../decisions/dec-2026-07-17-two-node-topology-resource-pins.md).

### Grafana

#### `grafana.ingress.enabled` = `false`

No ingress and no SSO: Grafana's UI is reached with `kubectl port-forward` over
SSH, the same posture as Argo CD's own server. Keeping the observability UI
non-public in this phase is a deliberate choice (publishing it with auth is a
later, separate decision) — recorded in Plan C and in Plan B's mandate note.

#### `grafana.admin.existingSecret` = `grafana-admin`

Grafana reads its admin credentials from an existing `Secret` rather than an
inline `adminPassword` that would sit in git in plaintext. `userKey` and
`passwordKey` are left at the chart defaults `admin-user` / `admin-password`,
which the rendered Secret matches. How that Secret gets onto the node is the
secret route below.

#### `grafana.defaultDashboardsEnabled` = `true`

Left on (the chart default), pinned explicitly because the cluster-overview
dashboard is a plan-C requirement and should not depend on a default not
flipping in a future chart bump.

### Alertmanager

`alertmanager.enabled` = `true` with a resource limit. The component comes up
with the stack's defaults; the actual alert **routing rules** and receiver are
plan C C3, not this task — so it runs but routes nowhere useful yet.

### node-exporter and kube-state-metrics

Both stay enabled (chart defaults). Their resource limits are set through the
subchart passthrough keys `prometheus-node-exporter.resources` and
`kube-state-metrics.resources` — each subchart exposes a top-level `resources`
key (verified in the subchart `values.yaml` at the versions this chart pins:
prometheus-node-exporter 4.56.1, kube-state-metrics 7.8.1).

heading_path: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana as one chart
The Grafana admin secret route
text:
Grafana's password is not in the `valuesObject`. It is stored SOPS-encrypted as
`grafana_admin_password` in `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml`, decrypted on the
controller by the `gitops_bootstrap` role (`community.sops.load_vars`,
`no_log: true`), and templated onto the node as the `grafana-admin` `Secret` in
namespace `monitoring`. The `Application`'s `existingSecret` then consumes it.

Why Ansible-out-of-SOPS rather than an in-cluster secrets operator (KSOPS,
external-secrets) is a recorded decision:
[dec-2026-07-17-app-secrets-ansible-sops](../decisions/dec-2026-07-17-app-secrets-ansible-sops.md).

heading_path: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana as one chart
Pitfalls
text:
### The CRDs overflow the annotation limit without server-side apply

Covered above under `syncOptions`: without `ServerSideApply=true` the first sync
fails on `metadata.annotations: Too long`. It is the single most common failure
when this chart meets Argo CD, so it is called out twice on purpose.

### The `grafana-admin` Secret's namespace does not exist at first write

The Secret targets namespace `monitoring`, which the monitoring `Application`
(`CreateNamespace=true`) creates. When Ansible writes the Secret manifest to the
node, the namespace may not exist yet; k3s' deploy controller retries the
manifest on its own poll until it does — the same reconcile-retry the Argo CD
bootstrap manifests rely on.
