heading_path: kubectl — the read-only routes this programme uses against the cluster
What it is
text:
`kubectl` is the Kubernetes command-line client — it turns commands into calls
against the API server. We do not install it separately: the k3s binary embeds
it, so on a node the command is **`k3s kubectl`** (or `sudo k3s kubectl`),
reading the node's own kubeconfig. There is no standalone `kubectl` package on
these nodes and no admin kubeconfig lying around off them (see
[topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md), `write-kubeconfig-mode`).

The point of this topic is narrow on purpose: not "everything kubectl can do",
but **the specific, read-only routes this programme actually uses**, and the
boundary that keeps them read-only.

heading_path: kubectl — the read-only routes this programme uses against the cluster
Why we use it (this way)
text:
The platform's discipline is that the cluster contains only what git declares,
and mutations flow through Argo CD from a commit — not from someone's shell
(see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)). That leaves `kubectl` two honest jobs
here: **looking** (has this actually synced? is that pod really running? what
does the API say?) and, for a human operator with direct consent, applying a
deliberate change. Day-to-day, agents use it to *observe*, because "green is not
the same as running" and only the cluster can answer whether something works.

heading_path: kubectl — the read-only routes this programme uses against the cluster
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ansible/roles/k3s/files/viewer-rbac.yaml` | The read-only identity: a namespace, a `viewer` ServiceAccount, a ClusterRoleBinding to the built-in `view` role |
| `scripts/viewer-kubeconfig.sh` | Mints a short-lived token for `viewer` and writes a kubeconfig (the token is not in git, not in the cluster) |

The copy-paste command forms live in the command cookbook
(`reference/command-cookbook.md`), recipes **14** (service proxy) and the SSH
tunnel in [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md).

heading_path: kubectl — the read-only routes this programme uses against the cluster
Flags & settings we use
text:
### The three read-only routes

**1. The viewer kubeconfig (`kubectl get` / `describe`, bound `view`).** The
default entry for looking at namespaced objects. It carries a token minted on
demand by `viewer-kubeconfig.sh` for the `viewer` ServiceAccount, bound to
Kubernetes' built-in **`view`** ClusterRole. `view` grants read on most
namespaced objects and pointedly **not** on Secrets (reading Secrets in a
namespace means reading ServiceAccount tokens — privilege escalation), nor on
cluster-scoped objects like `nodes`. All of this — why `view`, why minted not
stored, why a ClusterRoleBinding — is documented in
[topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md#the-viewer-serviceaccount-and-how-it-gets-a-token);
this topic just names it as route 1.

**2. `kubectl get --raw` and the API service proxy.** For reading an in-cluster
HTTP service without a port-forward, an ingress, or session state — one GET
through the API server (cookbook recipe 14):

```bash
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/services/http:<svc>:<port>/proxy/<path>"
```

Proven in use for Grafana `/api/health`, Prometheus
`/api/v1/targets|query|alerts|rules`, Alertmanager `/api/v2/status|alerts`, and
Loki `/loki/api/v1/query_range` (verified 2026-07-17, Plan C, tens of calls).
This is how `verify:observability` checks components *through* the k3s API proxy
over one SSH connection, instead of opening a port per service. `--raw` takes a
literal API path and prints the raw response, which is what makes the proxy
subresource reachable from a script.

**3. The SSH tunnel is a precondition, not a route.** Port 6443 is open to the
peer node only (see [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md), [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)),
so any `kubectl` from the workstation runs through
`ssh -N -L 6443:127.0.0.1:6443 deploy@<server-ip>` first, against a kubeconfig
pointing at `127.0.0.1:6443`. Being at an SSH prompt is therefore already the
cost of looking at the cluster — which is also why minting a fresh short-lived
token each time costs nothing (the argument is worked through in
[topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md)).

### The RBAC boundary: viewer vs admin

The read-only route is a real boundary, not a convention, and it has already
been hit. **`view` cannot create CRDs or ClusterRoles and cannot list
cluster-scoped `nodes`** — so a tool that needs to *write* cluster-scoped
objects fails on the viewer route. Observed verbatim running the Haven
compliancy checker on the viewer identity
([topic-haven-compliancy-checker](topic-haven-compliancy-checker.md)):

```
clusterroles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io is forbidden: User
"system:serviceaccount:...:viewer" cannot create resource "clusterroles" ...
at the cluster scope
```

That is the boundary doing its job: a checker that must deploy a CRD needs a
**cluster-admin** kubeconfig (or a temporary binding torn down after), which is
an operator decision reached over the same SSH tunnel — not something the
viewer route grants and not something a subagent can be handed.

### Mutations are operator work — the consent principle

`kubectl apply`, `edit`, `delete`, `create` against this cluster are **not**
agent operations. Two reasons, both structural:

- **They fight Argo CD.** `kubectl edit` on anything under `gitops/` is
  reverted on the next sync (`selfHeal`), and deleting an object it manages is
  undone; the durable way to change managed state is a commit
  (see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)). A `kubectl` mutation of managed
  state is at best temporary and at worst drift the platform will fight.
- **Consent does not travel.** Per the programme's execution harness, a
  cluster mutation requires consent in the executing session; a mandate quoted
  into a subagent's prompt never counts. So direct cluster changes are the
  operator's (or the orchestrator's, in-session with a direct mandate), with
  pre-state captured and reversal logged — never delegated.

The net rule: agents reach for `kubectl` to **read**. Writing is a human at a
prompt who owns the consequence.

heading_path: kubectl — the read-only routes this programme uses against the cluster
Alternatives (why CLI + read-only)
text:
Brief, per the convention's "why ours":

- **k9s** — "a terminal based UI to interact with your Kubernetes clusters"
  (k9scli.io). A live, navigable TUI over the same kubeconfig. Pleasant for
  browsing, but it is an interactive terminal app: it does not fit a scripted
  verify step, and its convenience is in fast *navigation*, which an agent
  driving one exact query does not need.
- **Lens** — a desktop application "that provides a graphical interface for
  managing Kubernetes clusters" (docs.k8slens.dev). A GUI on the workstation;
  it would still need the SSH tunnel and a kubeconfig, and it invites
  point-and-click mutation, which is the opposite of "changes are commits".
- **The Argo CD UI** — the in-cluster web UI for sync state. We run it without
  ingress and reach it by `kubectl port-forward` when needed
  (see [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md)); it shows *Argo's* view of sync
  health, not arbitrary cluster reads.

Why ours: a plain `kubectl` command is scriptable (it *is* how the `verify:*`
jobs read the cluster), leaves no interactive surface that quietly mutates, and
composes with the SSH tunnel and the minted viewer token we already require.
The other tools are strictly nicer for a human browsing — and none of them
changes what the RBAC boundary allows.

heading_path: kubectl — the read-only routes this programme uses against the cluster
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### Read-only means it cannot score, not that it is safe to run blind

Running a *write*-needing tool on the viewer route mutates nothing (every write
is RBAC-rejected) but also cannot complete — and the Haven checker exited `0`
despite a fatal `[F]` line. Trust the tool's own error output, not the exit
code, and do not read "it ran read-only" as "it succeeded". See
[topic-haven-compliancy-checker](topic-haven-compliancy-checker.md).

### `view` cannot see Secrets — that is correct, do not "fix" it

The recurring temptation when a read fails on a Secret is to bind the viewer to
a wider role. Don't: a viewer that could read Secrets could read every
ServiceAccount token in the cluster and stop being a viewer. The exclusion is
the design. [topic-k3s](topic-k3s.md) works through why at length.

heading_path: Kustomize — rendering manifests, and the generated-name hash that makes a config change reach a running pod
What it is
text:
Kustomize renders a directory of Kubernetes manifests into the YAML that is
actually applied. It is not a templating language: it reads plain, valid
manifests and applies declared transformations to them — set a namespace on
everything, add labels, patch a field, or *generate* a ConfigMap or Secret from
files. It ships inside `kubectl` (`kubectl kustomize <dir>`, and
`kubectl apply -k`), so there is usually nothing to install.

The piece we care about most is **`configMapGenerator`**. Instead of writing a
ConfigMap by hand, you point it at a file; Kustomize builds the ConfigMap, hashes
its content, and appends that hash to the object's name
(`ntfy-config` → `ntfy-config-fbbf9224fh`). It then rewrites every reference to
that ConfigMap elsewhere in the same build — a Deployment's `volumes` entry, an
`envFrom`, a `valueFrom` — so the manifests stay internally consistent.

heading_path: Kustomize — rendering manifests, and the generated-name hash that makes a config change reach a running pod
Why we use it
text:
Because of a defect class that has cost us three incidents in one month:
**written is not the same as re-read.** A ConfigMap or Secret can change in git,
Argo CD can apply it, every dashboard can go green — and the process that
consumes it never notices, because it read that value once at startup. Nothing is
out of sync. Nothing is unhealthy. The workload is simply running old data.

The generated-name hash converts a *data* change into a *pod template* change:
new content → new ConfigMap name → different pod template → Kubernetes rolls the
pod → the new container reads the new data. It is the same trick as a checksum
annotation, with one decisive difference: **it cannot be forgotten.** A
hand-maintained `checksum:` annotation works exactly as long as every future
author remembers to update it, and this whole class of incident is about
mechanisms that quietly stopped being true.

There is a second reason it is Kustomize specifically and not an Ansible-side
checksum: this ConfigMap comes from **git, via Argo CD**, not from a playbook run
on the node. A checksum computed during `apply` never reaches it. Kustomize
computes the hash where the content actually lives.

heading_path: Kustomize — rendering manifests, and the generated-name hash that makes a config change reach a running pod
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

- `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/kustomization.yaml` — the only kustomization in the
  platform (as of 2026-08-04). It generates `ntfy-config` from `server.yml`.
- `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/server.yml` — the generator's input; the ntfy
  server configuration as a real file rather than an indented YAML block.
- `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/deployment.yaml` — consumer. Its volume still names
  `ntfy-config`; Kustomize rewrites that to the generated name at render time.
- `gitops/apps/ntfy/app.yaml` — the Argo CD `Application`. It names **no**
  Kustomize options at all: it points `path:` at the directory, and Argo detects
  the `kustomization.yaml` and switches its source type by itself.

Rendering happens in two places, and they must agree: locally with
`kubectl kustomize gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests` (how a change is proven before it
is pushed), and in-cluster by Argo CD's repo-server.

heading_path: Kustomize — rendering manifests, and the generated-name hash that makes a config change reach a running pod
Flags & settings we use
text:
Everything set in `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/kustomization.yaml`, completely.

### `apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1` + `kind: Kustomization`

The only stable pairing for a kustomization file. `v1alpha1` exists for some
newer sub-features; we have no reason to leave the stable API.

### `namespace: ntfy`

Sets `metadata.namespace` on every rendered resource. Its real job here is the
**generated** ConfigMap: the deleted `configmap.yaml` carried its own namespace
field, and a generated object has no file of its own to carry one. The other
three resources still declare `namespace: ntfy` themselves; this field agrees
with them rather than replacing them. Leaving it out would render the ConfigMap
without a namespace, and Argo would place it in the `Application`'s destination
namespace — which happens to be the same, so it would work *by coincidence*.
Stating it removes the coincidence.

### `resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml, ingress.yaml]`

The plain manifests to include. This list is **exhaustive by design**: a file in
the directory that is not listed is silently not applied. That is the opposite of
the directory-source behaviour it replaced (where every YAML file was picked up),
and it is the single most likely way a future addition goes missing — add a
manifest, forget the list, and nothing anywhere goes red.

Note `server.yml` is deliberately *not* in `resources`. It is generator input,
not a manifest; listing it there would fail the build.

### `configMapGenerator[].name: ntfy-config` + `files: [server.yml]`

Generates a ConfigMap named `ntfy-config` with one key, `server.yml`, whose value
is that file's content. The key defaults to the filename; `files: [key=path]`
would rename it, which we do not need because the container mounts it as
`server.yml` anyway.

Alternatives we do not use: `literals:` (inline `key=value` pairs — fine for one
or two short values, hopeless for a 20-line config), and `envs:` (a
`KEY=VALUE`-per-line file rendered as *many* keys rather than one file-shaped
value — wrong shape for a config file that is mounted whole).

### `generatorOptions.labels: {app.kubernetes.io/name: ntfy}`

Labels added to generated objects only. Chosen key deliberately: Argo CD's
default resource tracking uses `app.kubernetes.io/instance`, so a *different* key
avoids any interaction with how Argo decides what it owns and what it may prune.

### `disableNameSuffixHash` — deliberately **absent**

This is the important non-setting, and the file carries a comment saying so.
Setting it to `true` keeps the name constant (`ntfy-config`), which means the pod
template does not change, which means the pod does not roll, which means the
running container keeps its old config — precisely the defect the generator was
introduced to fix. It looks like a tidiness flag ("stop the ugly suffix") and it
is actually the off-switch for the entire mechanism.

Legitimate uses exist — a ConfigMap referenced by name from outside the build, or
one consumed by something that cannot tolerate a changing name. Neither applies
here. If a future object *must* have a stable name, the honest route is to write
it as a plain manifest and accept that it will not roll anything, not to disable
the hash on a generator.

heading_path: Kustomize — rendering manifests, and the generated-name hash that makes a config change reach a running pod
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### The three-strike class: written ≠ re-read

Within a single month, the same failure mode surfaced three times in this
platform, each needing a different fix because the data arrived by a different
road:

1. **A Secret consumed with `envFrom`.** Kubernetes resolves environment
   variables exactly once, when kubelet starts the container. A rewritten Secret
   reaches nothing already running. Observed: a pod 6d9h old with 0 restarts
   while its Secret had changed twice, so the phone was authenticating with a
   password that no longer existed. Fixed by stamping the Secret's data checksum
   onto the pod template during `apply` — the value is SOPS-encrypted and never
   enters git, so only the node can compute it.
2. **A ConfigMap consumed as a volume** (`ntfy-config`). ntfy reads `server.yml`
   once, at start. Same silence. Fixed with the `configMapGenerator` documented
   here, because this data *does* live in git and the checksum can be computed
   there.
3. **The class itself**, which is the actual lesson: *green* meant "the file was
   written", not "the process is using it". Every check that looks at
   declarations rather than at what a running container actually read will keep
   passing through this failure.

The generalisation worth carrying to the next workload: whenever a manifest hands
data to a process, ask **when that process reads it** — at start, on every
request, or on a watch. If the answer is "at start", something must change the
pod template when the data changes, or the change does not land.

### A `subPath` mount never refreshes at all

kubelet keeps ordinary ConfigMap volume mounts up to date, which is why "the pod
is older than the file" proves nothing on its own. That does **not** hold for a
mount with `subPath:` — documented Kubernetes behaviour is that a container using
a ConfigMap as a `subPath` volume mount does not receive updates at all. Our ntfy
Deployment mounts `server.yml` with `subPath`, so both mechanisms were failing at
once: the file in the container never changed, *and* ntfy would not have re-read
it if it had. Worth knowing before relying on "kubelet will refresh it" for any
other workload.

### The source type flips silently

An Argo CD `Application` whose `path:` points at a plain directory renders every
manifest it finds. The moment a `kustomization.yaml` appears in that directory,
Argo treats it as a Kustomize source instead — no field changes in the
`Application`, no announcement. That is a behaviour change of the workload
delivered by adding one file, so it deserves its own change window rather than
riding along with something else. Ours shipped as a standalone merge request for
exactly this reason.

### Prove the reference rewrite; do not assume it

The rewrite is the step that fails quietly: if it did not happen, the Deployment
would reference a ConfigMap name that no longer exists and the pod would fail to
mount — but you would only discover that on the cluster. Render locally, twice,
with a changed input in between, and check three things:

```
kubectl kustomize gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests
```

- (a) the generated ConfigMap's name carries a hash suffix;
- (b) editing the input file moves that suffix, and restoring the file brings the
  original suffix back (so the name is a function of content, not of build order
  or time);
- (c) the rendered Deployment's `volumes` entry carries **that same generated
  name**, even though the file on disk still says the bare name.

### The hashes do agree between workstation and cluster

A reasonable worry is that the workstation's Kustomize and Argo CD's bundled one
compute different suffixes, making local rendering useless as proof. Observed
2026-08-04: the local build (`kubectl kustomize`, Kustomize v5.5.0) and the
object Argo CD created on the cluster carried the **identical** suffix. Local
rendering is therefore evidence about the cluster, not merely about the laptop.
Worth re-checking after a major Kustomize or Argo CD bump, since this is an
observation, not a guarantee.

### A generator sync rewrites the pod template — check what else lives there

Switching a workload to a generator changes its pod template, which means Argo CD
re-applies the whole Deployment. If any field on that pod template is owned by
something *other* than git, this is exactly the moment it can be silently wiped.

Ours has one: `soevereinlab.nl/checksum.secret.ntfy-auth`, written onto the ntfy
pod template by Ansible during `apply`, because the Secret it hashes is
SOPS-encrypted and never enters git. The `Application` protects it with
`ignoreDifferences` on that one JSON pointer plus
`syncOptions: [RespectIgnoreDifferences=true]` — the second one existing
precisely so that "a sync triggered by any *other* change" cannot strip it while
re-applying.

Until this change, that protection had never been exercised by a sync that
actually rewrote the pod template. Verified on 2026-08-04, after the generator
landed: both the Deployment's pod template and the newly rolled pod still carried
the annotation. Had it been stripped, the workload would have quietly returned to
the "a rewritten Secret reaches nothing already running" behaviour, and only
`verify:config-freshness` would eventually have said so.

Worth repeating as a habit: after any change that rewrites a pod template, list
that template's annotations and confirm the externally-owned ones are still
there. It costs one `kubectl get ... -o jsonpath` and it checks a protection that
is otherwise only theoretical.

### Prune removes the old, suffix-less object — if prune is on

Switching to a generator leaves the previous hand-written ConfigMap (`ntfy-config`
with no suffix) orphaned on the cluster. With `syncPolicy.automated.prune: true`
on the `Application`, Argo removes it on the sync that applies the change;
observed on 2026-08-04, `ntfy-config` was gone and no manual cleanup was needed.
Without `prune`, it lingers forever — harmless but confusing, and it will
outlive everyone's memory of why there are two.

### What a clean roll looks like

For the record, so a future sync can be compared against it. Merge at
`20:49:17Z`; the generated ConfigMap appeared at `20:49:23Z`, the new ReplicaSet
at `20:49:23Z`, the new pod at `20:49:24Z`, its container running at `20:49:25Z`
with 0 restarts. Total: seven seconds from merge to a pod reading the new config.

heading_path: Loki + Alloy — log aggregation for the mini-cloud
What it is
text:
**Loki** is Grafana's log store: it indexes only labels (not full text), which
keeps it cheap, and stores the log lines as compressed chunks. **Alloy** is
Grafana's collector (the successor to Promtail, which Grafana Labs deprecated in
favour of Alloy and which reached end-of-life on 2 March 2026 — source: the
official [Promtail agent](https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/send-data/promtail/)
page in the Grafana Loki docs): it discovers pods, reads their logs, and pushes
them to Loki.
Together they are the logging half of plan C observability — the metrics half
is [kube-prometheus-stack](topic-kube-prometheus-stack.md). Logs are queried
from the **same Grafana** as the metrics, via a Loki datasource.

heading_path: Loki + Alloy — log aggregation for the mini-cloud
Why we use it
text:
Loki + Alloy is the logging half of the observability stack; the choice (and the
alternatives VictoriaLogs / an ELK stack / a hosted service) is recorded in
[dec-2026-07-17-observability-prometheus-loki](../decisions/dec-2026-07-17-observability-prometheus-loki.md).
In short: label-indexed logs are cheap enough to run on 8 GB nodes with 7-day
retention, and sharing one Grafana with the metrics keeps the operator's mental
model small.

heading_path: Loki + Alloy — log aggregation for the mini-cloud
Why two charts / two Applications
text:
Loki and Alloy are two distinct Helm charts. An Argo CD `Application` points at
exactly one chart, so this is **two Applications** (`loki`, `alloy`) under
`gitops/platform/logging/`, not one. That is the natural structure, not a
workaround: they version, sync and roll back independently. Loki is sync-wave
`0`, Alloy `1`, so Loki's push endpoint is up first — soft ordering, since
Alloy retries writes regardless.

heading_path: Loki + Alloy — log aggregation for the mini-cloud
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gitops/platform/logging/loki-app.yaml` | Argo `Application` for the Loki chart |
| `gitops/platform/logging/alloy-app.yaml` | Argo `Application` for the Alloy chart |
| `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml` | Grafana's `additionalDataSources` holds the Loki datasource |

heading_path: Loki + Alloy — log aggregation for the mini-cloud
Flags & settings we use
text:
The values we set on the two charts, grouped by component (Loki, Alloy, and the
Grafana datasource that joins them).

### Loki: the single-binary, storage-light shape

The chart default is `SimpleScalable` (a read/write/backend split, 3 replicas
each) — far too much for a 2-node 8 GB cluster. We run **single-binary**: one
process, `-target=all`. The values that matter and why:

| Value | Setting | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `deploymentMode` | `SingleBinary` | one process runs all of Loki |
| `singleBinary.replicas` | `1` | **the chart does not set this from `deploymentMode`** — default is `0`, so you must set it or nothing runs |
| `fullnameOverride` | `loki` | deterministic Service name `loki` (used by the datasource and Alloy's write URL) instead of `loki-loki` |
| `loki.auth_enabled` | `false` | single-tenant; no `X-Scope-OrgID` header needed from Grafana or Alloy |
| `loki.commonConfig.replication_factor` | `1` | one replica cannot form the default quorum of 3 |
| `loki.schemaConfig` | TSDB, schema `v13`, `object_store: filesystem` | a real install must declare a schema (only test setups may skip it); v13 is the Loki 3.x default and is required for structured metadata |
| `loki.storage.type` | `filesystem` | no S3/MinIO in this phase |
| `loki.limits_config.retention_period` | `168h` | ~7 days (plan C spec); merges over the chart's other limits defaults |
| `loki.compactor` | `retention_enabled: true`, `delete_request_store: filesystem` | retention only actually deletes when the compactor runs it |
| `singleBinary.persistence.enabled` | `false` | no CSI/StorageClass this phase (same as Prometheus) — a PVC would stay `Pending`. But **this alone leaves the pod with no volume on `/var/loki`** — see the storage note below |
| `singleBinary.extraVolumes` / `extraVolumeMounts` | `emptyDir` at `/var/loki` | the chart provides **no** emptyDir fallback when persistence is off; without this the pod crashloops `mkdir /var/loki: read-only file system` |
| `chunksCache` / `resultsCache` | `enabled: false` | the memcached caches are the biggest footprint: `chunksCache` requests **8Gi**, `resultsCache` **1Gi** by default |
| `gateway` | `enabled: false` | no nginx front — Grafana/Alloy reach `loki:3100` directly |
| `lokiCanary` / `test` | `enabled: false` | a synthetic log-loss DaemonSet and CI scaffolding, not worth the memory |

**Retention option space (`retention_period: 168h`):** 168h is ~7 days, the
plan C target (spec §6). A shorter value (say `72h`) keeps less history and less
disk; a longer one (say `720h` ≈ 30 days) needs proportionally more filesystem
space — and that trade is sharp *because* `loki.storage.type` is `filesystem` on
the pod's `emptyDir` this phase: retention is bounded by the node's disk and the
logs are lost on a pod reschedule anyway (see the storage note below). Moving
storage to an S3/MinIO object store would decouple retention from node disk and
make long retention cheap, but the provider offers no S3-compatible object
storage this phase
([dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection](../decisions/dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection.md)),
so short, filesystem-bound retention is a deliberate interim, not a tuning knob.
Retention only actually *deletes* when the compactor runs it
(`compactor.retention_enabled: true`, in the table above).

**Storage — an explicit `emptyDir`, not a chart default:** `persistence.enabled:
false` alone does **not** hand Loki a writable data dir — the earlier note here
that it "yields an emptyDir" was wrong and cost a crashloop. On chart tag
`helm-loki-7.1.0` the single-binary `templates/single-binary/statefulset.yaml`
gates **both** the `/var/loki` mount and the volumeClaimTemplate on
`singleBinary.persistence.enabled` and offers no emptyDir fallback; meanwhile the
default `containerSecurityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` makes the root FS
read-only and `commonConfig.path_prefix` is `/var/loki` — so with persistence off
the pod crashloops `mkdir /var/loki: read-only file system` (also failing
`ruler-storage` init). The fix is a writable **`emptyDir` at `/var/loki`** mounted
via the chart's own `singleBinary.extraVolumes` + `extraVolumeMounts`; one volume
covers chunks/rules/compactor/ruler-wal (all under `path_prefix`). **Trade-off:**
logs are still lost if the Loki pod is rescheduled — an intentional interim state.
A persistent storage layer is a later phase; it is added then, rather than
flipping `persistence.enabled` in isolation (which is what broke). **Hedge:** the
512Mi limit is conservative; Loki 3.x single-binary can want more under real log
volume — raise `singleBinary.resources.limits.memory` if it OOMs.

### Alloy: collect pod logs via the Kubernetes API

Alloy runs as a **DaemonSet** (`controller.type: daemonset`) — one collector
per node so it sees every node's pods. The config (River) reads logs through
the **Kubernetes API** with `loki.source.kubernetes`, which needs **no host log
mount** (`mounts.varlog` stays `false`):

```river
discovery.kubernetes "pods" {
  role = "pod"
}

discovery.relabel "pod_logs" {
  targets = discovery.kubernetes.pods.targets
  rule { source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_namespace"];          target_label = "namespace" }
  rule { source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_name"];           target_label = "pod" }
  rule { source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_name"]; target_label = "container" }
  rule { source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app_kubernetes_io_name"]; target_label = "app" }
}

loki.source.kubernetes "pods" {
  targets    = discovery.relabel.pod_logs.output
  forward_to = [loki.write.default.receiver]
}

loki.write "default" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://loki.logging.svc.cluster.local:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
  }
}
```

Why the API method over the file method (`loki.source.file` on `/var/log/pods`):
no host mount, and no dependence on k3s' container-log paths — cleaner and more
portable for a small cluster. **Trade-off:** it streams each container's logs
through the API server; fine at this scale, reconsider if log volume grows.

Two things that keep it working:

- **RBAC is already covered.** The Alloy chart's default `rbac.rules` grant
  `pods`, `pods/log` and `namespaces` (the rules `discovery.kubernetes` and
  `loki.source.kubernetes` need). `rbac.create` defaults to `true`, so **no
  override is required**.
- **Stability level.** `loki.source.kubernetes` is a **generally-available**
  component, so it loads under the chart's default
  `stabilityLevel: generally-available`. A public-preview/experimental
  component would need `--stability.level` raised — not the case here.

### The Grafana datasource

Added via the kube-prometheus-stack values (not the Loki chart):

```yaml
grafana:
  additionalDataSources:
    - name: Loki
      type: loki
      access: proxy
      url: http://loki.logging.svc.cluster.local:3100
```

The URL is the single-binary Service (`fullnameOverride: loki`, gateway
disabled) on the HTTP port 3100. Single-tenant, so no header config.

heading_path: Loki + Alloy — log aggregation for the mini-cloud
Pitfalls
text:
- **`deploymentMode: SingleBinary` with `singleBinary.replicas: 0`** (the
  default) → nothing runs and it is not obvious why. Set replicas to 1.
- **A PVC with no StorageClass** → the Loki pod sits `Pending` forever. Disable
  persistence until a CSI exists.
- **Leaving the memcached caches on** → 9Gi of requests the 8 GB nodes cannot
  satisfy; pods `Pending`.
- **Pointing the datasource/Alloy at `loki-gateway`** → 503s, because the
  gateway is disabled. Use the `loki` Service directly.
- **Version drift on the chart lineage:** the OSS Loki chart is moving toward
  `grafana-community/helm-charts`; chart 7.1.0 is still served from
  `https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts` (index.yaml, verified 2026-07-17).
  Re-check the repo when bumping the pin.

heading_path: NFS — the cluster's PersistentVolume layer (single-server export)
text:
> **Build phase.** This topic documents the storage layer as it is **declared
> in the repos** (the `nfs` role, the `nfs-storage` Argo Application,
> `verify-storage.sh`). At the time of writing it has not yet been applied to a
> node or bound a live PVC — nothing below is a cluster observation. The green
> path (a PVC actually binding) is proven only by the first `verify:storage`
> run after merge + apply, which is a Jelle/orchestrator gate.

heading_path: NFS — the cluster's PersistentVolume layer (single-server export)
What it is
text:
NFS (Network File System) lets a server export a directory over the network so
that other hosts mount it as if it were local. In this platform it is the
**PersistentVolume layer**: one NFS server on the k3s server node (vps1) exports
a single directory, and an in-cluster provisioner
(`nfs-subdir-external-provisioner`) hands each PersistentVolumeClaim its own
subdirectory under that export. Until this layer existed the cluster had no
persistent storage at all — k3s' local-path provisioner was the only class and
observability ran on `emptyDir` (spec §4).

The mount protocol is **NFSv4-only**. NFSv4 carries everything (mount,
lock, the file traffic itself) over a single TCP port, 2049, so there is no
portmapper (111) / `mountd` / `statd` port dance and the firewall stays one peer
rule. The client half (`nfs-common`) is installed on every node by the
`baseline` role; the server half (`nfs-kernel-server`) runs on vps1 only. With
the export granting **every** node IP — the server node's own address included
(see the client-list note below) — any node's kubelet, vps1's own included, can
mount an `nfs-client` PV.

heading_path: NFS — the cluster's PersistentVolume layer (single-server export)
Why we use it
text:
Of the three storage candidates weighed in the scaling design (§3.3 — Longhorn,
NFS, provider block-storage), NFS is the lowest-cost way to get a working PV
layer onto two 8 GB nodes: a single provisioner pod (64–128Mi) instead of
Longhorn's per-node manager/engine replicas, and no coupling to a specific
infra provider's CSI. The trade — the NFS server is a single point of failure
and there is no replication — is accepted deliberately and recorded, with the
ideal end-state and the migration path, in
[dec-2026-07-20-storage-nfs](../decisions/dec-2026-07-20-storage-nfs.md).

heading_path: NFS — the cluster's PersistentVolume layer (single-server export)
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

- **Server role:** `ansible/roles/nfs/` — `tasks/main.yml` installs
  `nfs-kernel-server`, forces NFSv4-only via `/etc/nfs.conf`, creates the export
  root, and writes the export drop-in; `defaults/main.yml` holds the client-list
  derivation and the export options; `templates/k8s-pv.exports.j2` renders one
  export line per allowed client; `handlers/main.yml` re-exports on change. It
  runs in its own server-scoped play in `site.yml`, not folded into `baseline`,
  because the daemon and export belong on the server node only.
- **Export path:** `nfs_export_path` (`/srv/nfs/k8s`) lives in
  `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml`, not in a role default — because two roles must
  agree on it: `nfs` serves it and `backup` backs it up. Single source of truth.
- **Firewall:** 2049/tcp is opened to the peer node(s) only, via the same
  `baseline_k3s_peer_ports` mechanism that opens 9100 for node-exporter
  (`ansible/roles/baseline/tasks/firewall.yml`). See [topic-ufw](topic-ufw.md).
- **Backup:** the export path is added to `backup_extra_paths` on the NFS host,
  so PV data rides the existing cross-node restic backup. See
  [topic-restic](topic-restic.md).
- **Provisioner app:** `gitops/platform/storage/app.yaml` — the
  `nfs-subdir-external-provisioner` Helm chart as an Argo Application. See
  [topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md), [topic-helm](topic-helm.md).
- **Verify:** `scripts/verify-storage.sh` drives a real PVC → pod →
  write/read/cleanup round-trip over one SSH connection; CI jobs follow the
  `verify:observability` pattern (main-only after apply + an on-demand manual
  job).

heading_path: NFS — the cluster's PersistentVolume layer (single-server export)
Flags & settings we use
text:
### Export options — `nfs_export_options` = `rw,sync,no_subtree_check,root_squash`

The export line rendered for each client (`roles/nfs/defaults/main.yml`).

- **`rw`** — read-write; the provisioner must create and populate per-PV
  subdirectories. `ro` would make every PV read-only, useless for a PVC.
- **`sync`** — the server acknowledges a write only once it is on stable
  storage. `async` is faster but can lose acknowledged writes on a server crash
  — the wrong default for the layer whose whole job is durability.
- **`no_subtree_check`** — skip the per-request check that a file still sits
  inside the exported subtree; the modern default, avoids a class of rename
  races and is a small speed win.
- **`root_squash`** (kept, stated explicitly rather than left to the NFS
  default) — a client mounting as root is mapped to `nobody:nogroup` on the
  server, so a compromised in-cluster provisioner cannot write as root on the
  host filesystem of the node that also runs the k3s control plane. The rejected
  alternative, `no_root_squash`, would hand client-root full root on the
  exported tree — exactly the privilege this SPOF host should not give out. The
  price of keeping it is the export-root mode below.

### Export root mode — `0777` (a consequence, not a free choice)

`roles/nfs/tasks/main.yml` creates `/srv/nfs/k8s` mode `0777`. This is the
**direct consequence** of `root_squash`: the squashed identity (`nobody`) must
still be able to create one subdirectory per PV under the root. It is acceptable
only because the export is network-restricted to the peer node (ufw 2049/tcp)
and holds nothing but PV data. Read it together with `root_squash` — the two are
one decision.

### Client list — `nfs_allowed_clients` (all node IPs)

`roles/nfs/defaults/main.yml` derives the allowed-client IPs from the inventory
(`groups['nodes']` → `ansible_host`) — **every** node, the server node's own
address **included**. It deliberately does **not** subtract the host's own
address the way `baseline/firewall.yml` does for its peer list: the NFS server
node also schedules pods, so its own kubelet must be able to mount the export
(self-access). A `difference()` that dropped the server's own IP — the shape the
firewall peer-list uses — would silently deny every PVC landing on the server
node while leaving the other node working, so the grant lists all node IPs
without subtraction. A node added or renamed still cannot leave a stale grant
behind — the exports file is regenerated from the inventory, the same
single-source-of-truth discipline the firewall uses.

> **Build phase — grant-all-IPs is the intended fix, not yet in the role.** As
> checked in, the role still derives the client list with a `difference()` that
> removes the server node's own address, which excludes the server node's own
> kubelet from the export. The corresponding mini-cloud fix (drop the
> `difference()`, grant all node IPs including self) is tracked in **mini-cloud
> MR !36** and must land and be applied before the "any node can mount" claim
> above holds on the server node. Until then, treat self-access on the server
> node as not yet granted.

### NFSv4-only — `/etc/nfs.conf` `[nfsd]` `vers3=n vers4=y`

`roles/nfs/tasks/main.yml` sets these via `community.general.ini_file`;
`rpc.nfsd` reads `/etc/nfs.conf` directly. **Disabling v3** (`vers3=n`) is the
step that does the work: it removes the portmapper/`mountd`/`statd` port dance
and collapses the firewall to a single 2049/tcp peer rule. NFSv2 needs no
toggle — it was dropped from `nfs-utils` upstream and is absent on Debian
bookworm/trixie, so a `vers2=n` line is a no-op against a dead, undocumented
`[nfsd]` option and is not relied on here.

### Provisioner chart — `targetRevision: 4.0.18` (pinned)

`gitops/platform/storage/app.yaml`. Chart **4.0.18** (appVersion 4.0.2) is the
newest entry served by the
`kubernetes-sigs.github.io/nfs-subdir-external-provisioner` Helm repo, verified
against its `index.yaml` on 2026-07-20 (digest + release-tarball URL recorded in
the app's comment). Pinned because a floating chart would change the platform
without a commit. Memory limit 128Mi / request 64Mi — a single tiny controller
pod, smallest sensible under the 8 GB memory-limit-only philosophy.

### StorageClass — `nfs-client`, **not** the cluster default

`valuesObject.storageClass`: `defaultClass: false`, `name: nfs-client`. local-path
stays the default (spec §4), so putting a PV on NFS is a **deliberate
per-workload choice** via an explicit `storageClassName: nfs-client`. Making it
default would silently pull every future PVC onto the single NFS server — the
SPOF. `archiveOnDelete: false` reclaims (deletes) a PV's subdirectory when its
PVC is deleted rather than renaming it to `archived-*`, so orphaned data does
not accumulate on the export; the cross-node restic backup is the durability
story, not archived subdirs.

### Provisioner `nfs.server` — vps1's **public** IP

The provisioner is pointed at vps1's public address (`<vps1-public-ip>`), not a
private/overlay one, for the same reason the restic backup uses the public peer
IP: the flannel wireguard-native device is a **pod** overlay (10.42.x), not a
node-management tunnel, and these VPSes share no private LAN. The ufw peer rule
restricts 2049/tcp to the peer node only; the NFS link itself is **unencrypted**
(NFSv4, no krb5) — a documented limitation in
[dec-2026-07-20-storage-nfs](../decisions/dec-2026-07-20-storage-nfs.md).

heading_path: NFS — the cluster's PersistentVolume layer (single-server export)
Pitfalls we hit
text:
> Build phase — these are design-time cautions and known limits, not incidents
> observed on a running cluster.

- **NFSv4-single-port is an assumption until an apply proves it.** The role
  disables v3 (v2 is already gone from `nfs-utils`) so the firewall needs only
  2049/tcp. A build-phase note in
  `roles/nfs/tasks/main.yml` flags the risk: if a Debian default still pulls in
  `rpcbind`/`mountd` for a v4 mount, that surfaces on the first apply +
  `verify:storage` run, and the extra peer ports would then be added to
  `baseline_k3s_peer_ports` exactly the way 9100 already was. Not yet verified
  against a node.
- **`root_squash` forces the 0777 export root** — a reviewer who reads the mode
  in isolation will read it as sloppy. It is the deliberate price of not handing
  out client-root (see the two settings above); the mitigation is that the
  export is peer-only over ufw and holds nothing but PV data.
- **The NFS server is a single point of failure.** If vps1 is down, no PV binds
  or serves. Data survives node loss only via the restic backup, **not** via
  replication — restore is a copy-back, not a failover. The default StorageClass
  stays local-path precisely so a stray PVC cannot land here unnoticed.
- **`nfs-client` is not default on purpose.** A PVC with no `storageClassName`
  gets local-path, not NFS. If a workload's data must survive a pod moving to
  another node, it must ask for `nfs-client` explicitly — forgetting the field
  is a silent "your data is node-local" bug, not an error.
- **"Green" is not "working."** Argo reporting the `nfs-storage` Application
  Synced/Healthy and the provisioner pod Running says nothing about whether a
  PVC binds — wrong server IP, ufw dropping 2049, or `root_squash` refusing the
  subdir create all leave the pod Running while every PVC stays Pending. That
  gap is exactly what `verify-storage.sh` exists to close.

heading_path: ntfy — the self-hosted push server that carries our alerts
What it is
text:
ntfy is a small push-notification server. A publisher does an HTTP `POST` to
`<server>/<topic>` with the message as the request body; every subscriber of
that topic — a phone app, a browser, a `curl` long-poll — receives it. There is
no account model to speak of and no per-device registration: the topic name *is*
the address. It ships as a single Go binary with an embedded SQLite database for
its message cache and its user/ACL store.

In our stack it is the **last hop of the alerting chain**: Prometheus evaluates
rules, Alertmanager groups and deduplicates, and ntfy turns the resulting webhook
`POST` into a notification on a phone. It is the piece that makes an alert
*arrive* rather than merely *fire* — see
[topic-prometheusrule-alerting](topic-prometheusrule-alerting.md) for the firing
half and [topic-kube-prometheus-stack](topic-kube-prometheus-stack.md) for the
Alertmanager that calls us.

heading_path: ntfy — the self-hosted push server that carries our alerts
Why we use it
text:
We run ntfy **on our own cluster** rather than using the hosted `ntfy.sh`,
because both external delivery routes are structurally blocked from the netcup
nodes: `ntfy.sh` is unreachable over IPv4 from both nodes (pods are IPv4-only),
and outbound SMTP (25/465/587) is blocked by the provider, which kills the
e-mail route as well. The full measurement and the alternatives weighed are in
[dec-2026-07-21-self-hosted-ntfy](../decisions/dec-2026-07-21-self-hosted-ntfy.md).

Self-hosting also fits the sovereignty goal of the platform: the whole path —
alert fires, Alertmanager posts, ntfy holds it, phone reads it — stays on
infrastructure we own. The cost we accepted is that patching the server is now
our job, which is why the image is both version- and digest-pinned.

heading_path: ntfy — the self-hosted push server that carries our alerts
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gitops/apps/ntfy/app.yaml` | The Argo CD `Application` (sync-wave `"1"`) that deploys the manifests below |
| `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/configmap.yaml` | `server.yml` — the **non-secret** half of the server config |
| `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/deployment.yaml` | The `Deployment`: image pin, `args`, probes, volumes, container hardening |
| `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/service.yaml` | ClusterIP `Service` — what Alertmanager publishes to |
| `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/ingress.yaml` | Traefik `Ingress` + Let's Encrypt certificate — what the phone subscribes to |
| `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml` | The **publisher** side: Alertmanager's `ntfy` receiver |
| `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml` | Holds the user hash and the two tokens (SOPS-encrypted; values never in git) |
| `ansible/roles/gitops_bootstrap/` | Renders the `ntfy-auth` and `ntfy-webhook-token` Secrets onto the node |
| `scripts/verify-ntfy.sh` | The check that proves delivery works — health, deny-all, round-trip, bogus token, Alertmanager rehang |
| `.gitlab-ci.yml` | Jobs `verify:ntfy` (after `apply`) and `verify:ntfy:on-demand` (read-only) |

The secret half never touches git: hashes and tokens travel the Ansible-out-of-
SOPS route (`dec-2026-07-17-app-secrets-ansible-sops`) into two Secrets —
`ntfy-auth` (namespace `ntfy`, consumed as environment variables) and
`ntfy-webhook-token` (namespace `monitoring`, mounted as a file for
Alertmanager).

heading_path: ntfy — the self-hosted push server that carries our alerts
Flags & settings we use
text:
ntfy merges its configuration from three sources, in increasing precedence:
`/etc/ntfy/server.yml`, environment variables (`NTFY_<KEY_IN_CAPS>`), and
command-line flags. **We use the first two and no flags** — the non-secret keys
sit in the ConfigMap, the secret ones (`NTFY_AUTH_USERS`, `NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS`)
arrive as env from a Secret. That split is deliberate: it puts everything a
reviewer needs to judge the security posture in git, and nothing that must stay
out of it.

### `args: ["serve"]` (Deployment)

ntfy's binary is multi-command (`serve`, `publish`, `subscribe`, `user`,
`access`, `token`, …) and the image's entrypoint does **not** default to
`serve`. Without this argument the container starts, prints usage and exits —
which reads as a crash-loop, not as a configuration error. Verified during
build: the subcommand is required.

### `base-url` = `https://ntfy.<your-domain>` (server.yml)

The public URL ntfy believes it is reachable at. It is not cosmetic: ntfy uses
it to build attachment links, the web app's own URLs and the `Location` headers
it returns. Leaving it empty makes ntfy guess from the request, which behind a
reverse proxy produces internal URLs (`http://ntfy.ntfy.svc.cluster.local/…`) in
links that a phone then cannot open. The concrete host lives in
`gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/ingress.yaml`; the knowledge base keeps hostnames as
placeholders (topics/README, spec §7).

### `behind-proxy` = `true` (server.yml)

Tells ntfy it sits behind a reverse proxy (Traefik, via the `Ingress`), so it
reads the client IP from `X-Forwarded-For` instead of taking the TCP peer
address. Without it, every request appears to come from the ingress controller's
pod IP — which collapses rate-limiting and visitor accounting onto a single
"visitor". Other value: `false` (the default), correct only for a directly
exposed server.

### `listen-http` = `:80` (server.yml)

The plain-HTTP listener. TLS terminates at Traefik with a cert-manager-issued
Let's Encrypt certificate (`ingress.yaml`), so ntfy itself speaks HTTP only —
the alternatives (`listen-https` plus `key-file`/`cert-file`) would duplicate
certificate management inside the pod. Port 80 (rather than ntfy's own default
of `:80` as well) matches the `Service`/probe ports; note the consequence in
"Pitfalls" — binding a privileged port keeps the container running as root.

### `auth-file` = `/var/lib/ntfy/user.db` (server.yml)

The SQLite database holding users, tokens and ACL entries. Setting it is what
*enables* the whole auth layer: with no `auth-file`, ntfy runs wide open and
`auth-default-access` is ignored.

The mount matters as much as the value. `/var/lib/ntfy` is an **`emptyDir`, not
a PVC**, because the auth database is **derived state**: `NTFY_AUTH_USERS`,
`NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS` and `auth-access` re-provision users, tokens and ACLs from
config on *every* start, so the file has no information the SOPS-encrypted
source does not have. That buys two things: the source of truth stays the
encrypted config rather than a running database, and — decisive here — **SQLite
never lands on NFS**. Our shared storage is NFS ([topic-nfs](topic-nfs.md)), and SQLite over
NFS is a classic corruption/locking hazard. An `emptyDir` sidesteps it at the
cost of nothing durable.

### `auth-default-access` = `deny-all` (server.yml)

The access level for anyone the ACL does not mention — including anonymous
requests. Options: `read-write` (the default: anyone may read and publish any
topic), `read-only`, `write-only`, `deny-all`. We use `deny-all`, so **both**
publishing and subscribing require a credential.

This is the flag that lets the topic name be non-secret. The hosted-ntfy.sh
pattern is "pick an unguessable topic name" — security by obscurity, with a
topic name that then leaks into every config file, log line and screenshot.
Under `deny-all` the protection is the token, so `soevereinlab-alerts` can be an
ordinary, readable name. `verify-ntfy.sh` asserts this every run: an
unauthenticated poll of the topic must return `403`.

### `auth-access` (server.yml)

The declarative ACL, in `user:topic:permission` form (supported from ntfy
v2.14.0; ours is v2.26.3):

```yaml
auth-access:
  - "alertmanager:soevereinlab-alerts:wo"
  - "phone:soevereinlab-alerts:ro"
```

Permissions: `rw` (read+write), `ro` (read-only), `wo` (write-only), `deny`. We
split the two directions deliberately — Alertmanager only ever *publishes*, the
phone only ever *reads*, so neither credential can do the other's job. A leaked
read token cannot forge alerts; a leaked publish token cannot exfiltrate the
alert history. `verify-ntfy.sh` proves the split holds by publishing with the
write token and reading the same message back with the read token.

Declaring the ACL here rather than running `ntfy access …` by hand is what keeps
it GitOps: Argo CD reconciles the ConfigMap, and a hand-edit inside the pod is
erased on the next restart along with the rest of the derived auth database.

### `cache-file` = `/var/cache/ntfy/cache.db` and `cache-duration` = `12h`

`cache-file` is the SQLite database of recent messages. Without it ntfy keeps
messages in memory only, and a subscriber that reconnects after a restart sees
nothing. With it, a phone that was offline can fetch what it missed
(`?since=…`). Same reasoning as the auth database: it is a cache, so it lives on
an `emptyDir` and stays off NFS.

`cache-duration` is how long a message stays fetchable (default `12h`, ntfy's
own default as well; `0` disables the cache entirely). Twelve hours is chosen
against `repeat_interval: 12h` on the Alertmanager side — a phone that was off
overnight still sees the outstanding alerts, and nothing older is worth
replaying. Note that a message *disappearing* after 12h is by design; ntfy is
not the alert history, Alertmanager and Prometheus are.

### `NTFY_AUTH_USERS` / `NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS` (env, from Secret `ntfy-auth`)

The declarative user and token provisioning, supplied as environment variables
because they contain a password hash and two tokens. Both are comma-separated
lists; the users list is `name:hash:role` and the tokens list is `name:token`
(plus optional label). The real values live only in
`ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml` (SOPS-encrypted) and reach the cluster as
Secret `ntfy-auth`; in this repo they are `<PLACEHOLDER>` and nothing else.

`envFrom.secretRef` (rather than individual `env` entries) means adding a key on
the Ansible side needs no manifest change. The users provisioned this way are
re-created on every start — see `auth-file` above.

### Deployment: probes, resources and hardening

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `image` | `binwiederhier/ntfy:v2.26.3@sha256:<digest>` | Tag **and** digest. The tag says which version a human reads; the digest makes the pull reproducible even if the tag is re-pushed. We own patching now, so the pin is deliberate and bumping it is a reviewed change. |
| `replicas` | `1` | Two replicas would each hold their own `emptyDir` cache and auth database, so a subscriber would see only half the messages. Horizontal scaling needs shared state ntfy does not have here. |
| `readinessProbe` / `livenessProbe` | `GET /v1/health` on port 80 | ntfy's own health endpoint; it answers `{"healthy":true}`. A probe on `/` would pass while auth is broken, because the web app renders regardless. |
| `resources` | requests `10m` CPU / `32Mi`, limit `64Mi` | A two-node lab: everything is resource-pinned so one workload cannot starve the others. ntfy is genuinely this small. |
| `readOnlyRootFilesystem` | `true` | Everything ntfy writes goes to the two `emptyDir`s; the rest of the filesystem has no reason to be writable. |
| `allowPrivilegeEscalation` | `false` | No setuid path out of the container's privileges. |
| `volumeMounts` (config) | `subPath: server.yml`, `readOnly: true` | `subPath` mounts the single file into `/etc/ntfy/` without hiding the rest of the directory. The trade-off is real: a `subPath` mount does **not** update when the ConfigMap changes, so a config edit needs a pod restart (Argo CD's sync does that when the Deployment changes; a ConfigMap-only edit does not). |

### Service and Ingress

The `Service` is a plain ClusterIP on port 80 → targetPort 80. **This is the
address Alertmanager uses** (`http://ntfy.ntfy.svc.cluster.local/<topic>`), and
the choice is load-bearing: publishing to the public URL would leave the cluster
and hairpin back over IPv4 — the exact failure class that killed the ntfy.sh
route. In-cluster traffic never touches the node's egress path.

The `Ingress` is the phone's door: `ingressClassName: traefik`, a single host
rule, `pathType: Prefix` on `/`, and TLS via
`cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod` into secret `ntfy-tls` (see
[topic-cert-manager](topic-cert-manager.md), [topic-traefik](topic-traefik.md)).

### Argo CD `Application`

`sync-wave: "1"` puts ntfy **after** the platform charts in wave `"0"` (which
include kube-prometheus-stack). `syncPolicy.automated` with `prune: true` and
`selfHeal: true` means a hand-edit on the cluster is reverted — including, by
design, any attempt to loosen `auth-default-access` outside git.
`CreateNamespace=true` creates the `ntfy` namespace, so no separate manifest
exists for it. The rest is the house default for an app: `project: default`,
`destination.server: https://kubernetes.default.svc` (the local cluster),
`source.targetRevision: HEAD` (track the default branch — we pin *images*, not
the manifest revision, because the manifests are ours) and
`source.path: gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests`. See
[topic-argo-cd](topic-argo-cd.md).

### The publisher side (Alertmanager)

Set in `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml`, documented here because it is half
of the contract:

```yaml
receivers:
  - name: 'ntfy'
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://ntfy.ntfy.svc.cluster.local/soevereinlab-alerts'
        send_resolved: true
        http_config:
          authorization:
            type: Bearer
            credentials_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/ntfy-webhook-token/token
```

- `type: Bearer` + `credentials_file`: the token is read from a file mounted via
  `alertmanagerSpec.secrets: [ntfy-webhook-token]`, at the operator's fixed path
  `/etc/alertmanager/secrets/<secret>/<key>`. Inline `credentials` would put the
  token in the values file, i.e. in git. Bearer was verified against the real
  server (good token `200`, wrong token `401`); ntfy also accepts basic auth as
  a fallback.
- `send_resolved: true`: ntfy also receives the resolved notification, so a
  phone sees an incident close. Without it an alert can only ever arrive, never
  clear, and the reader has to guess.
- The `Watchdog` alert keeps a subroute to the `null` receiver: it is a ~30s
  heartbeat whose *purpose* is to fire forever, and routing it here would mean a
  notification every 30 seconds.

heading_path: ntfy — the self-hosted push server that carries our alerts
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### The raw webhook body exceeds ntfy's message size

Alertmanager's webhook payload is JSON with the full alert group, labels and
annotations; ntfy's default maximum message size is **~4096 bytes**. We
deliberately post the raw JSON as the message body ("begin ruw, verfijn later"),
which means **a notification with several alerts in the group is truncated —
the reader sees the start of a JSON document and not necessarily the alert
names**. That is the consequence to know before trusting what a phone shows: the
notification is a *signal that something fired*, not the authoritative content;
the authority is Alertmanager's UI/API. The follow-up is templating (ntfy has a
pre-defined `alertmanager` template, addressable as `?template=alertmanager` or
an `X-Template` header) so the notification carries a title and a short body
instead of a JSON dump; that work is not done. Note the accepted state is
truncation, not attachment conversion: attachment behaviour depends on how the
body is posted, and the observed effect for us is a clipped message.

### The auth database is not durable — and must not be

Losing `/var/lib/ntfy` costs nothing, because the pod re-provisions from
`NTFY_AUTH_USERS`/`NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS`/`auth-access` on start. The failure mode to
avoid is the *opposite* one: "fixing" this by moving the mount to a PVC would
put SQLite on NFS. If durable state is ever genuinely needed (message history,
attachments), the choice reopens — see the decision's "Revisit when".

### The two emptyDirs are functionally required

They are not just hygiene. With `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and no writable
directory for `auth-file`, ntfy exits **fatally** at start — it cannot create the
user database. Both mounts must exist for the pod to run at all.

### One password hash served both users — resolved, and how it failed twice

`NTFY_AUTH_USERS` originally provisioned `alertmanager` and `phone` with the
**same password hash**. Tokens were separate and the ACL correctly split, but
the phone app offers no token field in its subscribe flow — it demands username
and password — so the handset carried a password that also opened the publishing
account. Each user now has its own hash, from its own key in the encrypted
secrets file, with the template falling back to the shared value only while the
new key does not exist yet.

Two failures on the way there, both worth more than the fix:

1. **A silent fallback is invisible.** The template's `default(...)` meant every
   render succeeded whether or not the new hash existed, so nothing went red
   while the accounts still shared a password. The gate that closed it reads the
   rendered Secret back off the cluster and compares the two hashes **without
   printing either**, emitting only `shared`, `distinct` or `unreadable`, and
   escalates from warning to failure by grepping the *encrypted* file for the
   key name (SOPS leaves keys in plaintext, so this needs no key and no network).
2. **A valid hash of the wrong password.** The replacement was minted by piping
   a password into `<image> user hash` from a Windows shell, so `password\r` was
   hashed. The device could not log in for a week while six independent checks
   stayed green — 60 characters, `$2a$` prefix, strict bcrypt regex, distinct
   from the other account, Secret written at 21:17:01Z, pod started 21:17:03Z.
   All true; none of them could see it. **A check on the form of a secret cannot
   see that it was made from something else.** Mint on a real TTY and prove the
   pair against a throwaway ntfy before deploying — recipe 20 in
   [command-cookbook](../reference/command-cookbook.md), procedure in
   [rb-2026-08-04-ntfy-password-hash-rotation](../runbooks/rb-2026-08-04-ntfy-password-hash-rotation.md).

Closed on the same day: giving `phone` its own hash stopped the phone's password
from opening the publishing account, but it did not *invalidate* the password
the two had shared — that one still logged in as `alertmanager` until its hash
was rotated too, by the same procedure. Rotating one account never revokes a
password shared with another; that always takes a second rotation. Nothing
authenticates as `alertmanager` with a password anyway — Alertmanager publishes
with the Bearer token from `NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS` — so the rotation is invisible to
delivery, which the post-`apply` verify run confirms rather than assumes.

No value, hash or token belongs anywhere in this repository.

### The container runs as root

ntfy binds port 80, a privileged port, and the upstream image runs as root; a
`runAsNonRoot` container would need `listen-http` on a high port plus a
`Service` `targetPort` change. We chose container hardening
(`readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`) over a non-root
UID for now. Worth revisiting when the manifests are next touched.

### Verifying delivery is its own discipline

Three separate defects in this stack lived in the *verification*, not in the
platform: Alertmanager masks a webhook URL so a check on it can never pass; a
heredoc body shipped to a remote shell is parsed by no local gate; and the
Kubernetes API service proxy carries neither `Authorization` nor `Content-Type`
headers. All three, with the working commands, are recipes 14, 18 and 19 in
[command-cookbook](../reference/command-cookbook.md).

### The round-trip probe now asks the client not to alert

`verify-ntfy.sh`'s round-trip check (`NTFY_PUBLISH`/`NTFY_READBACK`) has to
publish onto the real `soevereinlab-alerts` topic — that is the assertion, and
a probe on a topic of its own would stop proving the path alerts actually
take. The consequence was that every `apply` and every `verify:ntfy:on-demand`
run put a `verify-ntfy-<epoch>-<pid>` message in front of whoever reads that
topic, indistinguishable in urgency from a real alert.

Since 2026-08-04 the publish call carries `X-Priority: min` and an explicit
`X-Title: verify:ntfy self-test (geen alert)` header. ntfy carries the
priority to the client; what a given client does with `min` is that client's
behaviour, not something the server side can assert — so it had to be
verified on a real device rather than assumed from the header alone.

**Observed, 2026-08-04, on the first `verify:ntfy` run on `main` after the
change:** no notification, message visible in the ntfy app. `X-Priority: min`
suppresses the notification (no buzz/sound) on this client without hiding the
message from the app itself — the outcome the change was written for. No
fallback (e.g. relying on the title alone) was needed.

heading_path: openssl s_client / x509 — reading a live TLS certificate from a script
What it is
text:
`openssl` is the command-line front end to the OpenSSL library. Two of its
subcommands read a server's live TLS certificate: `s_client` opens a TLS
connection and prints the certificate the server presented, and `x509` parses a
certificate and answers questions about it (who issued it, when it expires).
Chained together they turn "what certificate is this host actually serving right
now?" into a scriptable check.

heading_path: openssl s_client / x509 — reading a live TLS certificate from a script
Why we use it
text:
The platform's outside-in check, `scripts/verify-platform.sh`, has to prove the
served certificate is a *real* one — issued by Let's Encrypt, not the staging
CA, and not about to expire — because a staging or stale certificate sits in a
Kubernetes Secret looking healthy while a browser rejects it or renewal has
quietly stopped. `curl` validates the chain but cannot show *which* chain: on
Windows it is built against schannel and prints no certificate fields at all
(see [topic-workstation-toolchain](topic-workstation-toolchain.md)). openssl is
the portable reader that shows the issuer and the expiry, so the check reads the
same on the CI runner and on the workstation.

heading_path: openssl s_client / x509 — reading a live TLS certificate from a script
Where it lives in our repos
text:
In `soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it does |
|---|---|
| `scripts/verify-platform.sh` | Reads the demo host's cert once via `s_client`, then checks issuer and expiry with `x509` |
| `.gitlab-ci.yml` (`verify:platform`) | Runs that script after `apply`, so a staging or expiring cert turns the pipeline red |

The issuers the certificate comes from are described in
[topic-cert-manager](topic-cert-manager.md).

heading_path: openssl s_client / x509 — reading a live TLS certificate from a script
Flags & settings we use
text:
The whole pattern is one handshake, then two local reads of the captured PEM:

```bash
cert=$(echo | openssl s_client -connect "$HOST:443" -servername "$HOST" 2>/dev/null)
printf '%s' "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -issuer
printf '%s' "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -checkend 1209600
```

### `s_client -connect <host>:443`

Opens a TLS connection to that host and port and prints the presented
certificate chain. Without a following `x509` it dumps the whole handshake; we
pipe it into `x509` to ask a specific question instead.

### `s_client -servername <host>`

Sends the hostname as SNI (Server Name Indication) in the handshake. This is
**required**, not cosmetic: an ingress serving several names hands out a default
(often wrong) certificate when no SNI is sent, so the check would inspect a
certificate the browser never sees. Setting it to the same host we connect to is
what makes the answer trustworthy.

### `echo | s_client`

`s_client` keeps the connection open for interactive input; piping an empty line
into it sends EOF so it closes and returns instead of hanging. `2>/dev/null`
drops its progress chatter, leaving only the PEM on stdout.

### `x509 -noout -issuer`

Prints just the issuer line (`-noout` suppresses re-printing the encoded
certificate). Verified 2026-07-16 against the live demo host: `issuer=C=US, O=Let's
Encrypt, CN=YR2`. The script fails if this line is empty, contains `STAGING`, or
does not name Let's Encrypt — the staging issuer reads `(STAGING) ...` and is
untrusted by browsers.

### `x509 -noout -checkend <seconds>`

Exits `0` if the certificate is valid for at least that many more seconds and
`1` if it will expire within the window; we pass `1209600` (14 days). A
certificate inside that window means renewal is already broken while everything
else still reads green, which is exactly the silent failure the check exists to
catch. Verified 2026-07-16 on the live cert (`notAfter Oct 14 2026`): `-checkend
1209600` printed `Certificate will not expire` and exited 0; a deliberately huge
window (`-checkend 999999999`) printed `Certificate will expire` and exited 1, so
the red path is real, not assumed.

heading_path: openssl s_client / x509 — reading a live TLS certificate from a script
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### Windows curl shows no certificate fields

`curl` on the workstation is built against schannel, and `curl -sv https://host
| grep issuer` matches nothing even on a fully successful handshake — the fields
are simply not printed. This cost time during task 5 before openssl replaced it
for every issuer/expiry check. `curl --fail` (no `-k`) is still the right tool
for the *other* question — does the chain validate? — because it exercises the
real trust store; it just cannot tell you which chain it validated. Use both
when you need both facts.

### Reading from stdin prints a warning

`openssl x509` without `-in` warns `Reading certificate from stdin ...` on
stderr. It is harmless and does not affect the exit code, but the script
redirects it (`2>/dev/null`) so it does not masquerade as an error in a job log.

heading_path: PrometheusRule alerting — how our alerts get picked up, and which ones we add
What it is
text:
A `PrometheusRule` is the custom resource the Prometheus Operator turns into
Prometheus' own recording/alerting rules. You declare alerts as Kubernetes
objects and the operator writes them into the running Prometheus — no
hand-editing of `prometheus.yml`. Alertmanager then groups, deduplicates and
routes whatever fires.

This topic covers the two things that are easy to get wrong on our platform:
**how a rule actually gets picked up** by the pinned chart, and **which alerts
are worth adding** given how many the chart already ships.

heading_path: PrometheusRule alerting — how our alerts get picked up, and which ones we add
Why we use it
text:
Declaring alerts as `PrometheusRule` objects (rather than editing Prometheus'
config) is the GitOps-native route: an alert is a committed, reviewed manifest
like any other resource, and the operator reconciles it — no drift, no
hand-editing of `prometheus.yml`. It is the alerting arm of the observability
choice recorded in
[dec-2026-07-17-observability-prometheus-loki](../decisions/dec-2026-07-17-observability-prometheus-loki.md).

heading_path: PrometheusRule alerting — how our alerts get picked up, and which ones we add
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gitops/platform/monitoring/alert-rules.yaml` | Our `PrometheusRule` (node + Argo alerts) and the `PodMonitor` the Argo alert needs |
| `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml` | The kube-prometheus-stack `Application`; its `alertmanager.config` holds the null-route |

heading_path: PrometheusRule alerting — how our alerts get picked up, and which ones we add
Flags & settings we use
text:
The settings and objects our repo actually sets to get alerts picked up, scoped
and routed — the pickup label, the rules we add, the Argo metrics `PodMonitor`,
and the Alertmanager null-route.

### The label that makes a rule get picked up

The pinned chart (87.16.1) keeps two selector defaults **on**:

- `prometheus.prometheusSpec.ruleSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: true`
- `prometheus.prometheusSpec.podMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: true`

With those `true`, a nil/`{}` selector is **not** treated as "match
everything". Instead the operator builds the selector from the Helm release
label, so Prometheus only picks up `PrometheusRule` and `PodMonitor` objects
carrying:

```yaml
metadata:
  labels:
    release: monitoring
```

`monitoring` is the Helm release name — which, under Argo CD, is the
`Application`'s `metadata.name`. **Forget this label and the rule is applied to
the cluster, looks healthy in Argo, and is silently never evaluated** — a clean
example of "green is not the same as working". Verify it landed by checking the
rule shows up under Prometheus' `/api/v1/rules` (or the Rules page), not just
that Argo says Synced.

> Note the asymmetry: `serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues` is deliberately
> set to `false` in our `app.yaml` (so any ServiceMonitor is scraped without a
> label). That flag only covers **ServiceMonitors**. Rules and PodMonitors keep
> the default, so they still need the `release` label. Source: values.yaml @
> chart 87.16.1.

### Which alerts we add (and which we do not)

The stack ships a large default rule set (`defaultRules.create: true`, almost
every group enabled). Before adding anything, inventory it — **duplicate alerts
are noise**. What is already there and relevant:

| Concern | Default rule(s) already shipped |
|---|---|
| A job's targets down | `TargetDown` (`general.rules`) — fires when >10% of a job's targets are down for 10m |
| A node not Ready | `KubeNodeNotReady`, `KubeNodeUnreachable` (`kubernetes-system`/`node`) |
| Disk near-full | `NodeFilesystemAlmostOutOfSpace` (<5%/<3% free ≈ >95% used), `NodeFilesystemSpaceFillingUp` (24h/4h fill prediction) |

So we add **only** what the plan C spec asks for that the defaults do not cover
at the shape/threshold wanted:

- **`NodeExporterDown`** — `up{job="node-exporter"} == 0`, `for: 5m`, critical.
  It overlaps `TargetDown` on purpose but is **per-instance** (names the node)
  and fires specifically on node-exporter reachability. That is exactly the gap
  the C2 monitoring rollout exposed: a node that was `Ready` (so
  `KubeNodeNotReady` stayed silent) whose node-exporter was unreachable through
  a firewall port gap. The alert answers "is this node's host-metrics
  endpoint reachable", which the aggregate `TargetDown` does not name.
- **`NodeFilesystemHighUsage`** — >80% used, `for: 15m`, warning, excluding
  `tmpfs|overlay|squashfs|ramfs` and read-only mounts. The default filesystem
  alerts only fire near-full (95%) or on a fill-rate prediction, so an 80%
  warning is a genuinely earlier signal, not a duplicate.
- **`ArgoCdAppNotSynced` / `ArgoCdAppNotHealthy`** — on `argocd_app_info`,
  `for: 15m`, warning. The `for` rides out the normal `OutOfSync`/`Progressing`
  blips during a sync.

### Getting Argo CD metrics without a metrics Service

The Argo alerts read `argocd_app_info`, a gauge the **application-controller**
exports with `sync_status` and `health_status` labels. The catch: our Argo is
installed by the `argo-cd` Helm chart (10.1.3), and that chart only creates the
metrics **Service** when `controller.metrics.enabled: true` — which our install
leaves off. So there is no Service to point a ServiceMonitor at.

The controller nonetheless serves metrics on container port **8082
unconditionally** (`containerPorts.metrics: 8082` in the chart). A `PodMonitor`
scrapes that port directly:

```yaml
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PodMonitor
metadata:
  name: argocd-application-controller
  namespace: monitoring
  labels:
    release: monitoring
spec:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames: ["argocd"]
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: argocd-application-controller
  podMetricsEndpoints:
    - port: metrics
```

This keeps the metric available with **no extra running component and no change
to the Ansible install** — the alternative (enabling `controller.metrics` in
`gitops_bootstrap/templates/argocd-helmchart.yaml.j2`) would be an Ansible
change. Hedge: this was built without cluster access; that the controller
actually answers on 8082 and the target comes up is an orchestrator
observation (rule + target visible in Prometheus).

### The null-route (no receiver yet, on purpose)

Alertmanager is configured but routes everything to a no-op `null` receiver, so
it groups and deduplicates but sends nothing outward. Choosing a real receiver
(e-mail / ntfy / webhook) is a deliberate later decision — a **JELLE-GATE**
(plan C SC 5). The swap is a ~5-minute change documented in
[alert-receiver-draaiboek](../reference/alert-receiver-draaiboek.md). We spell
the route out in `app.yaml` (rather than inherit the chart default) so the
null-route reads as a declared choice, and we keep the default `inhibit_rules`
(a firing `critical` silences a matching `warning`/`info`) so nothing
regresses. The `Watchdog` alert (always firing) is what the C5
`verify:observability` check will assert still reaches Alertmanager.

heading_path: PrometheusRule alerting — how our alerts get picked up, and which ones we add
Pitfalls
text:
- **Missing `release: monitoring` label** → rule/PodMonitor silently ignored.
  The single most common kube-prometheus-stack alerting mistake here.
- **Adding a rule that duplicates a default** → double pages. Inventory
  `defaultRules` first.
- **Alertmanager `config` is a map, but `receivers`/`routes` are lists.** Lists
  replace on merge, they do not deep-merge — so provide the whole route +
  receivers block, not a fragment, or you lose the chart's defaults.
- **`for:` too short on Argo alerts** → every routine sync pages. 15m is a
  deliberate floor.
