heading_path: The workstation toolchain — Git Bash on Windows, and what it is not
What it is
text:
The maintainer's machine: Windows, with **Git Bash** (Git for Windows, which
ships an MSYS2 environment) as the shell the repos are used from. `uname`
reports `MINGW64_NT ... Msys`. It is a real bash with a real coreutils, and it
is close enough to Linux that scripts written for Linux usually run — which is
precisely what makes the places it differs expensive. The differences are not
loud. They do not error; they succeed and mean something else.

This topic exists because the workstation is a **deployment target for our own
scripts** and nobody was treating it as one. Almost everything in the
soevereinlab ecosystem runs in the pipeline, on a Linux runner. A small number
of things cannot: minting a credential a human is about to use, for one. Those
run here, and "it passed CI" says nothing at all about them.

heading_path: The workstation toolchain — Git Bash on Windows, and what it is not
Why we use it
text:
Not a choice so much as a fact: it is the machine the repos are cloned on. The
choice worth recording is what we **refuse** to put on it.

**Ansible is deliberately not installed on the workstation.** The pipeline is
the route to the nodes — that is the founding property of the config repo, and
it is what makes "nothing is configured by hand" checkable. See
[topic-ansible](topic-ansible.md) and [topic-gitlab-ci](topic-gitlab-ci.md).
The consequence is easy to state and was still missed: **any script meant to
run on the workstation cannot use `ansible`, `ansible-inventory`, or anything
else that only exists because Ansible is installed.** A CI script and a
workstation script are different programs, however similar they look.

heading_path: The workstation toolchain — Git Bash on Windows, and what it is not
Where it lives in our repos
text:
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`:

- `scripts/viewer-kubeconfig.sh` — the one script written to be run **here**
  rather than in the pipeline. Reads the inventory with a bare Python and
  PyYAML, probes the interpreter by running it, and writes a credential file.
- `scripts/test-viewer-kubeconfig-no-leak.sh` — its test, which runs offline
  and therefore runs both here and in CI.
- `scripts/verify-hardening.sh`, `scripts/bootstrap-if-needed.sh` — the
  contrast: **pipeline** scripts. They use `ansible-inventory` and are correct
  to. Do not copy their inventory-reading pattern into a workstation script.

heading_path: The workstation toolchain — Git Bash on Windows, and what it is not
What the workstation has, and what it deliberately lacks
text:
Verified 2026-07-15 by running each, not by locating it — see the pitfalls
below for why that distinction is the whole page.

| | state |
|---|---|
| `ansible`, `ansible-inventory` | **absent, by design** — the pipeline is the route to the nodes |
| `python` | **present and working** — Python 3.12.2, with PyYAML 6.0.3 |
| `python3` | **present and broken** — the Microsoft Store alias stub, not Python |
| `ssh`, `git`, `jq`, `docker`, `kubectl`, `glab` | present |
| `yq` | absent |

On a Linux CI runner the first two rows are usually **inverted**: `python3` is
the working one, and `python` may not exist at all. Neither name is portable.
A script that must run in both places has to establish which one is real.

### The probe pattern we use

```bash
PYTHON=""
for candidate in python3 python; do
  if [ "$("$candidate" -c 'import yaml; print("ok")' 2>/dev/null)" = "ok" ]; then
    PYTHON="$candidate"
    break
  fi
done
[ -n "$PYTHON" ] || { echo "FAIL: no working Python with PyYAML" >&2; exit 1; }
```

Three properties are load-bearing, and each is there because the obvious
version fails:

- It **executes** the candidate. `command -v python3` is not a probe (below).
- It compares **stdout to a sentinel**, not just the exit status. A stub that
  printed nothing and exited 0 would pass an exit-status check.
- It tests the **capability actually needed** (`import yaml`), not merely the
  interpreter. A Python without PyYAML is not a Python this script can use.

`python3` is tried first so the CI runner keeps taking the name it prefers; the
workstation falls through to `python`. Note a bash subtlety that makes this
safe: a failing command substitution **inside an `if` condition does not trip
`set -e`**, so a candidate that does not exist is skipped rather than fatal.

heading_path: The workstation toolchain — Git Bash on Windows, and what it is not
Pitfalls we hit
text:
### `command -v python3` succeeds and proves nothing

Windows ships **App Execution Aliases**: zero-byte stubs on the PATH, under
`C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\`, that exist to send you
to the Microsoft Store. One of them is called `python3`.

```
$ command -v python3
/c/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Microsoft/WindowsApps/python3    <- succeeds
$ python3 -c 'print(1)'
Python was not found; run without arguments to install from the Microsoft Store...
$ echo $?
49
```

It resolves. It is on the PATH. It is not Python. Any probe of the shape
`command -v python3 || die` selects it and reports success, and the script then
fails somewhere further down with a message about the Store.

**This is the same failure class as the sshd incident** (see
[topic-sshd](topic-sshd.md)): the config file said the right thing and the
running daemon had never loaded it. Here the path resolves and the interpreter
has never run. **Existence is not behaviour.** The rule generalises well past
Python: if a script's correctness depends on a program *doing* something, the
check must make it do that thing. Locating it is not a check.

Real cost: `scripts/viewer-kubeconfig.sh` was merged after two reviews,
`shellcheck`, `bash -n` and a rigorous leak test, and had never worked on the
workstation it was written for. Its test stubbed the very commands that would
have reached the failure.

### `chmod` and `umask` are silent no-ops under `noacl`

Git Bash mounts everything `noacl`:

```
$ mount
C: on /c type ntfs (binary,noacl,posix=0,user,noumount,auto)
                    ^^^^^
$ touch f; chmod 600 f; echo $?; stat -c '%a' f
0
644
```

`chmod` **exits 0 and changes nothing.** `umask 077` changes nothing. The file
reports 644 to any later process, forever. A script that writes a credential
and then "secures" it with `chmod 0600` has not secured anything here, and
nothing goes red to say so.

Two traps inside the trap:

- **In-process caching.** MSYS caches the mode for the life of the process, so
  `stat` *immediately after* the `chmod`, in the same script, can still say
  `600` while every other observer sees `644`. A self-check inside the script
  would pass. This is worse than no check.
- **`mktemp` is not the umask.** On a real POSIX system `mktemp` creates `0600`
  **unconditionally and never consults the umask** — verified at umask 022, 000
  and 077, always 600, and still 600 after a same-filesystem rename. If a
  script's comment credits `umask 077` for the mode of a `mktemp` file, the
  comment is wrong on Linux too. Keep the umask as defence-in-depth for a
  future edit that creates the file by plain redirect (where it *is*
  load-bearing: 666 at umask 000, 600 at 077), but do not credit it for what
  `mktemp` did.

**What actually protects the file on Windows is the NTFS ACL**, which it
inherits from the user's profile directory:

```
$ icacls C:\Users\<user>\...\viewer.kubeconfig
    NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
    BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)
    <DOMAIN>\<user>:(I)(F)
```

Every entry is `(I)` — **inherited**. No `Everyone`, no `Users`. So a
credential written under the user profile is in practice not readable by other
unprivileged local users, and the outcome is correct. But it is correct for a
reason the script neither controls nor may claim credit for: move the output
somewhere with different inheritance and the protection is simply gone, with
`chmod 0600` still exiting 0.

Practical rule: on Windows, **POSIX modes are not the access control in play**.
Checking the mode there is not a weak test, it is a meaningless one. Check the
ACL with `icacls`, or check nothing and say so.

**A tool that trips over this in our stack:** `age-keygen` warns `writing
secret key to a world-readable file` when it writes the age identity here, and
the warning is a false alarm — it is reading the 644 fiction, while `icacls`
shows only inherited `SYSTEM` / `Administrators` / the user. The trap is not
the warning, it is the obvious response to it: a `chmod 600` that exits 0,
changes nothing, silences nothing, and leaves the reader believing they fixed
it. See [topic-age](topic-age.md), which also states the uncomfortable half —
the key's protection is *entirely* profile-directory ACL inheritance, so moving
it somewhere else loses that protection silently.

### A credential written to the repo root is a credential `git add -A` stages

Not Windows-specific, but it bites here first, because the workstation is where
credential-minting scripts run. A script that defaults its output to a relative
path writes into **the current directory**, and repo scripts are usually run
from the repo root (often forced, if the script pins something like
`ansible/known_hosts` relatively).

If the filename is not in `.gitignore`, `git add -A` stages it. Patterns like
`*.pem`, `*.key`, `*_key`, `id_*` look comprehensive and match **none** of
`viewer.kubeconfig`. Check with the tool rather than by reading:

```
$ git check-ignore -v <the-file>          # names the rule, or exits 1 if none
$ git add -A --dry-run | grep <the-file>  # the question actually being asked
```

Ignore the temp file too. A `mktemp`-based script has a window in which
`<name>.XXXXXX` holds the full credential and is not ignored by a rule written
for `<name>`.

### `pipx`-installed Ansible has PyYAML that `python3` cannot see

Worth knowing before making a tidy-sounding argument. "ansible-core requires
PyYAML, so any machine with `ansible-inventory` can `import yaml`" is **false**.
PyYAML is required in *Ansible's* environment. `pipx install ansible-core` — an
install method upstream recommends — puts `ansible-inventory` on the PATH and
PyYAML in a venv the PATH `python3` cannot see:

```
$ ansible-inventory --version     # works
$ python3 -c 'import yaml'        # ModuleNotFoundError
```

So a bare-Python script is **not** universally a weaker dependency than an
Ansible script; it is a different one. Where we run it the trade is clearly
right (the workstation has no Ansible at all and does have a Python; CI
`pip install`s into the image's system Python), but the general claim does not
hold, and the specific one is the only one worth writing down.

### MSYS converts POSIX paths in argv — which is usually a rescue, and occasionally the bug

This section previously claimed the opposite of what happens: that native
Windows binaries cannot open MSYS paths like `/tmp/x` or `/c/Users/...`, and
that you should convert with `cygpath -w`. Two reviewers independently
disproved it by experiment, and it was rewritten on 2026-07-15. It is recorded
rather than quietly deleted because the false version was actively harmful: it
pushed readers toward pointless conversions while saying nothing about the case
that does bite.

**What actually happens: MSYS rewrites POSIX-looking paths in argv into Windows
paths *before* the native binary is executed.** The binary never sees `/tmp/x`.
It does not need to understand MSYS paths, because it is never handed one:

```
$ W=$(mktemp -d)                    # /tmp/tmp.Qf9Bqyvz1v
$ python -c 'import sys; print(sys.argv[1])' "$W/k.txt"
C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Temp/tmp.Qf9Bqyvz1v/k.txt     <- already converted
```

So the things the old text said were impossible all work, verified 2026-07-15:

```
$ python -c 'import sys; print(open(sys.argv[1]).read())' "$W/k.txt"   # reads it
$ age-keygen -o "$W/id.txt"                                            # writes it
$ age-keygen -y "$W/id.txt"                                            # reads it back
```

**It applies to environment variables too**, which is the load-bearing case for
[topic-sops](topic-sops.md) — native `sops.exe` finds its identity through a
POSIX path in `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE`:

```
$ SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE=/c/Users/<user>/.soevereinlab/mini-cloud-age.txt \
    sops decrypt ci/sops-canary.sops.yaml
sops_canary: decryption-works
```

That was checked with negative controls, because "it decrypted" on its own does
not prove the variable was the reason: **unset** → `no master key was able to
decrypt`; **wrong path** → same failure. So the variable was load-bearing and
the POSIX path resolved.

`cygpath -w` is therefore usually unnecessary. It is not *wrong* — a converted
path also works — it is just solving a problem the shell already solved.

**Where the conversion is the bug** is when a path was never meant to become a
Windows path:

- **`/dev/stdin` has no Windows equivalent.** MSYS maps it to `/proc/self/fd/0`
  and then converts that to `C:\proc\self\fd\0`, and sops reports `cannot
  operate on non-existent file "C:\proc\self\fd\0"`. A pipe works; the
  `/dev/stdin` path does not. See [topic-sops](topic-sops.md).
- **`docker -v <host>:<container>`** — the *container-side* path is a Linux
  path that must survive intact, and MSYS converts it anyway:

  ```
  $ cmd //c echo /data
  "C:/Program Files/Git/data"                <- the container path, mangled

  $ docker run --rm -v "$(pwd -W):/data" python:3.12-slim ls /data
  ls: cannot access 'C:/Program Files/Git/data': No such file or directory

  $ MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker run --rm -v "$(pwd -W):/data" python:3.12-slim ls /data
  <the directory listing>                    <- works
  ```

  So `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` plus a `pwd -W` host path is the right recipe, and
  the reason is not "docker cannot read MSYS paths" — it is that half the
  argument is not a host path at all.

  **Prefix it, do not export it.** `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` in front of the one
  command is a fix; `export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` in a shell breaks unrelated
  things, because the conversion it disables is also what makes a POSIX path in
  an *environment variable* reach a native binary correctly. Observed
  2026-07-15: with it exported, `sops decrypt` fails on a `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE`
  holding a POSIX path ("cannot find the path specified"); unset, the same
  command works. The variable is a scalpel with a blast radius — the same
  mechanism, wanted here and unwanted there.

The rule that survives: **suppress the conversion when a POSIX path must stay
POSIX; otherwise let it happen.** Reaching for `cygpath` because a native
binary is involved is cargo cult.

The general lesson is the same one this page keeps relearning: the old text was
plausible, matched a real mental model of how MSYS "must" work, and was never
executed. One `python -c 'print(sys.argv[1])'` would have settled it.

heading_path: Set up the bootstrap pipeline for a new node set
Goal
text:
From an empty `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` repo to a pipeline that configures both
nodes: `lint` on merge requests, `bootstrap` (creates the deploy user, as root),
`apply` (the baseline hardening) and `verify` (proves the hardening is live).
After this, changing a node is a merge request, not an SSH session.

heading_path: Set up the bootstrap pipeline for a new node set
Preconditions
text:
- The nodes are installed and hold the deploy key for root:
  `rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning` has been executed on each.
- The deploy keypair exists at `~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy` on the operator
  workstation. **The private key lives in exactly two places: that file, and a
  protected GitLab CI file variable. It is never committed, anywhere.**
- Maintainer on the GitLab project (to set variables and protect `main`).

heading_path: Set up the bootstrap pipeline for a new node set
Steps
text:
1. **Protect `main` so nothing reaches the nodes without review.**

   ```
   glab api --method POST "projects/<project-path-urlencoded>/protected_branches" \
     -f name=main -f push_access_level=0 -f merge_access_level=40 -f allow_force_push=false
   ```

   *Expected result:* the response shows `"access_level":0` ("No one") for push
   and `40` ("Maintainers") for merge.

2. **Add the private key as a protected CI file variable.**

   Settings → CI/CD → Variables → Add variable:

   - Key: `ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY`
   - Type: **File**
   - **Protect variable**: on (so it exists only on protected branches)
   - **Mask variable**: off (a multi-line key cannot be masked)
   - **Expand variable reference**: off
   - Value: the entire contents of `~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy`, including the
     `-----BEGIN`/`-----END` lines **and the trailing newline**

   *Expected result:*

   ```
   glab api "projects/<project-path-urlencoded>/variables/ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY"
   ```

   reports `"variable_type":"file"` and `"protected":true`.

   A key without its trailing newline is rejected by OpenSSH with an
   unhelpful error inside CI. Check the value ends with one.

3. **Fill in the node IPs in `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml`.**

   Public IPs are committed here on purpose: this is the config repo.

   *Expected result:* `ansible-inventory -i ansible/inventory/hosts.yml --list`
   lists both hosts with their `ansible_host`.

4. **Pin the node host keys (trust on first scan).**

   ```
   ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 <node-1-ip> <node-2-ip> > ansible/known_hosts
   ```

   *Expected result:* two lines of the form `<ip> ssh-ed25519 AAAA...`. Verify
   before committing that strict checking works against the file:

   ```
   ssh -i ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
       -o UserKnownHostsFile=ansible/known_hosts root@<node-ip> 'cat /etc/debian_version'
   ```

   prints `13.x` with no prompt. Do this **after** the nodes are finally
   installed: reinstalling a node changes its host key and the pipeline will
   then refuse to connect.

5. **Merge the pipeline and roles to `main` via a merge request.**

   *Expected result:* the MR pipeline's `lint` job passes (`ansible-lint` plus
   `--syntax-check` on both playbooks).

6. **Let `bootstrap` run.**

   It starts automatically on `main` and only bootstraps nodes that do not yet
   answer as the deploy user with working sudo.

   *Expected result:* on fresh nodes, `PLAY RECAP` with `failed=0` and
   `changed=3` per host. On nodes that already have a deploy user:
   `Nothing to bootstrap. All nodes already have a working deploy user.` and a
   green job.

7. **Play `apply` (manual).**

   *Expected result:* `PLAY RECAP` with `failed=0` on every host. The first
   successful run shows `changed` > 0.

8. **Let `verify` run.**

   It starts by itself when `apply` succeeds.

   *Expected result:*

   ```
   --- <node-ip>
   ok: root login refused
   ok: password login refused
   ok: ufw, fail2ban and unattended-upgrades as declared
   ...
   All nodes verified: hardening is in effect, not just written down.
   ```

heading_path: Set up the bootstrap pipeline for a new node set
Verification
text:
- `apply` reports `failed=0` on both nodes.
- `verify` passes — this is the check that matters. It tests behaviour from
  outside; the other checks only read files.
- Playing `apply` a second time reports `changed=0, failed=0` on every host.
  Anything else means a task is not idempotent: find it and fix it, do not
  re-run until it looks quiet.

heading_path: Set up the bootstrap pipeline for a new node set
Rollback
text:
Reinstall the nodes via `rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning` and run this
runbook again. Before the baseline lands, the nodes hold no state worth
keeping, so a rebuild costs only the install.

After reinstalling, regenerate `ansible/known_hosts` (step 4): the host keys
change and strict host key checking is deliberate.

heading_path: Set up the bootstrap pipeline for a new node set
Traps this pipeline has already fallen into
text:
Recorded because each one cost real time, and none of them is obvious from the
code:

- **ufw's rate-limit bans CI.** `ufw limit` on 22/tcp rejects a source that
  opens 6 new connections within 30 seconds. Ansible's default SSH multiplexing
  keeps that at one connection per host — but setting `ssh_args` in
  `ansible.cfg` *replaces* the default (`-C -o ControlMaster=auto
  -o ControlPersist=60s`) instead of extending it. Without those options every
  task reconnects, and the play dies mid-run with `Connection refused` (REJECT,
  not a timeout — hence "refused" rather than a hang). Keep the multiplexing
  options whenever you touch `ssh_args`.
- **`verify` must wait out that same window** before probing, or the firewall
  fails its own verification.
- **A blocking manual job jams every later stage.** Under `rules`,
  `when: manual` defaults to `allow_failure: false`. An unplayed `bootstrap`
  once left `apply` stuck in `created` — and since bootstrap only works before
  hardening closes root login, it would have jammed `apply` permanently.
- **A failed play skips its handlers,** which is how a config file ends up
  correct on disk while the daemon never loads it. `force_handlers = True` in
  `ansible.cfg` closes that. See `rb-2026-07-14-debian-hardening` for the full
  story — it is the most dangerous failure here, because everything reports
  green.

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
Goal
text:
Every node reachable only by SSH key, only as the `deploy` user, behind a
default-deny firewall, with fail2ban watching and security updates installing
themselves — all of it applied by the `apply` job and proven by `verify`.

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
Preconditions
text:
- `rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline` completed: the deploy user exists on every
  node and CI can reach them.

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
What the baseline enforces
text:
| Area | Enforced | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SSH | `PermitRootLogin no`, `PasswordAuthentication no`, `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no`, `X11Forwarding no`, `MaxAuthTries 3` | A drop-in at `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf`, validated with `sshd -t` before it is written. |
| Firewall | ufw: default deny incoming, allow outgoing, `limit` on 22/tcp | Phase A opens nothing else. |
| Brute force | fail2ban, `sshd` jail, 5 tries / 10 min, 1h ban | **`backend = systemd`** — see the traps below. |
| Updates | `unattended-upgrades` enabled and running | |
| Clock | Timezone Europe/Amsterdam | |

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
Steps
text:
1. **Play the `apply` job on the `main` pipeline.**

   *Expected result:* `PLAY RECAP` with `failed=0` on every host.

2. **Let `verify` run.** It starts by itself when `apply` succeeds and fails the
   pipeline if the hardening is not actually in effect.

   *Expected result:*

   ```
   --- <node-ip>
   ok: root login refused
   ok: password login refused
   ok: ufw, fail2ban and unattended-upgrades as declared
   ```

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
Verification
text:
`verify` does all of this automatically. To check by hand:

```
ssh -i ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy -o UserKnownHostsFile=ansible/known_hosts \
    deploy@<node-ip> 'sudo ufw status verbose; sudo fail2ban-client status sshd; systemctl is-enabled unattended-upgrades'
```

*Expected result:* `Status: active`, `Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing)`,
a `22/tcp LIMIT IN` rule, an active `sshd` jail, and `enabled`.

```
ssh -i ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy -o UserKnownHostsFile=ansible/known_hosts root@<node-ip> 'echo no'
ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile=ansible/known_hosts -o PubkeyAuthentication=no \
    -o PreferredAuthentications=password deploy@<node-ip> 'echo no'
```

*Expected result:* both `Permission denied (publickey)`, with no password
prompt.

**Do not verify by reading the config.** See the first trap below: that is
exactly what hid a wide-open root login behind a green pipeline.

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
Rollback
text:
If the hardening locks you out, the drop-in is the only thing to remove:

1. Open the node's VNC console in the netcup SCP (this works when SSH does not).
2. Log in as root, `rm /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf`, then
   `systemctl restart ssh`.

*Expected result:* the previous SSH behaviour returns. Fix the cause in git and
run `apply` again — do not leave the node repaired by hand, or the next `apply`
will simply reapply the same mistake.

heading_path: Baseline hardening of a Debian 13 node (via pipeline)
Traps
text:
### A green pipeline is not proof (the important one)

The first `apply` reported `failed=0` and passed while **root login was still
open on both nodes**. `sshd -T` printed `permitrootlogin no` throughout.
Nothing was lying: the config file really did say that.

The chain: an earlier run died on the ufw rate-limit *after* writing the
drop-in. On the retry the file was already correct, so Ansible's template task
did not report `changed`, so its handler never fired, so sshd went on running
the config it had loaded at boot. Reading configuration cannot catch this,
because the configuration is correct. Only the running daemon knows, and it
only tells you if you try to log in.

Three defences now, because any one of them can be defeated:

- `force_handlers = True` in `ansible.cfg` — a failed play still runs its
  handlers, so the drift never forms.
- The baseline role compares the running sshd's start time (the mtime of
  `/proc/<pid>`, same host so no clock skew) with the drop-in's mtime, and
  restarts sshd when the daemon is older than its own config.
- The `verify` job tests behaviour over the network. It is the only defence a
  correct-looking file cannot fool.

The general lesson outlives sshd: **"the config says X" and "the service does
X" are different claims.** Anything that reloads config on change can drift
this way. Verify the behaviour, not the file.

### fail2ban finds no log

Debian ships no `/var/log/auth.log` without rsyslog, so fail2ban's default
`sshd` jail silently watches a file that does not exist and bans nobody. The
jail sets `backend = systemd` to read the journal instead. If you ever see the
jail active with a permanently empty ban list, check this first.

### sshd may be socket-activated

Debian 13 documents socket activation (`ssh.socket` owning port 22, sshd
spawned per connection) as the default for fresh installs. The netcup image
does not do this — `ssh.socket` is inactive there and plain `ssh.service` is in
charge. The role detects which unit is running rather than assuming, because
restarting `ssh.service` while the socket holds port 22 fails with
`Cannot bind any address`. Under socket activation no restart is needed at all:
each connection spawns an sshd that reads the config fresh.

### ufw rate-limits your automation too

`limit` on 22/tcp rejects a source after 6 new connections in 30 seconds — your
CI runner included. See `rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline` for the SSH
multiplexing setting that keeps Ansible under it.

heading_path: Provision or reinstall a netcup VPS (Debian 13)
Goal
text:
A freshly installed Debian 13 VPS, reachable over SSH as `root` with the
mini-cloud deploy key. This is the only manual head-end of the platform:
netcup has no Terraform provider, so the image install and the first key
handover are done by hand. Everything after this point is done by the
pipeline in the `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` repo.

Use this runbook when adding a node, rebuilding a node that has drifted or
broken, or recovering from a lost SSH key.

heading_path: Provision or reinstall a netcup VPS (Debian 13)
Preconditions
text:
- Access to the netcup Server Control Panel (SCP) for the target VPS.
- The mini-cloud deploy keypair exists on the operator workstation:
  `~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy` and `~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy.pub`.
  Verify: `ls ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy.pub` prints the path.
- A POSIX shell. On Windows: **Git Bash**. Step 4 needs `ssh-copy-id`, which
  Windows' bundled OpenSSH does not provide (a PowerShell alternative is
  given inline).
- The node holds no data you still need — step 2 erases the disk.

heading_path: Provision or reinstall a netcup VPS (Debian 13)
Steps
text:
1. **Log in to the netcup Server Control Panel.**

   Open <https://www.servercontrolpanel.de/> and select the target VPS from
   the server list.

   *Expected result:* the server's status page is shown, with the current
   power state and the assigned public IP.

2. **Install the Debian 13 image.**

   A new netcup VPS ships with Debian 13 minimal already installed — if the
   node is fresh and untouched, skip to step 3.

   To reinstall, go to *Media* → *Images*, pick **Debian 13** (minimal), set
   a strong root password when prompted, and start the installation.

   Debian 13 (trixie) is deliberate, not just the default: Debian 12
   (bookworm) left regular security support on 2026-07-12 and is now on LTS
   until June 2028, while trixie has full support until August 2028 and LTS
   until June 2030. Starting a new node on bookworm would mean planning a
   distro upgrade inside the platform's first years. See
   `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection` for the surrounding choices.

   The root password is only needed for the few minutes until step 4
   completes; after that, password login is never used again and the
   baseline hardening disables it entirely. Do not store it in a repo, a
   runbook, or a chat.

   *Expected result:* the install runs to completion (a few minutes) and the
   server reports as running.

3. **Note the public IP.**

   Read the IPv4 address from the server's status page.

   *Expected result:* an IPv4 address, e.g. `203.0.113.10`. This value goes
   into `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` in the `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` repo —
   public node IPs are committed there by design (that is the config repo).

4. **Copy the deploy key to root.**

   On a Windows workstation, run this **in Git Bash, not in PowerShell**.
   Windows' bundled OpenSSH has no `ssh-copy-id`, and calling Git Bash from
   PowerShell breaks the path: PowerShell expands `~` to `C:\Users\...` and
   the shell then eats the backslashes.

   ```
   ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy.pub root@<node-ip>
   ```

   Accept the host key fingerprint when asked — this is the trust-on-first-use
   moment; the same key is pinned into `ansible/known_hosts` later. Then enter
   the root password from step 2.

   *Expected result:* `Number of key(s) added: 1`.

   If you must stay in PowerShell, do it without `ssh-copy-id`:

   ```
   Get-Content ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy.pub -Raw | ssh root@<node-ip> "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && tr -d '\r' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && sort -u -o ~/.ssh/authorized_keys ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"
   ```

   `tr -d '\r'` strips the Windows line endings PowerShell sends; `sort -u`
   keeps the file clean if you run this twice.

   *Expected result:* a password prompt, then no output and no error.

5. **Verify key-based login.**

   ```
   ssh -i ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy root@<node-ip> 'echo ok'
   ```

   *Expected result:* `ok`, with no password prompt.

heading_path: Provision or reinstall a netcup VPS (Debian 13)
Verification
text:
Key-based root login works and the node reports Debian 13:

```
ssh -i ~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy root@<node-ip> 'cat /etc/debian_version'
```

*Expected result:* `13.x` (e.g. `13.6`), no password prompt. From here on
the root password is not needed; the bootstrap pipeline takes over.

heading_path: Provision or reinstall a netcup VPS (Debian 13)
Rollback
text:
Re-run the image install from step 2 in the SCP. At this stage the node
holds no state, so a reinstall costs only the minutes of the install itself.

If the node was already in service, note that a reinstall changes the SSH
host key: rerun `ssh-keyscan` and update `ansible/known_hosts` in the
`soevereinlab-mini-cloud` repo, otherwise the pipeline will refuse to
connect (strict host key checking is deliberate).

heading_path: Keep public DNS IPv4-only until the platform serves IPv6
Goal
text:
Public DNS for the platform domain serves **only** the records the platform
can actually answer: A records pointing at the ingress node, and **no AAAA
(IPv6) records** as long as the platform is IPv4-only. Use this runbook when
setting up a new domain, after any change in the DNS panel, and whenever the
automated check (below) turns red.

Why this matters more than a missing record would:

- **Certificate issuance breaks.** Let's Encrypt prefers IPv6 whenever an
  AAAA record exists. The HTTP-01 challenge then lands on whatever answers
  that address — not your node — and issuance fails with a misleading
  "unauthorized" error that makes you debug the wrong machine.
- **IPv6 visitors silently land elsewhere.** Dual-stack clients prefer AAAA
  too, so they reach the wrong server while everything looks fine from an
  IPv4-only workstation.

The trap is that you rarely create these records yourself: **DNS hosters add
AAAA records by default**, pointing at their own parking platform. Observed
2026-07-15 at Yourhosting: fresh apex and wildcard AAAA records into
`2a05:1500::/27` (their infrastructure) that were never asked for. Deleting
an A record or changing hosting packages can re-apply such defaults — DNS
drifts without any commit.

heading_path: Keep public DNS IPv4-only until the platform serves IPv6
Preconditions
text:
- Access to the DNS panel of the domain.
- `dig` (package `dnsutils`) on any Linux/WSL shell, or `nslookup` on Windows.
- You know the ingress node's public IPv4 address (`<ingress-node-ip>`; it
  lives in the config repo's inventory, not here).

heading_path: Keep public DNS IPv4-only until the platform serves IPv6
Steps
text:
1. **Audit what public resolvers actually serve.** Query a public resolver
   directly — your own cache lies:

   ```
   dig +short A   <your-domain>       @1.1.1.1
   dig +short A   demo.<your-domain>  @1.1.1.1
   dig +short AAAA <your-domain>      @1.1.1.1
   dig +short AAAA demo.<your-domain> @1.1.1.1
   dig +short AAAA random-label.<your-domain> @1.1.1.1
   ```

   *Expected result:* every A query returns exactly `<ingress-node-ip>`;
   every AAAA query returns **nothing**. The random label matters: parking
   defaults live on the wildcard, so records you never created only show up
   on names you never created.

2. **Delete any AAAA records in the DNS panel.** Look for AAAA entries on
   the apex (`<your-domain>`) *and* the wildcard (`*.<your-domain>`) — panels
   sometimes list defaults separately from user-created records.

   *Expected result:* the panel lists only the A records you created.

3. **Confirm the deletion has propagated.** Re-run the AAAA queries from
   step 1 against two resolvers (`@1.1.1.1` and `@8.8.8.8`).

   *Expected result:* no addresses returned by either. Allow up to the
   record's TTL for cached answers to age out before treating a leftover as
   a failure.

4. **Rely on the automated check from here on.** The config repo
   (`soevereinlab-mini-cloud`) carries `scripts/verify-dns.sh` and a
   `verify:dns` CI job that runs on every `main` pipeline **and on a daily
   schedule**, asking two public resolvers whether the records still match
   the policy. A hoster re-applying its defaults turns the scheduled
   pipeline red instead of waiting to be discovered during a failed
   certificate renewal.

   *Expected result:* the `verify:dns` job in the latest scheduled pipeline
   is green.

heading_path: Keep public DNS IPv4-only until the platform serves IPv6
Verification
text:
Run the check exactly as CI does, from the config repo:

```
bash scripts/verify-dns.sh
```

*Expected output:* `ok` lines for every name/resolver combination, ending in
`DNS verified: IPv4 records point at <ingress-node-name> and the IPv6 policy
holds.` with exit code 0. The failure mode is proven too: pointed at a
dual-stack domain, the script reports each stray AAAA record and exits 1.

> The real line names the node outright. That string is correct where it lives
> — the config repo may hold hostnames (spec §7) — and cannot be quoted here,
> where the same §7 says they do not belong. Substituted rather than dropped,
> because the line is how you know the check passed. Expect this shape
> whenever a runbook quotes observed output: **the quoting is the leak**, not
> the tool, and the fix is always here rather than in the thing being quoted.

heading_path: Keep public DNS IPv4-only until the platform serves IPv6
Rollback
text:
Not applicable as a repair — the pre-runbook state (stray AAAA records) is
the defect. When the platform deliberately goes dual-stack later:

1. Add AAAA records pointing at the node's own IPv6 addresses (not the
   hoster's).
2. Set `EXPECTED_IPV6` in `scripts/verify-dns.sh` to that address instead of
   deleting the check — the guard then enforces the *new* policy.

heading_path: Bootstrap GitOps with Argo CD on k3s
Goal
text:
Install Argo CD on the cluster once, via Ansible, so that from then on **every
platform or app change is a git commit** — no `ansible-playbook`, no
`kubectl apply`, no cluster-admin in anyone's shell. This runbook covers the
one-time bootstrap, how a new app arrives afterwards (with the clocked proof
that it does), and a repeatable break/heal test that proves the loop actually
reconciles rather than merely reads green. Use it for the first GitOps
stand-up and whenever you need to re-prove the sync loop.

heading_path: Bootstrap GitOps with Argo CD on k3s
Preconditions
text:
- A working cluster (`rb-2026-07-17-k3s-cluster-bootstrap`): the server node
  serves 6443, both nodes `Ready`.
- SOPS and the age identity are available to the **controller** (the machine or
  CI job running `apply`), not the node: the workstation key at
  `~/.soevereinlab/mini-cloud-age.txt` and CI's `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE` — the
  private key lives in exactly those two places and nowhere else.
- A read-only GitLab deploy token for the config repo, SOPS-encrypted in
  `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml`.

heading_path: Bootstrap GitOps with Argo CD on k3s
Steps
text:
### Stage 1 — Ansible lays Argo CD and the root app (once)

1. **Understand the two-stage design before running it.** `apply` runs
   `roles/gitops_bootstrap`, which does only the bootstrap: it decrypts the
   deploy token on the controller (`community.sops.load_vars`, `no_log: true`),
   writes **three** manifests into the k3s server's manifests directory
   (`/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/`) — the `HelmChart` that installs
   Argo CD, the `repo-secret` (the deploy token as a repository Secret), and the
   `root` `Application` — and then waits on the cluster. After that the role gets
   out of the way: the `root` Application watches `gitops/` on `main` and
   everything else arrives as a commit.

   *Expected result:* the role completes both waits — `argo-cd-argocd-server`
   becomes `available`, and `root` reaches `Synced:Healthy`. Observed on the
   task-4 apply (pipeline `2680045590`): Argo CD installed, root Application
   synced; a second apply `changed=0`; the node showing `root  Synced  Healthy`
   with the controller/repo-server/server/redis pods `Running`.

2. **Know the manifests-dir retry behaviour — it is expected, not a race.** k3s'
   helm/deploy controller polls `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` on its
   own ~15s clock and **retries on failure**. Two of the three manifests — the
   Argo CD `HelmChart` and the `root` Application — land before the CRDs they
   need exist and are rejected until the chart creates them; the controller keeps
   retrying until they apply. (The `repo-secret` is a plain core `Secret` with no
   CRD dependency, so it applies straight away — it is not part of this race.)
   The role comment states this outright: "the two manifests below land before
   the CRDs they need exist and are rejected until the chart creates them. That
   is expected, not a race."

   *Expected result:* transient rejections in the controller log during the
   first sync, resolving on their own once the Argo CD chart is up. The role's
   `kubectl wait` retries (20×15s for the server Deployment, 40×15s for
   `root` Synced:Healthy) cover exactly the window between "manifest written"
   and "object created".

3. **Know the deploy-token + SOPS flow.** The token is decrypted on the
   controller and templated into `repo-secret.yaml`, which lands on the node in
   **plaintext** (0600, root) — k3s' manifests directory has no other mode. The
   encryption protects the token *in git*, not on the server. One repo URL feeds
   both the repository Secret and the root Application: Argo CD matches a
   repository Secret to an Application by URL, and if the two disagree it fails
   quietly as "authentication required" on a repo whose secret is sitting right
   there, so both read `gitops_bootstrap_repo_url` from one default.

   *Expected result:* Argo CD authenticates to the repo; the `root` Application
   shows no "authentication required" condition.

4. **Apply the root-app `directory.exclude` — the lesson that cost a red sync.**
   The `root` Application syncs `gitops/` with `recurse: true`. Without an
   exclude it also applies the child apps' *manifests* (`apps/*/manifests/**`),
   which are namespaced to `demo` — but `root` has no `CreateNamespace` sync
   option, so its direct apply strands. **Observed failure** (mini-cloud !19,
   commit `1858d3d`): the root sync failed with

   ```
   namespaces "demo" not found (retried 5 times)
   ```

   The fix is one line under `spec.source.directory`:

   ```
   exclude: "apps/*/manifests/**"
   ```

   Now `root` manages Applications and platform resources only; each child
   Application owns its own manifests **with** `CreateNamespace=true`. Why the
   root must not apply them itself: two controllers applying the same namespaced
   objects, one of which cannot create the namespace, is a sync that fails on
   the missing namespace while the child that *can* create it is right there.

   *Expected result:* after the exclude, `root` reaches `Synced/Healthy`, the
   `demo` child Application creates namespace `demo` and applies the app
   manifests, and certificate issuance starts.

### Stage 2 — every new app is a commit

5. **Add an app by committing a manifest.** A new app is a file under `gitops/`
   merged to `main`; Argo CD applies it, prunes what you remove, and reverts
   out-of-band edits (`prune: true`, `selfHeal: true`). Nothing is
   `kubectl apply`-ed by hand.

   *Expected result — the clocked proof (task 5, succescriterium 3):* merging
   `replicas: 1 → 2` on the whoami Deployment (mini-cloud !21, `merged_at`
   07:27:28) brought
   a **second** pod `Running` at ≈ **07:29** — about **2 minutes**, within Argo's
   sync interval, with no manual action, and the scheduler placed it on the
   **other** node (the agent), so the cross-node encrypted overlay carries real
   traffic. End state: `deployment.apps/whoami 2/2`, all Applications
   `Synced/Healthy`.

   *Window nuance (audit taak 5, A-1), stated so the proof is honest:* at
   07:29:07 the `apply` job was also started manually (pipeline `2680695819`), so
   the observation window was not clean. It is causally excluded: since the !19
   exclude the root app does not touch the demo manifests and the role never
   writes them, so `replicas: 2` can only have arrived via Argo's git-sync — and
   at mini-cloud !20 a certificate renewal demonstrably arrived with **no** apply
   at all.
   The proof stands, with the note.

### Break/heal test — prove the loop reconciles

> These steps are **destructive cluster mutations** (`kubectl patch`/`scale`).
> Per the execution harness they require direct authorization in the executing
> session — they cannot be delegated to a sub-agent. Save the pre-state first;
> restore from the saved JSON exactly.

6. **Save the pre-state.** Capture both syncPolicies verbatim — these are your
   exact restore values:

   ```
   root .spec.syncPolicy: {"automated":{"prune":true,"selfHeal":true}}
   demo .spec.syncPolicy: {"automated":{"prune":true,"selfHeal":true},"syncOptions":["CreateNamespace=true"]}
   ```

7. **Break it — pause the OUTER app first.** Null the syncPolicy on `root`, then
   on `demo` (outer before inner, so selfHeal cannot re-enable the inner from the
   outer), then scale the workload to zero:

   ```
   kubectl patch application root --type merge -p '{"spec":{"syncPolicy":null}}'
   kubectl patch application demo --type merge -p '{"spec":{"syncPolicy":null}}'
   kubectl scale deploy whoami -n demo --replicas=0
   ```

   *Expected result (observed 2026-07-16 21:49:53, +30s):* `whoami 0/0`, `demo`
   `OutOfSync` — the break held; selfHeal was effectively off. Then run the
   external check (`verify:platform:on-demand`): it **fails** with exactly

   ```
   FAIL: https://demo.<your-domain> did not return success without -k
   FAIL: Application(s) not Synced/Healthy: demo=OutOfSync/Healthy
   ```

   the other 7 checks ok → `2 check(s) failed` (on-demand job `15383679279`).

8. **Heal it — restore the INNER app first.** Re-apply the saved syncPolicies to
   `demo`, then `root` (inner before outer):

   ```
   kubectl patch application demo --type merge -p '<demo syncPolicy JSON>'
   kubectl patch application root --type merge -p '<root syncPolicy JSON>'
   ```

   *Expected result (observed 21:54:30 → 21:54:40):* selfHeal already had
   whoami back to `2/2` (pods age 11s); all Applications `Synced/Healthy`; both
   policies byte-identical to the pre-state. Re-run the external check via retry
   (`POST .../jobs/<id>/retry`, which mints a **new** job-id because the first
   is now `failed` — job `15387392320`): **success**, all 9 checks ok, ending
   "All checks passed: the platform works from the outside, not just on paper."

heading_path: Bootstrap GitOps with Argo CD on k3s
Verification
text:
The break/heal test above is the verification: a red external check on a real
break, green after restore, both in CI job traces, with the workload and the
saved syncPolicies proving the restore was exact. For a quick standing check:

```
ssh deploy@<server-ip> 'sudo k3s kubectl -n argocd get applications.argoproj.io'
```

*Expected output:* `root`, `cert-manager` and `demo` all `Synced` / `Healthy`.

**The lesson that changes how you read this:** Argo CD's status flags are
snapshots, not break evidence. During the break above, `root`'s sync status
flipped back to `Synced` (trace 21:53:15) while the drift was still present and
the restore was still needed. Base your break/heal judgement on **primary
symptoms** — the workload being down (`whoami 0/0`) and the external endpoint
failing — and treat the reconciler's status flag as secondary (audit taak 6,
les 3).

heading_path: Bootstrap GitOps with Argo CD on k3s
Rollback
text:
The break/heal test is self-reversing — step 8 is its rollback, and the saved
pre-state JSONs from step 6 are what make it exact. Do not leave a session with
a nulled syncPolicy or a scaled-down deployment; re-apply the saved policies and
confirm `2/2` and `Synced/Healthy` before ending.

Removing Argo CD itself is not a step taken here. Because `prune: true` is on,
deleting a manifest from `main` removes what it created; deleting the `root`
Application stops reconciliation but leaves the objects it synced in place.
Uninstalling k3s (the other runbook's rollback) removes everything with the
datastore.

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
Goal
text:
Back up the one piece of state that a rebuilt k3s cluster cannot regenerate —
the SQLite datastore — from each node to the *other* node, encrypted, with a
live-safe snapshot, a daily timer, and a CI guard. Then prove the backups are
restorable **on a copy** without ever touching the live datastore. Use this
runbook for the first bring-up, for the recurring restore drill, and as the
reference for what is and is not backed up (and why). A real cutover onto
restored data is out of scope here — that is the DR exercise (C8).

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
Preconditions
text:
- A working 2-node cluster (`rb-2026-07-17-k3s-cluster-bootstrap`): the server
  node runs the embedded SQLite datastore in WAL mode (observed: `state.db` +
  `-wal` + `-shm`, no `etcd/`).
- SOPS + age available to the controller running `apply`: `restic_password`
  lives in `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml`.
- Peer-to-peer reachability on the SSH port between the two nodes' public IPs
  (see the transport note in step 3).

All role paths are in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` (`ansible/roles/backup/`).

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
The cross-node design — what is backed up, and what never is
text:
The `backup` role runs on **both** nodes in one non-serial play: each node is a
restic *source* backing up to the *other* node as an SFTP *receiver*, so a lost
node's state lives on its peer.

- **Server node backs up:** a live-safe snapshot of the SQLite datastore
  (`state.db`), the **k3s server token**, and `config.yaml`.
- **Agent node backs up:** `config.yaml` (keeps the cross-backup verifiable in
  both directions).
- **Never backed up: the admin kubeconfig.** A backup that carries
  cluster-admin credentials turns every offsite copy into a root key to the
  cluster. The token is enough to decrypt the datastore for a restore
  (`docs.k3s.io/datastore/backup-restore`); the admin kubeconfig is
  regenerable and is deliberately excluded (spec §7).

Extension hooks are stubbed, not wired: `backup_extra_paths: []` (for future
PV data) and `backup_offsite_repository: ""` (the offsite target — gate 2).

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
Steps
text:
### Stage 1 — install and initialise

1. **Install a pinned restic binary by SHA.** Debian 13 trixie ships
   `restic 0.18.0-1+b4` in apt (documented as the fallback), but the role
   installs the **upstream binary 0.18.0 pinned by SHA-256**
   (`98f6dd8bf5b59058d04bfd8dab58e196cc2a680666ccee90275a3b722374438e`, asset
   `restic_0.18.0_linux_amd64.bz2`) via `get_url` with `checksum:` — which fails
   hard on a mismatch, the same pattern used for the sops binary. `sqlite3` and
   `bzip2` come from apt (ordinary distro tools).

   *Expected result (design expectation from the SHA-pinned install, not
   separately clocked):* `restic version` should report `0.18.0` on both nodes.

2. **Initialise the repo idempotently.** A dedicated `nologin` `restic` receive
   user, a repo directory per peer, the repo password decrypted from SOPS into a
   node-local `no_log` file, and `restic cat config || restic init` so a re-run
   does not re-init an existing repo.

   *Expected result (design expectation from the `restic cat config || restic
   init` construct, not separately clocked):* on the first apply the repo
   initialises; on any later apply it is left as-is. See step 5 for the SFTP
   receiver that makes the remote repo reachable.

### Stage 2 — the live-safe snapshot

3. **Snapshot SQLite with the Online Backup API — not a raw file copy.** The k3s
   datastore is a live SQLite database; copying the three files
   (`state.db`/`-wal`/`-shm`) under active writes can capture a torn state. The
   role instead runs:

   ```
   sqlite3 <state.db> ".backup '<dest>'"
   ```

   The `.backup` CLI uses SQLite's **Online Backup API**
   (`sqlite3_backup_init/step/finish`), which produces a transactionally
   consistent snapshot even under concurrent writes and restarts the copy if the
   source changes mid-copy (`sqlite.org/backup.html`); WAL mode lets this reader
   run alongside k3s' writer (`sqlite.org/wal.html`). The server token is backed
   up with it because it decrypts the datastore on restore. Full flag reasoning:
   [topic-restic](../topics/topic-restic.md).

   *Expected result:* a single consistent `state.db` snapshot per run, taken
   without stopping k3s.

### Stage 3 — transport and the SFTP receiver

4. **Know the transport: public peer IP, because there is no management tunnel
   (gate 2b).** The design brief assumed a "WireGuard IP of the peer" — it does
   not exist. The only WireGuard on these nodes is flannel's **pod overlay**
   (`flannel-wg 10.42.0.0/32`, observed), which is not a node-to-node management
   tunnel. The role therefore defaults transport to the **public peer IP**
   (`backup_peer_address`, configurable): restic and SSH both encrypt the
   traffic, and — the DR argument — a backup must keep working precisely when the
   overlay is broken. Routing over `flannel-wg` instead is a one-variable change.
   **The public-vs-overlay choice is a gate for Jelle (gate 2b).**

5. **The receiver must be SFTP-only via sshd, not `authorized_keys command=`.**
   The `restic` user has `/usr/sbin/nologin` as its shell. An `authorized_keys`
   forced command runs **via the login shell**, so with `nologin` the command
   never starts and nologin's message pollutes the SFTP stream. This bit the
   first init:

   ```
   unable to start the sftp session ... packet too long
   ```

   with the handshake showing the pollution verbatim: `This account is currently
   not available.` The canonical fix (**command-cookbook recipe 17**) is
   server-side — an sshd drop-in (`/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-restic-sftp.conf`):

   ```
   Match User restic
       ForceCommand internal-sftp
   ```

   `internal-sftp` is in-process (no shell, no support files) and sshd's
   `ForceCommand` overrides any client command; `authorized_keys` keeps only
   `restrict,from="<peer-ip>"` for key-level scoping.

   *Expected result:* `restic init` completes over SFTP; no "packet too long".

### Stage 4 — schedule and guard

6. **Daily timer plus a CI guard.** A systemd timer runs the backup daily
   (jitter + `Persistent`), and a seed backup runs at apply time. The standing
   guard is the CI job `verify:backup` (`scripts/verify-backup.sh`): per node it
   checks the repo is reachable, runs `restic check --read-data-subset=5%`, and
   asserts the latest snapshot is < 26h old. It runs main-only after `apply`,
   not `allow_failure`.

   *Expected result (observed, first real run):* apply success
   (`changed=11`/node: init + seed) → **`verify:backup` green** on the first real
   run. The red route (a bogus `VERIFY_BACKUP_NODES`) hits `fail()` and exits 1
   in ~10s without touching a real backup.

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
The restore drill — restore on a copy, never over the live datastore
text:
Restoring is the half of "backup" that is usually untested. This drill proves a
snapshot restores to real, openable data — **onto a scratch path**, never over
the live `state.db`.

7. **Restore the latest snapshot to a throwaway target and inspect it.**

   ```
   restic restore latest --target /tmp/restore-check
   ```

   Then confirm the restored datastore is real and intact:

   ```
   ls -l /tmp/restore-check/<path>/state.db
   sqlite3 /tmp/restore-check/<path>/state.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"
   sqlite3 /tmp/restore-check/<path>/state.db ".tables"     # expect the kine table
   ```

   *Expected result (observed 2026-07-17 04:12:14–16Z):* the restored snapshot
   was **34.7 MiB**; `state.db` was **36,417,536 B**; `PRAGMA integrity_check`
   returned **`ok`**; the **`kine`** table (k3s' datastore table) was present;
   the **token** was **109 B**. The scratch target was removed afterwards.

8. **Heed the vacuous-restore warning — check the path first.** The **first**
   attempt was **vacuous**: an `integrity_check` was run against a path where no
   database had actually been restored (a wrong environment assumption), and
   SQLite happily reported **`ok`** on that non-existent/empty path. `PRAGMA
   integrity_check` on a path with no real database still says `ok` — so it
   proves nothing on its own. **Always confirm the restored `state.db` exists at
   the expected path (a real, multi-MB file) *before* trusting the
   integrity_check.** The clocked result in step 7 is the redone,
   non-vacuous run.

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
Verification
text:
The standing verification is the CI job `verify:backup` (step 6): per node repo
reachable + `restic check --read-data-subset=5%` + latest snapshot < 26h,
main-only after apply, green on the first real run. The restore drill (steps
7–8) is the periodic manual proof that the snapshots are not just present but
restorable — run it on a copy, on the schedule the DR plan sets.

For a quick manual snapshot check on a node:

```
sudo restic snapshots           # latest snapshot present and recent
```

heading_path: Cross-node backups of the k3s datastore with restic, and restore-on-a-copy
Rollback / scope boundary
text:
There is no destructive rollback here — the backup path only reads the live
datastore and writes to the peer; the restore drill writes only to a scratch
target it then deletes. Tearing the role down removes the timer, the receiver
user and the repos; it does not touch cluster state.

**A real cutover onto restored data — stopping k3s, replacing `state.db`,
re-seeding the token — is *not* in this runbook.** That is a destructive,
cluster-wide operation and belongs to the **DR exercise (C8)**; this runbook
proves the snapshots are good, the DR runbook uses them. The offsite copy
(`backup_offsite_repository`) is gate 2.

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
Goal
text:
Take the mini-cloud from **freshly delivered nodes** — reinstalled at netcup,
holding nothing — back to a working platform with its data, using only what
lives in git plus the two secrets that live on the operator workstation. This
runbook is the single script for the full DR drill required by spec §6: *both
nodes fresh → platform and data back*, checkable on paper and executable with
Jelle present.

Every rebuild step here **references an existing, tested runbook** rather than
repeating it — this file is the *order* and the *DR-specific decisions*
(what to safeguard first, when a datastore restore is actually needed, the
both-nodes gap, and the IPv6 dual-stack option). Use it for the planned drill,
and as the reference for a real recovery.

> **Status is `draft` on purpose.** This procedure has **not** been executed
> end to end. Each step leans on a runbook that *is* tested, but the sequence
> as a whole — and especially the live datastore cutover (not the
> restore-on-a-copy that C6 proved) and the IPv6 block (§4a, entirely design) —
> is unproven until the drill with Jelle. It becomes `tested` only after that
> drill, with the observed timings filled in where this file now hedges.

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
Scope & assumptions
text:
**"Freshly delivered" means** each node reinstalled to a clean Debian 13 image
via the netcup Server Control Panel — the manual head-end in
[rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning](rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning.md).
netcup has no Terraform provider, so the image install and the first key
handover are by hand; everything after is the pipeline. A reinstall changes the
node's SSH host key — `ansible/known_hosts` in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` must be
regenerated (that runbook's step 4 / rollback), or the pipeline refuses to
connect (strict host-key checking is deliberate).

**What lives outside git and must be safeguarded *before* a disaster, because
the rebuild cannot regenerate it:**

- **The age private key** — `~/.soevereinlab/mini-cloud-age.txt` on the
  workstation, and CI's `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE`. It lives in exactly those two
  places (per
  [rb-2026-07-17-argocd-gitops-bootstrap](rb-2026-07-17-argocd-gitops-bootstrap.md)).
  **Without it, nothing in `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml` decrypts** — that
  envelope holds the GitLab deploy token, the Grafana admin password, and the
  **restic repo password** (`restic_password`, added in C6). So the restic
  password is *not* a separate offsite item to store — it rides inside the SOPS
  envelope and is recovered with the age key. Lose the age key and both the
  platform bootstrap *and* any backup restore are blocked.
- **The deploy SSH keypair** — `~/.ssh/mini-cloud-deploy` on the workstation and
  the protected CI **file** variable `ANSIBLE_DEPLOY_KEY` (per
  [rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline](rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline.md)).
  Without it CI cannot reach the fresh nodes to bootstrap them.
- **The GitLab repos themselves** — `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` (config: inventory,
  roles, `gitops/`, the SOPS envelope) and `soevereinlab-knowledge` (these
  runbooks). GitLab is the source of everything the rebuild replays. Its own
  resilience (a hosted service, plus these local working clones) is a DR
  dimension of its own; naming it is in scope, hardening it is not.

**Access Jelle must hold:** the netcup SCP (to reinstall), and the DNS panel
(to check/repair records). Neither is automatable here.

**What this runbook does *not* cover:** creating the offsite backup target
(gate 2) or activating IPv6 (the §4a block is design only). See "The
both-nodes gap" and §4a.

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
Preconditions
text:
- The two out-of-git secrets above are in hand (age key, deploy key) and known
  to be current.
- Local clones of `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` and `soevereinlab-knowledge`, `glab`
  authenticated, and the workstation toolchain from the phase-A runbooks.
- A decision on the **disaster scope** (see gate, below): *one node lost* (the
  surviving node still holds the peer's backup) or *both nodes lost* (backups
  are gone unless an offsite copy exists — read "The both-nodes gap" first).

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
The rebuild order
text:
Each numbered step is a reference to a runbook that owns the detail and its own
expected result. Do them in order; do not skip the verifications each runbook
carries.

### 1. Provision the fresh node(s)

Reinstall Debian 13 and hand over the deploy key:
[rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning](rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning.md).
Then **regenerate `ansible/known_hosts`** for the reinstalled node(s)
(`ssh-keyscan`, that runbook's step 4) and commit it — the host keys changed.

*Reference expected result:* key-based root login works, node reports Debian
13.x. **Jelle** drives the SCP; the rest is the workstation/pipeline.

### 2. Check DNS before issuing any certificate

Confirm public DNS still serves only the A records the platform can answer and
**no stray AAAA records**:
[rb-2026-07-15-dns-ipv4-only](rb-2026-07-15-dns-ipv4-only.md). A reinstall does
not touch DNS, but a hoster can re-apply parking defaults at any time, and a
stray AAAA sends the Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenge to the wrong address —
issuance then fails with a misleading "unauthorized". Do this *before* the
platform tries to issue, not after it fails. (If the drill goes dual-stack,
this step changes — see §4a step D.)

*Reference expected result:* every A query returns the ingress node IP; every
AAAA query returns nothing; `verify:dns` green.

### 3. Bootstrap the pipeline and apply the baseline

Bring the config repo's pipeline up against the fresh node(s) and harden them:
[rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline](rb-2026-07-14-bootstrap-pipeline.md) then
[rb-2026-07-14-debian-hardening](rb-2026-07-14-debian-hardening.md). `bootstrap`
creates the deploy user as root (only works before hardening closes root
login); `apply` lays the ufw default-deny baseline — including the peer-only k3s
ports (6443/51820/10250 plus 9100 for node-exporter, added in the C2 repair,
mini-cloud !26) — sshd hardening, fail2ban and unattended-upgrades; `verify`
proves the hardening is live over the network, not just on disk.

*Reference expected result:* `bootstrap` green, `apply` `failed=0`, `verify`
green ("hardening is in effect, not just written down"). **Jelle** merges to
protected `main` and plays the gated `apply`.

### 4. Stand up k3s

Rebuild the two-node cluster through the pipeline:
[rb-2026-07-17-k3s-cluster-bootstrap](rb-2026-07-17-k3s-cluster-bootstrap.md).
The role installs the pinned server first (`v1.36.2+k3s1`), the agent joins over
the WireGuard-encrypted pod overlay, and the viewer RBAC is applied from git (the
peer-only ports these need were already opened by the baseline layer in step 3).

*Reference expected result:* both nodes `Ready`, 6443 closed from the internet,
a recent WireGuard handshake. **This is the step the IPv6 block (§4a) modifies**
— dual-stack cannot be turned on later, so if the drill is going dual-stack it
must be decided *here*, at cluster creation.

### 5. Bootstrap GitOps — Argo CD rebuilds the platform from git

Install Argo CD once via Ansible; from there every platform and app object is a
git commit that Argo re-syncs:
[rb-2026-07-17-argocd-gitops-bootstrap](rb-2026-07-17-argocd-gitops-bootstrap.md).
The `root` Application pulls `gitops/` and Argo rebuilds cert-manager, the
demo app, and — via
[rb-2026-07-17-observability-bootstrap](rb-2026-07-17-observability-bootstrap.md)
— the monitoring, logging and alerting stack. App secrets (Grafana admin, etc.)
are re-templated from SOPS at `apply` time; cert-manager issues certificates
fresh.

*Reference expected result:* `root`, `cert-manager` and `demo` all
`Synced/Healthy`; the observability Applications `Synced/Healthy`; a certificate
issued. **This is where "platform back" is reached** — everything under
`gitops/` plus everything Ansible lays down is now reconstructed *from git
alone*.

### 6. Restore the data — only if there is data that git cannot replay

This is the "and data back" half, and it needs a decision, not a reflex.

**The decision tree — datastore restore vs GitOps-only:**

- **GitOps alone suffices** when the loss is confined to the *platform* layer —
  everything under `gitops/` and everything Ansible writes. A fresh rebuild plus
  Argo re-sync reproduces it. For the platform **as it stands today** this is
  essentially the whole picture: Loki storage is an ephemeral `emptyDir` by
  design, there are no PersistentVolumes, and `backup_extra_paths: []` — so
  after step 5 there is little or no state that lives *only* in the datastore.
- **A datastore restore is warranted** only when state exists that lives in the
  cluster and **nowhere in git or Ansible**, and must be preserved rather than
  regenerated. Today the clearest candidate is **cert-manager's issued
  certificates and its ACME account key** — these live in cluster Secrets (in
  the datastore), not in git. A from-git rebuild makes cert-manager *re-request*
  them, which spends Let's Encrypt's production budget: the duplicate-issuance
  limit is **5 certificates per exact set of identifiers per 7 days** (see
  [rb-2026-07-17-ingress-tls-cert-manager](rb-2026-07-17-ingress-tls-cert-manager.md),
  corrected in C7 against `letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits`). If earlier drill
  attempts have already burned that budget, restoring those Secrets from the
  datastore avoids re-issuance. As the platform grows, this branch also covers
  any future PV/app data wired through `backup_extra_paths`.

**How to restore (when the tree says you must):** follow
[rb-2026-07-17-backup-restore](rb-2026-07-17-backup-restore.md). That runbook
proved **restore-on-a-copy** (snapshot 34.7 MiB, `state.db` opens,
`integrity_check: ok`, `kine` table present, token 109 B — observed
2026-07-17). The DR-specific part it deliberately leaves here is the **live
cutover**, which is destructive and untested:

> **Live datastore cutover (design — not yet executed).** On the rebuilt server
> node: stop k3s, restore the latest snapshot to a scratch path and verify it is
> a real multi-MB `state.db` with `integrity_check: ok` and the `kine` table
> (never trust an `integrity_check` on a path you have not confirmed holds a
> real database — the vacuous-restore trap in that runbook), then replace the
> live `state.db` and re-seed the k3s server token that was backed up with it
> (the token decrypts the datastore — `docs.k3s.io/datastore/backup-restore`),
> and start k3s. This is a **destructive, cluster-wide** operation: it requires
> direct authorization in the executing session (execution harness — it cannot
> be delegated to a sub-agent) and pre-state capture. The exact stop/replace/
> re-seed commands and their observed results are to be filled in **from the
> drill** — they are not asserted here.

*Expected result (to be observed in the drill):* the cluster comes up on the
restored datastore; the objects that were not in git (e.g. the cert-manager
Secrets) are present; `kubectl get nodes` and the Applications reconcile against
the restored state.

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
The both-nodes gap (state it honestly)
text:
The C6 backups are **cross-node**: each node backs up to the *other* node. That
protects a **single** node loss — the survivor holds the lost node's snapshot,
and after rebuilding the lost node its state is on its peer.

**If both nodes are lost, the backups are lost with them** — they live *on the
nodes*. In that scenario, this runbook can rebuild only what lives **in git plus
the workstation** (age key + deploy key): the platform comes back in full (step
5), but there is **no datastore snapshot to restore** (step 6 has no source).
That is the real gap, and the honest limit of the current design.

**What closes it:** an **offsite backup target** — `backup_offsite_repository`
in the C6 role, stubbed empty today, and **gate 2** for Jelle. Until an offsite
copy exists, a genuine *both-nodes* DR drill can only prove the git+workstation
rebuild, not a datastore restore. This is why the drill's scope is itself a gate
(below): with no offsite decision, the exercise is a **one-node-loss** drill.

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
§4a. IPv6 dual-stack — design, NOT yet executed
text:
> **This entire section is design.** Nothing here has been run. It is Jelle's
> input for the drill: the steps to bring the rebuild up dual-stack instead of
> IPv4-only. Sources are the current k3s docs
> (`docs.k3s.io/networking/basic-network-options`, section "Dual-stack (IPv4 +
> IPv6) Networking", fetched 2026-07-17) and this repo's own DNS runbook; every
> value below is an example/expectation to be confirmed against the nodes'
> actual IPv6 allocation, not an observed result.

**Why it belongs in the DR runbook and nowhere else.** The k3s docs state, on
that page, verbatim: *"Dual-stack networking must be configured when the cluster
is first created. It cannot be enabled on an existing cluster once it has been
started as IPv4-only."* The cluster today is IPv4-only, so the **only** moment to
adopt dual-stack without a deliberate teardown is a **fresh cluster creation** —
which is exactly what a DR rebuild is. That makes the DR drill the natural, and
cheapest, window to go dual-stack.

**A. k3s dual-stack CIDRs at (re)install (modifies rebuild step 4).** Per the
k3s docs, verbatim: *"To enable dual-stack in K3s, you must provide valid
dual-stack `cluster-cidr` and `service-cidr` on all server nodes."* The docs'
own recommended example is:

```
--cluster-cidr=10.42.0.0/16,2001:db8:42::/56 --service-cidr=10.43.0.0/16,2001:db8:43::/112
```

The IPv6 CIDRs above are the docs' example ranges; the real ranges come from the
nodes' netcup IPv6 allocation and must be chosen before the drill. In the
`k3s` role these would be set on the **server** config
(`config-server.yaml.j2`), alongside the existing pinned version and
`flannel-backend: wireguard-native`. Two further docs points, verbatim:

- Node IP ordering, if IPv6 is the primary family: *"When defining cluster-cidr
  and service-cidr with IPv6 as the primary family, the node-ip of all cluster
  members should be explicitly set, placing node's desired IPv6 address as the
  first address."*
- NAT for non-routed IPv6: *"When using IPv6 addresses that are not publicly
  routed, for example in the ULA range, you might want to add the
  `--flannel-ipv6-masq` option to enable IPv6 NAT, as per default pods use their
  pod IPv6 address for outgoing traffic."* (netcup hands out routable IPv6, so
  this is likely *not* needed — to confirm.)

*Design expectation (to verify in the drill):* both nodes `Ready` with an IPv6
`InternalIP` alongside the IPv4 one; Services able to allocate from the v6
service CIDR.

**B. ufw peer rules for IPv6.** The baseline firewall
(`ansible/roles/baseline/tasks/firewall.yml`) opens the peer-only ports
(6443/51820/10250/9100) from the peer's **IPv4** address. Dual-stack node-to-node
traffic (the flannel overlay, the API server, kubelet) will also traverse IPv6,
so the same peer rules need an IPv6 counterpart keyed on the peer's IPv6 address.
The rule shape is the same "from the peer only" pattern already in that file;
the address family is the change. *Design — the exact rule entries are to be
written and tested in the drill.*

**C. AAAA records to the netcup addresses.** Today the DNS policy is IPv4-only
and the guard actively deletes stray AAAA records
([rb-2026-07-15-dns-ipv4-only](rb-2026-07-15-dns-ipv4-only.md)). Going
dual-stack **inverts that policy**: add AAAA records pointing at the node's *own*
IPv6 address (not the hoster's parking range), and — per that runbook's rollback
section — set `EXPECTED_IPV6` in `scripts/verify-dns.sh` to that address so the
guard **enforces** the new policy instead of deleting the record. Only do this
once the platform actually answers on IPv6 (step A verified), or Let's Encrypt
will prefer the AAAA and the challenge will land on an address that is not yet
serving.

**D. Verify over both families.** The verify layers currently probe IPv4. A
dual-stack drill extends them to prove the platform answers on **both** families:
the external endpoint reachable over IPv6 (e.g. `curl -6`), the ingress
certificate valid over IPv6, and `verify:dns` enforcing the AAAA policy from
step C. *Design — the specific check additions are part of the drill, not
asserted here.*

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
Verification (the DR success criterion)
text:
The drill is complete when **every standing verify layer is green** on the
rebuilt cluster — these are the same guards each source runbook defines, run in
order:

| Layer | Job / script | Proves |
|---|---|---|
| Hardening | `verify` (phase A) | root/password login refused; ufw, fail2ban, unattended-upgrades live |
| Platform | `verify:platform` | both nodes `Ready`; 6443 closed from the internet; WireGuard handshake < 3 min; all Applications `Synced/Healthy` |
| Observability | `verify:observability` | Prometheus targets up; Alertmanager reachable; ≥1 Loki stream; Grafana `database: ok`; no stuck pods; apps `Synced/Healthy` |
| Backup | `verify:backup` | per node: repo reachable, `restic check --read-data-subset=5%`, latest snapshot < 26h |
| DNS | `verify:dns` | A records correct; IPv6 policy holds (IPv4-only today, or the AAAA policy from §4a-D if dual-stack) |

Plus the DoD checks the source runbooks carry (both nodes `Ready`, a certificate
issued and valid, the demo endpoint reachable from the outside). **The spec §6
success criterion — "platform and data back" — is met when** the platform verify
layers are green (platform back) **and** either the datastore restore of step 6
is confirmed or the decision tree recorded that GitOps-only was sufficient (data
back, or accounted for). In a *both-nodes* drill without an offsite copy, "data
back" is limited to what git replays — record that limit explicitly (see the
gap, above).

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
Roles and timing
text:
*Timing is a design estimate, not measured — this drill has not been run. Fill
in real durations after the first execution.*

| Actor | Does |
|---|---|
| **Jelle** | Reinstalls the node(s) in the netcup SCP; checks/repairs the DNS panel; merges each MR to protected `main` and plays the gated `apply` jobs; authorizes the destructive live datastore cutover (step 6) in-session; decides the drill scope and the offsite/IPv6 gates. |
| **Pipeline / orchestrator** | Everything automatable: `bootstrap`/`apply`/`verify` runs, Argo re-sync, the verify layers, read-only observation of the rebuild. The orchestrator captures pre-state and clocks the destructive cutover when it runs with direct mandate. |

Rough order-of-magnitude estimate (to be replaced with measured values): node
reinstall + key handover ~15 min/node (Jelle + SCP); baseline+k3s+GitOps apply
and Argo re-sync tens of minutes (pipeline-paced, Argo sync intervals); datastore
restore + cutover unknown until measured; DNS propagation up to the record TTL.

heading_path: Disaster recovery — rebuild both nodes and bring platform and data back
Rollback
text:
DR *is* the rollback for a lost cluster — there is no "undo" beyond it. The one
reversible caution is in step 6: the live datastore cutover is destructive, so
capture pre-state and restore to a scratch path first (never over the live
`state.db` until verified). If the drill is a rehearsal on a healthy cluster,
do **not** perform the live cutover on the production datastore — rehearse the
restore on a copy (the C6 runbook's proven path) and stop before the replace.

heading_path: Run the Haven compliancy checker against the mini-cloud
Goal
text:
Measure the cluster against the official VNG Haven compliancy checker, and do it
honestly: the **tooling route** (pin the CLI, verify its SHA, and try the
least-privileged access first) is `tested` and its result — an RBAC block on the
read-only route — is the useful finding. The **cluster-admin run** that produces
the actual pass/fail per check is also `tested` as of 2026-08-11: executed via a
temporary, torn-down-after grant (see stage 3). Use this runbook to reproduce
either the baseline (viewer route) or the real measurement
([haven-meting-2026-08](../reference/haven-meting-2026-08.md)).

> **Status note.** Steps 1–3 were run on 2026-07-16 (baseline) and re-run on
> 2026-08-11 with identical results. Step 4 (the cluster-admin run) was
> executed twice on 2026-08-11 with operator consent — fast variant (11/15)
> and full variant with CNCF (12/15) — each behind an operator-created
> temporary grant with a read-only-verified teardown. The observed results
> live in the end-measurement reference doc.

heading_path: Run the Haven compliancy checker against the mini-cloud
Preconditions
text:
- The Haven CLI pinned on the **workstation** (not on the nodes — the checker is
  an operator tool, not a cluster component).
- An SSH tunnel to the k3s API: 6443 is peer-only, so the checker reaches it
  through a tunnel (see `rb-2026-07-17-k3s-cluster-bootstrap`, step 8).
- A kubeconfig. Step 3 uses the read-only `viewer`; step 4 needs cluster-admin.

heading_path: Run the Haven compliancy checker against the mini-cloud
Steps
text:
### Stage 1 — pin the tool and verify the SHA (tested)

1. **Pin the Haven CLI and verify its SHA-256 before trusting it.** The checker
   is the **Haven CLI** (`haven check`), VNG Realisatie / Common Ground,
   distributed through the GitLab generic package registry
   `commonground/haven/haven` (package `cli`). Pin the version and check the
   downloaded artifact's SHA against the registry's `file_sha256` — the registry
   packages API serves both read-only without auth.
