requirements. Plan C's monitoring stack (task C2) is the first such app:
Grafana needs an admin password, and that password must not sit in git in
plaintext.

The repository already has a proven route for exactly one secret — the Argo CD
read-only deploy token:

- The value is stored SOPS-encrypted in `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml`
  (age recipient in `.sops.yaml`; the private identity lives only on the
  maintainer's workstation and in CI's protected `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE`).
- The `gitops_bootstrap` role decrypts it *on the controller* with
  `community.sops.load_vars` (`no_log: true`) and templates it onto the node as
  a `kind: Secret` under k3s' manifests directory, which the k3s deploy
  controller applies.
- CI proves the layer works: `verify:sops` decrypts on `main` with the real
  key, and `test:verify-sops` / `test:deploy-token` prove the red paths without
  it. See [topic-gitlab-ci](../topics/topic-gitlab-ci.md).

The choice: reuse that route for Grafana's password, or introduce an in-cluster
secrets mechanism (KSOPS in Argo CD's repo-server, or the external-secrets
operator with a backing store).

heading_path: App-level secrets reach the cluster via Ansible-out-of-SOPS, not an in-cluster operator
Decision
text:
App-level secrets follow the **same Ansible-out-of-SOPS route** to k3s' manifests
directory. The `gitops_bootstrap` role is extended with one extra task and one
template (`grafana-admin-secret.yaml.j2`) rather than a new role or a new
mechanism — the smallest form that reuses what already exists. Grafana's
`Application` consumes the resulting Secret with `grafana.admin.existingSecret`,
so no password ever appears in a `valuesObject` in git.

heading_path: App-level secrets reach the cluster via Ansible-out-of-SOPS, not an in-cluster operator
Consequences
text:
- **No extra cluster component.** Nothing new to run, patch and secure on
  8 GB two-node hardware — the decrypt happens on the controller, the cluster
  only ever sees an already-rendered `Secret`.
- **The secret never touches git in plaintext.** SOPS/age protects it at rest;
  the same protected-variable boundary that keeps unreviewed branches from
  decrypting production secrets applies unchanged.
- **A proven, CI-guarded pattern** is extended rather than a new one introduced,
  so the existing `verify:sops` guard already covers the new key.
- **Trade-off — the secret is applied by Ansible, not reconciled by Argo CD.**
  The app is GitOps but its secret arrives on the apply path, so the two are
  slightly split: rotating the password needs an `apply` run, and Argo CD will
  not self-heal a hand-deleted Secret (k3s' manifests controller re-applies it
  on its own poll, which covers the common case but is a different mechanism).
- **Ordering is eventual, not immediate.** The Secret targets namespace
  `monitoring`, which does not exist until the monitoring `Application` creates
  it; k3s retries the manifest until then — the same reconcile-retry the Argo CD
  bootstrap manifests already rely on.

heading_path: App-level secrets reach the cluster via Ansible-out-of-SOPS, not an in-cluster operator
Alternatives considered
text:
- **KSOPS (Argo CD repo-server plugin).** Decrypts SOPS files in-cluster, so the
  whole app *including* its secret is one Argo CD `Application` and reconciles
  the same way everything else does. Rejected for now: it puts the age private
  key into the repo-server and adds a custom-plugin build to Argo CD — more
  moving parts and a larger key blast-radius for a handful of secrets.
- **external-secrets operator.** Syncs secrets from an external store
  (Vault, a cloud secret manager) into Kubernetes `Secret`s. Rejected: it needs
  a backing store this platform does not run and does not want to run yet; it
  solves a problem (many secrets, many consumers, central rotation) we do not
  have on two nodes.

Both are the right answer at scale; neither earns its complexity here.

heading_path: App-level secrets reach the cluster via Ansible-out-of-SOPS, not an in-cluster operator
Revisit when
text:
App secrets multiply (many apps × many secrets), or rotation cadence makes
apply-time rotation painful, or a secrets backend appears for other reasons —
at that point KSOPS or external-secrets becomes worth its weight and this
decision should be reopened.

heading_path: Argo CD is the GitOps engine that reconciles the cluster from git
Context
text:
The platform's thesis is that the cluster contains nothing that is not in git.
k3s' manifests directory converges *towards* the cluster but never away from it
— it applies files and never prunes, so "nothing manual that is not in git" is
an intention with no enforcement (`topic-k3s`; `topic-argo-cd`, "Why we use
it"). Closing that half of the loop needs a GitOps engine: a controller that
continuously compares the running cluster to a git revision and both prunes what
git no longer declares and reverts out-of-band edits.

The spec chose the engine up front (`docs/specs/2026-07-14-mini-cloud-bootstrap-design.md`,
§4): Argo CD, "herkenbaar bij NL-klanten (Haven-context), web-UI versterkt
runbooks en demo's", with Flux named there as the alternative ("~0,5 GB
zuiniger, geen UI — decision-record"). That parenthetical is the decision record
the spec promised; this is it. `topic-argo-cd` documents the resulting install;
this record makes the engine choice explicit with its alternatives. Argo CD is
layer L5 in the portability design (`docs/plans/2026-07-17-portability-design.md`,
§1).

heading_path: Argo CD is the GitOps engine that reconciles the cluster from git
Decision
text:
We use **Argo CD** (chart `argo-cd` 10.1.3, appVersion v3.4.5 at
`last_verified`) as the GitOps engine, installed through k3s' manifests
directory and driven by a single **app-of-apps** root `Application` that watches
`gitops/` on `main` with `prune` and `selfHeal` both on. Dex, notifications,
applicationSet and redis-ha are all disabled, and the UI is reached only over
`kubectl port-forward` (no public ingress, no SSO). The full configuration and
its reasoning are in `topic-argo-cd`.

heading_path: Argo CD is the GitOps engine that reconciles the cluster from git
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **"The cluster equals git" becomes checkable, not aspirational.** With
  `prune` on, deleting a file deletes its objects; with `selfHeal` on, a
  `kubectl edit` against anything under `gitops/` is reverted on the next sync
  (`topic-argo-cd`). A platform change becomes a reviewed commit on protected
  `main`, with no `ansible-playbook` run and no operator holding cluster-admin.
- **One entry point grows the whole platform.** The app-of-apps root means new
  platform components and apps are added as commits under `gitops/`, not as new
  bootstrap steps (`topic-argo-cd`; mini-cloud README).
- **A recognisable tool with a UI.** For the Haven/NL-client context the spec
  cares about, Argo CD is familiar and its UI strengthens demos and runbooks
  (spec §4).

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **A controller to run and bound on 8 GB nodes.** The application controller
  holds cluster state and was observed **OOMKilled in a crashloop (lastState
  OOMKilled, restarts 17) with 6 managed apps**, forcing its memory limit up
  512Mi→1Gi (scaling design §4.1). That pin is a real operating cost of the
  choice, not a rounding error.
- **Bootstrap is tied to k3s' front door.** Argo CD is born through k3s'
  `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` directory (`topic-argo-cd`,
  `topic-k3s`); a distribution swap re-designs that birth channel (portability
  design §2·L4).
- **"Green" still is not "running".** Writing a manifest is not the controller
  applying it; the role waits on `Synced:Healthy` precisely because a green
  Ansible run only proves bytes are on disk (`topic-argo-cd`, "The waits").

heading_path: Argo CD is the GitOps engine that reconciles the cluster from git
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Flux** — the other mainstream GitOps engine. Roughly 0.5 GB lighter and with
  no UI (spec §4). Rejected on recognisability and the UI's demo/runbook value,
  not on capability. The swap is judged "middel" cost: Flux has no
  `directory.recurse` app-of-apps but `Kustomization`/`GitRepository` objects
  with explicit `dependsOn`, so the app-of-apps root and its learned
  `directory.exclude` become a different solution to the same apply-ordering
  problem (portability design §2·L5). It stays the first alternative if the
  ~0.5 GB and the smaller attack surface start to matter.
- **No GitOps — pure pipeline push** (`kubectl`/`helm` from CI). The
  portability design names this a deliberate **degradation path**, not an equal
  swap: it is the only option that weakens the L5 contract itself rather than
  re-filling it, because it loses prune + self-heal, so drift detection would
  have to become a verify script instead of a controller (§2·L5). Rejected as a
  regression from the property this layer exists to provide.
- **Argo CD with a public UI + SSO** (Dex/an external IdP). Rejected for this
  phase: it is a public login page and a certificate for a UI one operator opens
  occasionally, on a cluster with no IdP (`topic-argo-cd`). Publishing it is a
  separate, later decision.

heading_path: Argo CD is the GitOps engine that reconciles the cluster from git
Revisit triggers
text:
- Node memory pressure or the controller's OOM history makes Flux's ~0.5 GB
  saving and smaller footprint worth the bootstrap rewrite (scaling design §4;
  portability design §2·L5).
- A second cluster or many environments appear — that is where
  `applicationSet` (disabled today) and Flux's multi-tenancy patterns earn their
  weight.
- An identity provider arrives and the UI needs to be published — reopens the
  Dex/SSO and ingress choices (`topic-argo-cd`).
- The platform moves off k3s, changing the bootstrap front door either engine
  depends on (portability design §2·L4/L5).

heading_path: k3s is the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Context
text:
The platform needs a Kubernetes distribution that runs a useful cluster on two
small VPSs (4 vCore / 8 GB each — `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`) and
that is credible as **Haven** material, since Haven's yardstick is a
CNCF-conformant Kubernetes (`topic-haven-compliancy-checker`, spec §1). The
choice sets the shape of most layers above it: the CNI, the ingress controller
and the storage provisioner all follow from which distribution ships them.

This choice was made in the design spec, not re-litigated later. The spec
(`docs/specs/2026-07-14-mini-cloud-bootstrap-design.md`, §4) records the two
reasons at the time: k3s is **CNCF-certified** ("echt Haven-materiaal") and
**light enough for these VPSs**, with its SQLite datastore called out as a
feature ("lichter dan etcd, backup is een simpele snapshot") rather than a
concession. `topic-k3s` documents what that produced in the repos; this record
promotes the spec's one-line argument to an explicit, revisable choice with its
alternatives written out. As `topic-k3s` puts it plainly: "there is no decision
record weighing k3s against k0s or plain Kubernetes. The spec chose it; this
page documents it." This record is that missing decision.

heading_path: k3s is the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Decision
text:
We run the mini-cloud on **k3s** (pinned `v1.36.2+k3s1` at `last_verified`),
one server node plus one agent, with its bundled batteries — flannel CNI
(WireGuard-native backend), Traefik ingress, ServiceLB, local-path storage —
and the default embedded **SQLite** datastore rather than etcd. The details of
every flag are in `topic-k3s`; the layer contract it fills (a CNCF-conformant
cluster API, a declarative front door to bootstrap GitOps, an encrypted node
network) is L4 in the portability design
(`docs/plans/2026-07-17-portability-design.md`, §1).

heading_path: k3s is the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **Fewer moving parts.** One binary carries the API server, scheduler,
  kubelet, container runtime, CNI, ingress and storage provisioner
  (`topic-k3s`). Traefik, flannel and local-path arrive bundled, so the ingress
  and CNI decisions become "keep the default" rather than "install and own a
  chart" (see `dec-2026-07-17-traefik-ingress`).
- **The datastore is a single file to snapshot.** SQLite in WAL mode means the
  backup of the control-plane state is one `sqlite3 .backup` of `state.db`, not
  an etcd snapshot regime — which is exactly how the backup layer is built
  (`topic-restic`, `dec-2026-07-17-restic-cross-node-backup`).
- **Encrypted node traffic without a provider add-on.** The flannel
  `wireguard-native` backend encrypts pod traffic over the public internet, so
  the two nodes need no netcup vLAN add-on (`topic-k3s`, "Flags & settings").

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **SQLite is single-server.** Most k3s writing online assumes embedded etcd,
  and its advice (quorum, `etcdctl`, snapshot schedules) does not apply here
  (`topic-k3s`). Real HA would mean migrating to embedded etcd **and** running
  ≥3 servers — a datastore migration, not a config flip
  (`dec-2026-07-17-two-node-topology-resource-pins`; scaling design §2).
- **The bundled components tie us to k3s' mechanisms.** Traefik is installed
  through k3s' `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/` "front door" and
  rewritten on every start; Argo CD is bootstrapped through that same directory
  (`topic-k3s`, `topic-argo-cd`). Replacing k3s means re-designing that
  bootstrap path (portability design §2·L4).
- **The install pipes `get.k3s.io` into a root shell.** The binary is checksum-
  verified but the checksum shares its origin with the binary, so this catches a
  corrupted download, not a compromised release; mirroring artifacts against a
  key we hold is a named, unbuilt gap (`topic-k3s`, "The supply chain, stated
  honestly").

heading_path: k3s is the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Alternatives considered
text:
- **k0s** — another single-binary distribution with a similar light footprint.
  Rejected on the same axis k3s won: no CNCF-conformance advantage, and it would
  give up the specific bundled-battery ergonomics (Traefik/flannel/local-path
  as k3s defaults) and the SQLite-snapshot-simple datastore the backup layer
  relies on, in exchange for nothing phase A needs. Listed as an L4 alternative
  in the portability design (§2·L4).
- **RKE2** — Rancher's security-hardened distribution with a comparable
  server/agent token model. The portability design judges an RKE2 swap
  "middel" cost: the role structure survives, the installer commands and unit
  names change (§2·L4). Rejected now as heavier than a two-node lab needs; it is
  the closest successor if a hardening/compliance requirement later demands it.
- **Talos** — an API-driven, immutable-OS Kubernetes. Rejected as the highest-
  cost swap: it replaces the whole SSH/Ansible configuration seam for this layer
  with a machine-config API (portability design §2·L4), which is a different
  operating model than the rest of the kit assumes.
- **Managed Kubernetes** (e.g. Scaleway Kapsule) — removes the bootstrap burden
  but reintroduces provider lock on L2/L4 and undercuts the sovereignty thesis
  the provider choice defends (`dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`). It is
  the alternative whose argument grows strongest only at scale, when self-managed
  HA becomes the operational cost it removes (scaling design §6.1).
- **Upstream ("vanilla") Kubernetes** — kubeadm plus a hand-assembled CNI,
  ingress and storage. Rejected: it is exactly the assembly work k3s packages,
  and it is heavier than 8 GB nodes comfortably carry, for no conformance gain.

heading_path: k3s is the Kubernetes distribution the mini-cloud runs on
Revisit triggers
text:
- The cluster needs real HA and therefore embedded etcd + ≥3 servers — that is a
  datastore migration off SQLite and reopens the distribution's fit
  (`dec-2026-07-17-two-node-topology-resource-pins`; scaling design §2).
- A client or compliance context arrives that mandates a hardened distribution
  (RKE2 is then the near-neighbour) or an immutable-OS posture (Talos).
- The platform moves to managed Kubernetes for operational reasons — a different
  category of decision that also changes L2 (portability design §2·L4).
- k3s' CNCF conformance or maintenance posture changes such that it stops being
  credible Haven material (`topic-haven-compliancy-checker`).

heading_path: Observability is kube-prometheus-stack for metrics and Loki/Alloy for logs
Context
text:
Plan C adds observability: success criterion 5 requires monitoring and logging
with at least one working dashboard and one demonstrably delivered alert (spec
§2.5, §6). The spec (§6) already names the metrics stack — kube-prometheus-stack
(Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager), "ingesnoerd voor deze schaal:
metrics-retentie ~7 dagen, resource-limits op alle componenten" — and the
constraint that shapes every choice here is the 8 GB two-node footprint. Logging
is the other half; the platform reads both metrics and logs from the **same
Grafana** (`topic-loki-alloy`).

The topics `topic-kube-prometheus-stack`, `topic-loki-alloy` and
`topic-prometheusrule-alerting` document the trimmed configuration in full; this
record promotes the stack choice to an explicit decision with the alternatives.
Observability is the platform's monitoring layer; the alerting *receiver* choice
is deliberately deferred to a JELLE-GATE (`topic-prometheusrule-alerting`) and is
not this record's subject.

heading_path: Observability is kube-prometheus-stack for metrics and Loki/Alloy for logs
Decision
text:
We run **kube-prometheus-stack** (chart 87.16.1) for metrics, alerting plumbing
and dashboards, and **Loki + Alloy** (loki chart 7.1.0, alloy chart 1.10.1) for
logs, all installed by Argo CD as GitOps `Application`s and all trimmed to the
8 GB footprint: memory limits on every component, Prometheus retention 7d on
`emptyDir`, Loki single-binary with caches off, Alloy as a log-collecting
DaemonSet reading via the Kubernetes API. No UI is exposed publicly — Grafana,
like Argo CD, is reached over `kubectl port-forward`. Full configuration in the
three topics named above.

heading_path: Observability is kube-prometheus-stack for metrics and Loki/Alloy for logs
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **One chart wires the metrics half together.** kube-prometheus-stack ships
  Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, node-exporter and kube-state-metrics with
  one pinned version and one `Application`, instead of assembling five
  components by hand (`topic-kube-prometheus-stack`, "Why we use it"). Its
  operator turns "what gets scraped and what fires" into declared Kubernetes
  objects.
- **Logs and metrics share one Grafana.** Loki indexes only labels (cheap) and
  Alloy (Promtail's GA successor) reads pod logs through the Kubernetes API with
  no host log mount; the Loki datasource lives in the same Grafana as the
  metrics (`topic-loki-alloy`).
- **It scales with the node count for free.** node-exporter is a DaemonSet and
  `verify-observability.sh` asserts "no target down" rather than an absolute
  count, so a third node is observed without a config change (scaling design
  §1.1, §5.1).

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **Heavily trimmed against upstream defaults, and the trims are load-bearing.**
  Loki must run single-binary with `replicas: 1` and an explicit `emptyDir` at
  `/var/loki` and its memcached caches off — leaving the caches on requests
  ~9 Gi the nodes cannot satisfy, and persistence-off without the emptyDir
  crashloops `mkdir /var/loki: read-only file system` (`topic-loki-alloy`).
  These are documented footguns, not defaults.
- **State is interim and lossy by design.** Prometheus keeps 7d on `emptyDir`
  and Loki logs are lost on pod reschedule — both accepted until a storage layer
  exists (`topic-kube-prometheus-stack`; `topic-loki-alloy`; scaling design §3).
- **Server-side apply is mandatory for the CRDs.** Without
  `ServerSideApply=true` the first sync fails on `metadata.annotations: Too
  long` — the single most common kube-prometheus-stack + Argo CD failure
  (`topic-kube-prometheus-stack`).
- **Much of this is not yet cluster-observed.** The topics carry explicit "not
  yet run against the cluster" hedges; claims about what values *do* come from
  the pinned charts' `values.yaml`, not a running instance
  (`topic-kube-prometheus-stack`, `topic-loki-alloy`). Cluster observations are
  added as the observation phase runs, the way `topic-cert-manager` was.

heading_path: Observability is kube-prometheus-stack for metrics and Loki/Alloy for logs
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Standalone Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager, wired by hand.** Rejected:
  it is exactly the assembly the chart packages, with the operator's declarative
  `ServiceMonitor`/`PrometheusRule` model lost. No footprint saving that a
  trimmed chart does not also achieve.
- **VictoriaMetrics** — a lighter, more memory-efficient Prometheus-compatible
  TSDB. A real contender on an 8 GB budget, and the strongest metrics
  alternative. Rejected for phase A on familiarity and the single-chart
  ergonomics (operator, default rules, default dashboards, Grafana all in one),
  which matter more here than the memory margin the trims already buy. It is the
  first thing to reconsider if Prometheus becomes the memory bottleneck.
- **ELK / EFK (Elasticsearch + Kibana) for logs** — the classic logging stack.
  Rejected outright on footprint: Elasticsearch is heavy for 8 GB nodes, and it
  would add a second UI instead of reading logs from the Grafana that already
  exists for metrics. Loki's label-only index is the deliberately cheap choice
  (`topic-loki-alloy`).
- **A hosted/SaaS observability backend** (e.g. Grafana Cloud, a hosted
  Prometheus). Rejected on the programme's sovereignty thesis — telemetry would
  leave the sovereign platform for a third party — and on cost for a self-funded
  lab (`dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection` sets that posture).

heading_path: Observability is kube-prometheus-stack for metrics and Loki/Alloy for logs
Revisit triggers
text:
- Prometheus becomes the memory bottleneck on these nodes — reconsider
  VictoriaMetrics (scaling design §4).
- A persistent-storage layer lands — Prometheus and Loki move off `emptyDir` to
  PVs, changing the retention/loss trade-offs (scaling design §3).
- Node size grows — the 8 GB pins become cramped and want a resource-profile
  mechanism (`dec-2026-07-17-two-node-topology-resource-pins`; scaling design
  §4.3).
- Log volume grows enough that Alloy streaming each container's logs through the
  API server strains it — reconsider the file-based collection method
  (`topic-loki-alloy`).

heading_path: Backups use restic, written cross-node between the two VPSs
Context
text:
The platform has exactly one piece of genuinely non-reproducible state: the k3s
control-plane datastore (embedded SQLite in WAL mode — everything else is
replayable from git via GitOps). Success criterion 6 requires a backup regime
**with a tested restore**, ending in a full DR exercise (spec §2.6, §6, §8).
Two questions had to be answered: which backup tool, and where the copies go.

The provider choice left the platform with **no S3-compatible object storage**
(`dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`), so an object-store-native backup tool
would have nothing to write to in phase A. The spec's answer (§6) is a
file/SFTP-based tool writing **cross-node**: each node backs up to the other, so
losing a node does not lose its backups. `topic-restic` documents the resulting
mechanism in full (the live-safe SQLite copy, the SFTP transport hardening, the
retention and the verify check); this record makes the tool-and-topology choice
explicit with its alternatives. This is the backup layer the portability and
scaling designs both reference.

heading_path: Backups use restic, written cross-node between the two VPSs
Decision
text:
We use **restic** (pinned binary 0.18.0, checksum-verified) writing encrypted,
deduplicated, incremental snapshots **cross-node over SFTP**: each node writes
its repository to its peer. The server backs up a live-safe `sqlite3 .backup`
snapshot of `state.db` plus the node token and `config.yaml`; the agent backs up
its `config.yaml` (a placeholder today that keeps the cross-backup verifiable in
both directions). Retention is `--keep` 7 daily / 4 weekly / 6 monthly on a
daily systemd timer, and `verify:backup` proves a fresh, sound snapshot exists
on the peer. The offsite target is a configurable hook, empty by default. Full
detail in `topic-restic`.

heading_path: Backups use restic, written cross-node between the two VPSs
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **A backup that keeps working when the cluster is broken.** restic over SSH to
  the peer's public IP depends on neither the pod overlay nor cluster health, so
  a DR backup still succeeds precisely when the overlay is what is broken
  (`topic-restic`, "Target address: public IP, not the WireGuard IP").
- **Encryption end-to-end, safely on a live database.** restic encrypts the
  repository and the `sqlite3 .backup` Online Backup API produces a
  transactionally consistent snapshot of the running datastore without blocking
  k3s (`topic-restic`, "The live-safe SQLite copy"). The snapshot is staged in
  tmpfs and deleted on exit, so plaintext state never lands on persistent disk.
- **Freshness is actually checked.** restic reports repository validity but not
  staleness; `verify:backup`'s <26h age check closes that gap with a proven red
  route (`topic-restic`, "verify-backup.sh").

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **Both copies live at the same provider, same datacentre.** Cross-node is
  honest for a lab but one correlated failure away from losing both copies — a
  named restrisico (spec §7; `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`). Closing
  it needs the offsite hook filled (most likely a Hetzner Storage Box) before
  the governance rollout — Plan C / deelproject 6 work, chosen by Jelle
  (`topic-restic`, "Offsite hook").
- **The datastore choice is baked into the backup.** The `sqlite3 .backup`
  route is SQLite-specific; moving to embedded etcd for HA replaces it with
  `k3s etcd-snapshot save` while the cross-node restic envelope stays (scaling
  design §2.3). The backup layer follows the L4 datastore decision.
- **A restore is only trusted once exercised.** A backup without a tested
  restore does not count (spec §2.6); the restore-on-copy drill and the full DR
  exercise are gated on Jelle (`topic-restic`, "Restore-on-copy").

heading_path: Backups use restic, written cross-node between the two VPSs
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Velero** — the standard Kubernetes-native backup tool (backs up cluster
  objects and, with restic/kopia under the hood, volumes; typically to an object
  store). Rejected for phase A: it targets object storage the provider does not
  offer, and it backs up Kubernetes API objects that here are already
  reproducible from git — the one thing that is *not* reproducible (the
  datastore file) is exactly what a file-level tool captures directly. Velero
  earns its weight once there are stateful PVs and an object store (scaling
  design §3).
- **borg** (BorgBackup) — an excellent deduplicating encrypted backup tool over
  SSH, very close in shape to restic. Rejected on a narrow margin: restic ships
  as a single static binary trivially pinned-and-checksummed the way this repo
  already installs sops, and its repository model needed no server-side borg
  install on the peer. The choice is convenience and install-surface, not
  capability.
- **kopia** — another modern deduplicating encrypted backup tool with strong
  object-store support. Rejected for the same reason as Velero's storage
  assumption: its strongest features assume the object store phase A lacks, and
  it adds no advantage over restic for cross-node SFTP.

heading_path: Backups use restic, written cross-node between the two VPSs
Revisit triggers
text:
- The offsite hook is filled (an external target such as a Hetzner Storage Box)
  — the "both copies at one provider" restrisico is what triggers it (spec §7;
  `topic-restic`).
- The cluster gains embedded etcd for HA — the SQLite `.backup` route is
  replaced by etcd snapshots; the restic envelope and cross-node form stay
  (scaling design §2.3; `dec-2026-07-17-two-node-topology-resource-pins`).
- A persistent-storage layer lands — PV paths go into `backup_extra_paths` and
  an object-store-native tool (Velero/kopia) becomes worth re-evaluating
  (scaling design §3).

heading_path: Terraform is not used in phases A–C; the head-end stays a manual runbook
Context
text:
The platform is coded end to end with one exception: the VPS install and the
first SSH key handover are performed by hand
([rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning](../runbooks/rb-2026-07-14-netcup-vps-provisioning.md)).
Everything after that first key handover is automated — Ansible hardens and
installs k3s, Argo CD runs the workloads. That one manual step is the natural
candidate for infrastructure-as-code, and the obvious tool for it is Terraform
(or its fork OpenTofu): a declarative provisioner that would call the
provider's API to bring the servers into existence and hand off their
addresses, replacing the runbook with code. What Terraform is and where it
would sit is documented in [topic-terraform](../topics/topic-terraform.md).

**Why we wanted it.** The programme's thesis is that the platform must be
rebuildable from code, and the manual head-end is the single place that thesis
has an asterisk. A Terraform head-end would make VPS (re)provisioning
reproducible and reviewable — a `plan`/`apply` instead of a click-path through
a control panel — closing the last hand-driven gap and letting the layered kit
be "code all the way down": Terraform provisions → Ansible hardens → GitOps
runs.

**Why it does not work here.** The provisioning tool is only as good as the
provider it can talk to, and Terraform "relies on plugins called providers to
interact with cloud providers, SaaS providers, and other APIs" (per
`developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/providers`, checked 2026-07-17).
The chosen VPS provider, netcup, has **no official Terraform provider — only
community providers**. This is not a new finding for this decision: it was
already established and recorded in phase A, in
[dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection](../decisions/dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection.md).
That record states it in three places — the comparison table row "Official
Terraform provider | **no** — only community providers (`rincedd/netcup-scp`,
`rincedd/netcup-ccp`, `hornc-greedy/netcup`)"; the Consequences section ("No
official Terraform provider. The VPS (re)install stays a manual runbook … the
one hand-driven step"); and the "Revisit triggers" ("A community netcup
Terraform provider reaches production-grade maturity — that would remove the
manual head-end"). The provisioning runbook records the same fact operationally:
"netcup has no Terraform provider, so the image install and the first key
handover are done by hand."

Depending on a community provider for the *most load-bearing* step of the
platform — the one that creates the servers everything else runs on — trades a
known, documented manual step for an unmaintained-plugin risk at exactly the
point where a failure is most expensive.

heading_path: Terraform is not used in phases A–C; the head-end stays a manual runbook
Decision
text:
We do **not** use Terraform or OpenTofu in phases A through C. The head-end
(VPS provisioning and first key handover) stays a manual runbook; everything
from the first key handover onward remains code (Ansible, then GitOps). This
ratifies, at the tooling level, the provider-level finding already accepted in
`dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`.

heading_path: Terraform is not used in phases A–C; the head-end stays a manual runbook
Consequences
text:
- **The "code all the way down" claim keeps its one honest asterisk.** The
  platform is reproducible from code from the first SSH handover onward; the
  image install is a documented manual step, not an automated one. The runbook
  is treated as a first-class deliverable precisely because it carries that
  weight — "a platform that can only be rebuilt by an API is a platform nobody
  understands" (per `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`).
- **No Terraform state to operate.** We avoid the operational surface state
  brings — a `terraform.tfstate` that "must store state about your workspace's
  managed infrastructure" (per `developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state`,
  checked 2026-07-17) and therefore needs storing, locking, and keeping secret.
  For a two-node, one-operator lab that is a real saving, not a rounding error.
- **The manual step is the scaling cost.** Adding or rebuilding a node means
  running the runbook by hand each time. On two nodes this is trivial; it
  becomes friction the moment node count grows (see the scaling backlog,
  deelopdracht 3).
- **The decision is provider-bound, not permanent.** It follows netcup. Move
  the platform to a provider with an official provider and the whole rationale
  inverts — the manual step becomes an unnecessary one.

heading_path: Terraform is not used in phases A–C; the head-end stays a manual runbook
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Terraform/OpenTofu with a community netcup provider.** Would have coded the
  head-end today. Rejected: the community providers
  (`rincedd/netcup-scp`, `rincedd/netcup-ccp`, `hornc-greedy/netcup`) are "not
  load-bearing enough to trust for the head-end of the platform" (per
  `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`). Taking an unmaintained dependency
  at the platform's most critical layer is a worse trade than a documented
  manual step.
- **Switch providers to get an official provider (e.g. Hetzner).** Hetzner
  ships an officially maintained Terraform provider and was the runner-up on
  jurisdiction-equal grounds. Rejected here because provider choice was already
  settled in phase A on sovereignty, cost, and availability, not on IaC support;
  reopening it to gain Terraform would be the tail wagging the dog. It remains
  the most likely successor if IaC or backup friction becomes the bottleneck
  (per `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`, "Alternatives considered").
- **cloud-init instead of Terraform.** A lighter provisioning path that some
  providers drive from their panel/API. Not pursued for the same root reason —
  it needs provider-side API support netcup does not expose for our flow — and
  it does not replace Terraform's declarative full-lifecycle management. Listed
  as a candidate in the portability backlog rather than adopted.

heading_path: Terraform is not used in phases A–C; the head-end stays a manual runbook
Revisit when
text:
The platform moves to any provider from the portability backlog's
infra-provider row that ships an **official** Terraform/OpenTofu provider (the
backlog table, `docs/plans/2026-07-17-portability-and-scaling-backlog.md`,
deelopdracht 1, "Infra-provider" and "Provisioning" rows, names Hetzner, OVH,
Scaleway and others as the candidates). The same trigger is already listed from
the provider side in `dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection` ("A community
netcup Terraform provider reaches production-grade maturity"). At that point the
head-end runbook should be replaced by a Terraform/OpenTofu configuration, and
this decision reopened. OpenTofu is the mild default over Terraform at that
point on licensing grounds (MPL-2.0 under the Linux Foundation vs. the BUSL) —
see [topic-terraform](../topics/topic-terraform.md).

heading_path: Traefik is the ingress controller, because it is the k3s default
Context
text:
The platform needs an ingress controller: something that turns `Ingress`
objects into live routing rules so a public request for a hostname reaches the
right in-cluster service, and that offers the attachment point for the ACME
HTTP-01 challenge cert-manager uses (`topic-traefik`; portability design L6,
`docs/plans/2026-07-17-portability-design.md`, §1). Because the platform runs
k3s (`dec-2026-07-17-k3s-kubernetes-distribution`), one controller — Traefik —
already ships bundled and installed through k3s' manifests directory. The choice
is therefore not "which controller do we install" but "do we keep the one we
already have running, or disable it and own a different chart."

The spec settled this at design time (`docs/specs/2026-07-14-mini-cloud-bootstrap-design.md`,
§4): Traefik, the k3s default, "minder bewegende delen dan ingress-nginx erbij
zetten". `topic-traefik` documents the one behaviour we configure over it (the
platform-wide web→websecure redirect) and already carries the "why Traefik"
comparison; this record promotes that to an explicit decision with the
alternatives written out.

heading_path: Traefik is the ingress controller, because it is the k3s default
Decision
text:
We use the **k3s-bundled Traefik** (packaged chart `traefik-40.1.3+up40.1.0` at
`last_verified`) as the ingress controller, configured only where the platform
needs it: a single `HelmChartConfig` adds an entrypoint-level `web`→`websecure`
redirect so the whole platform is HTTPS-only and every `Ingress` inherits it.
We do not disable it or run a second controller. The configuration and its
version-dependent value shape are in `topic-traefik`.

heading_path: Traefik is the ingress controller, because it is the k3s default
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **Ingress is "already running", not "a chart we maintain".** Keeping the
  default means the routing we need exists with zero install work; the platform
  spends its novelty budget elsewhere (`topic-traefik`, "why Traefik, briefly").
- **One place sets the HTTPS-only policy.** Because the redirect is on the
  shared entrypoint, new apps get it for free — no per-`Ingress` middleware to
  remember (`topic-traefik`, "The web→websecure redirect").
- **cert-manager's HTTP-01 challenge has its attachment point** on the same
  `web` entrypoint (`topic-traefik`, `topic-cert-manager`).

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **Configuration is chart-version-dependent.** We configure Traefik by merging
  values over a chart k3s packages, so the correct key path
  (`ports.web.http.redirections.entryPoint` at v40.1.0, not the older flat
  `ports.web.redirectTo`) is a property of the pinned version. A bad bump
  produces **no error** — helm-controller merges a key the chart ignores — so
  the redirect silently stops, caught only by `verify:platform`'s 3xx check
  (`topic-traefik`, "The values shape is chart-version-dependent").
- **Traefik is tied to k3s here.** The `HelmChartConfig` route only exists
  because k3s ships Traefik; on a non-k3s distribution Traefik is not a default
  and this route disappears (portability design §2·L6). The ingress choice is
  therefore coupled to L4.

heading_path: Traefik is the ingress controller, because it is the k3s default
Alternatives considered
text:
Each alternative would replace the packaged Traefik: disable it with k3s'
`--disable=traefik`, then own a controller chart as a GitOps app.

- **ingress-nginx** — the Kubernetes-community NGINX-based controller. Rejected,
  and not only on inertia: its own docs state the project is in a retirement
  phase with best-effort maintenance only until March 2026 (`topic-traefik`) —
  a positive reason not to adopt it now. It routes nothing the bundled Traefik
  does not.
- **HAProxy Kubernetes Ingress Controller** — strong on L4/TCP routing
  (`topic-traefik`). Rejected as more than a two-node lab's plain HTTP needs,
  and it too turns "already running" into "a chart we own".
- **Caddy** — attractive for its automatic HTTPS. Rejected because cert-manager
  already owns certificate issuance on this platform (`topic-cert-manager`), so
  Caddy's signature feature would duplicate a solved layer, and Caddy as an
  ingress controller is a separate community project — again a chart we would
  maintain. It is a genuine outlier only if we ever want the ingress to absorb
  the certs layer (portability design §2·L6/L7).
- **A per-`Ingress` `RedirectScheme` middleware** instead of the entrypoint
  redirect — not a controller alternative but the alternative *mechanism* for
  the one thing we configure. Rejected because the HTTPS-only policy is a
  property of the platform, not of any one app, so it belongs in one inherited
  place rather than a stanza every app author must copy (`topic-traefik`).

heading_path: Traefik is the ingress controller, because it is the k3s default
Revisit triggers
text:
- The platform moves off k3s — Traefik stops being a default and the ingress
  choice is genuinely reopened (portability design §2·L4/L6).
- A requirement appears that Traefik does not serve well (heavy L4/TCP routing →
  HAProxy; wanting the ingress to also manage certs → Caddy).
- A k3s (and thus Traefik chart) version bump changes the redirect value schema
  — re-verify the key against the new tag's `values.yaml` (`topic-traefik`,
  pitfalls).

heading_path: The platform is a 2-node cluster with memory limits pinned to 8 GB nodes
Context
text:
The lab has two netcup VPS 1000 G12 instances (4 vCore / 8 GB / 256 GB NVMe
each), already procured (`dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`, spec §1). Two
questions of shape follow from that hardware: how the nodes form a cluster, and
how much memory each workload is allowed. Both are answered against the same
constraint — two nodes, 8 GB each — and both were decided in the design spec
(§3 topology, §7 restrisico's; §6 the "resource-limits op alle componenten"
posture). This record promotes those to an explicit decision with alternatives,
because the topology sets the platform's single largest accepted risk (one
control-plane node) and the pins are the discipline that keeps the stack alive
on small nodes. The scaling design
(`docs/plans/2026-07-17-scaling-design.md`) is the forward-looking companion:
this record fixes the *current* shape, that plan describes growing out of it.

heading_path: The platform is a 2-node cluster with memory limits pinned to 8 GB nodes
Decision
text:
The platform is **one 2-node k3s cluster**: VPS 1 is the server (control-plane
**and** worker, and the ingress node the public A-records point at), VPS 2 joins
as an agent (spec §3). We accept **one control-plane node** as a named residual
risk. Every workload carries a **memory limit tuned to an 8 GB node** (CPU as a
request, not a limit — a CPU limit throttles rather than protects): Prometheus
1Gi, Argo application-controller 1Gi, Loki 512Mi, Alloy 256Mi, cert-manager
128Mi, Argo CD server/repo-server 256Mi each, demo-app 32Mi, with the rest in
`topic-kube-prometheus-stack` and the gitops manifests. The cluster shape is
derived from the inventory, not hard-coded to "2".

heading_path: The platform is a 2-node cluster with memory limits pinned to 8 GB nodes
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **The multi-node lesson is real, now.** A 2-node cluster exercises the join
  flow, cross-node WireGuard and cross-node backup for real, rather than
  deferring "the instructive step" behind a single-node stopgap (spec §3,
  rejected alternatives).
- **Costs stay small and predictable** — roughly €18/month for the pair
  (`dec-2026-07-14-vps-provider-selection`).
- **The pins keep the stack alive on small nodes.** Memory limits stop any one
  component OOMing the node out from under the rest; the Argo controller pin is
  a *observed* lesson (OOMKilled crashloop, restarts 17, at 6 managed apps →
  512Mi bumped to 1Gi), not a guess (scaling design §4.1).
- **Growth is designed for.** The inventory is the single source of node facts,
  so the firewall peer rules and node-exporter DaemonSet already grow to N nodes
  without edits (scaling design §1.1).

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **No HA control plane.** If VPS 1 is down, workloads on VPS 2 keep running but
  nothing schedules or heals, `kubectl` answers nothing, and — because VPS 1 is
  also the ingress node — in practice the lab is down (`topic-k3s`, "Only one
  control-plane node"; spec §7). This is accepted on purpose and recorded as a
  restrisico in the Haven measurement.
- **Real HA is not a small step.** It needs **≥3 servers** (etcd quorum is
  (n/2)+1, so two servers is *worse* than one) and a migration off SQLite onto
  embedded etcd — a datastore migration plus a VIP/LB in front of the API
  (`topic-k3s`; scaling design §2).
- **The pins are correct only for this context.** They are lower bounds that
  protect an 8 GB node; on a 32 GB node they are cramped (Prometheus still capped
  at 1Gi with 24Gi free). They are context-dependent, which is why a
  node-size-aware resource-profile mechanism is the designed way out, not raising
  each number by hand (scaling design §4.2–4.3).

heading_path: The platform is a 2-node cluster with memory limits pinned to 8 GB nodes
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Platform + a separate tenant VPS** (hard physical isolation). Rejected in the
  spec (§3): a single-node cluster fails more Haven checks, costs double (two
  stacks on 8 GB each), and tenant-as-a-separate-VPS is not how Haven intends
  multi-tenancy — a namespace with its own RBAC/quota/network-policies is.
- **Single node now, grow later.** The smallest step. Rejected (spec §3): it
  defers precisely the instructive multi-node step, and "prepared for later"
  without a test is false assurance.
- **HA 3-node control plane now.** Rejected as premature: with only two nodes it
  is not possible (quorum needs an odd ≥3), and three servers without workload
  growth is "quorum without a reason" (scaling design §2; spec §7). It is the
  logical step *after* horizontal growth, not before.
- **Larger nodes (vertical scale) instead of pinning.** Rejected for phase A on
  cost and because the pins are needed regardless — a bigger node still wants
  bounded components; the right answer is a resource *profile* per node-size
  class, designed but not built (scaling design §4.3).
- **No memory limits (rely on requests/scheduling).** Rejected: the observed
  Argo OOM shows an unbounded component can crashloop and threaten the node; on
  8 GB the limits are protection, not tidiness (scaling design §4.1).

heading_path: The platform is a 2-node cluster with memory limits pinned to 8 GB nodes
Revisit triggers
text:
- Workloads grow enough to need more nodes — horizontal growth is
  inventory-driven and mostly N-ready today (scaling design §1); it is the
  precondition for HA.
- HA becomes required — that reopens the "precisely one server" assert (to "1 or
  ≥3 odd"), the SQLite→etcd datastore migration, and a VIP/LB for the API
  (scaling design §2; `topic-k3s`).
- Node size grows (16/32 GB) — the 8 GB pins become the bottleneck and want the
  resource-profile mechanism (scaling design §4.3).
- A storage layer lands, adding stateful workloads whose availability makes the
  single control-plane risk less acceptable (scaling design §3).

heading_path: Cross-node backup transport stays on the public peer IP
Context
text:
The mini-cloud writes restic backups from each node to its peer over SFTP
(see `dec-2026-07-17-restic-cross-node-backup` and
`rb-2026-07-17-backup-restore`). The peer is addressed by its **public IP**,
configurable through `backup_peer_address`. The question raised at gate 2b was
whether that transport should instead ride the cluster's flannel WireGuard
overlay (the `flannel-wg` pod network), so backup traffic would traverse an
encrypted tunnel between the nodes rather than the public internet.

heading_path: Cross-node backup transport stays on the public peer IP
Decision
text:
Cross-node backup transport **stays on the public peer IP**. We do not move it
onto the flannel-wg overlay. `backup_peer_address` remains the configurable
hook, so the transport can be repointed without code changes if the topology
later demands it.

heading_path: Cross-node backup transport stays on the public peer IP
Consequences
text:
- **Disaster recovery keeps working when the cluster does not.** The backup
  path must be available precisely in the failure modes where the platform is
  broken. `flannel-wg` is the k3s **pod overlay**: it exists only while k3s and
  its CNI are healthy. Binding backups to it would couple "can I restore?" to
  "is the cluster up?" — the exact coupling DR must avoid.
- **No confidentiality is lost.** Both layers already encrypt: restic encrypts
  every blob at rest with the repository key, and SFTP runs over SSH on the
  wire. The overlay would add a third encryption layer over data that is
  already doubly protected — cost without a matching gain.
- **Operational simplicity.** The transport depends only on sshd and a routable
  address, not on the CNI being converged. One fewer moving part in the restore
  path.
- **Trade-off accepted:** backup traffic crosses the public network (encrypted
  end to end). The peer's `authorized_keys` entry scopes the SFTP receive
  account to the peer source address (`restrict,from="<peer-ip>"`), so exposure
  stays narrow.

heading_path: Cross-node backup transport stays on the public peer IP
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Route backups over the flannel-wg overlay address** — rejected. It is a pod
  overlay, not a management tunnel: it disappears in the very DR scenarios where
  the backup must still reach its peer, and it adds a third encryption layer
  over already-encrypted, already-SSH-tunnelled data for no confidentiality
  gain.

heading_path: The PersistentVolume layer is a single NFS server, for now
text:
> Legend: **⟐** = a design estimate for a not-yet-built step (harness §4a) — an
> intention, not an observed fact. Everything not marked ⟐ is derivable from the
> repos today.

heading_path: The PersistentVolume layer is a single NFS server, for now
Context
text:
The mini-cloud had **no persistent storage layer**. The spec (§4) deliberately
chose k3s' local-path provisioner and left it there; observability runs on
`emptyDir` as a result, and any data that must survive a pod restart survives
today only via git-replay plus the datastore snapshot, never via a
PersistentVolume. The scaling design (`soevereinlab-marketplace/docs/plans/
2026-07-17-scaling-design.md` §3) named this the **largest missing building
block for real recoverability** and left the choice of storage layer open as
the "twelfth layer", weighing three candidates without picking one.

On 2026-07-20 (live, in session) Jelle chose to build the layer now as **NFS** —
explicitly **with** the limitations, the ideal end-state, and the migration path
documented, rather than presenting NFS as the finished answer.

heading_path: The PersistentVolume layer is a single NFS server, for now
Decision
text:
The PersistentVolume layer is a **single NFS server on the k3s server node
(vps1)** exporting one directory (`/srv/nfs/k8s`), with the
**`nfs-subdir-external-provisioner`** (Helm chart 4.0.18, pinned) as a GitOps
Argo Application handing each PVC its own subdirectory. Specifically:

- The StorageClass `nfs-client` is **not** the cluster default — local-path
  stays default, so a PV lands on NFS only through an explicit
  `storageClassName: nfs-client`, a deliberate per-workload choice.
- The export uses **`root_squash`** (client-root maps to `nobody`); the export
  root is therefore mode `0777` so the squashed identity can create per-PV
  subdirectories — one linked decision, not two.
- NFSv4-only, reachable on **2049/tcp from the peer node(s) only**, fenced by
  the same `baseline_k3s_peer_ports` ufw peer rule that already opens 9100.
- The export path is added to `backup_extra_paths` on the NFS host, so PV data
  rides the existing cross-node restic backup.

We do **not** build Longhorn or a provider CSI, and we do not move any existing
workload (Prometheus/Loki stay `emptyDir`) onto a PVC — those are separate,
later, per-component decisions.

heading_path: The PersistentVolume layer is a single NFS server, for now
Consequences
text:
Stateful workloads become possible for the first time: a workload that asks for
`nfs-client` gets a volume that survives its pod moving to another node, and its
data is carried in the restic backup. The layer is cheap in-cluster — one small
provisioner pod — and adds nothing to cert-manager or the other apps' load. What
becomes harder is the honest part, below.

One build-phase caveat on "moving to another node": for a pod landing on the
**server** node itself to mount the export, the client-list grant must include
the server node's own IP — the "grant all node IPs, no `difference()`" shape
tracked in mini-cloud MR !36 (see [topic-nfs](../topics/topic-nfs.md)). Until
that fix lands and is applied, self-access on the server node is not yet
granted.

### Limitations (the reason this decision is written, not just made)

- **The NFS server is a single point of failure.** It runs on vps1, the same
  node as the k3s control plane. If vps1 is down, **no PVC binds or serves**.
  The blast radius of losing that one node now includes all cluster PV data.
- **No replication — recovery is copy-back, not failover.** PV data survives
  node loss **only** via the restic backup; there is no second live copy. A
  restore is a deliberate operator action (restic → re-populate the export),
  not an automatic takeover. This is the durability story, and it is a recovery
  story, not an availability one.
- **The NFS traffic is unencrypted over the public peer IP.** vps1 and vps2
  share no private LAN and the flannel wireguard device is a *pod* overlay, not
  a node tunnel, so the provisioner mounts over the **public** IP (the same
  reasoning as [dec-2026-07-20-backup-transport-public-peer-ip](dec-2026-07-20-backup-transport-public-peer-ip.md)).
  NFSv4 here runs without krb5, so the file traffic is in clear. The **primary,
  network-level** mitigation is the ufw peer restriction: the
  `baseline_k3s_peer_ports` rule scopes 2049/tcp to the peer node's source
  address, so nothing off the peer can reach the export. A second fence sits at
  the NFS layer itself — the export is granted only to the node IPs in
  `nfs_allowed_clients` (see [topic-nfs](../topics/topic-nfs.md)), so even a host
  that reached 2049 would still have to match an allowed client address. Both are
  network-reachability fences, **not** on-the-wire confidentiality — unlike
  restic's SFTP transport, which is additionally SSH-encrypted end to end. Anyone
  able to observe traffic between the two public IPs would see PV contents.
- **`root_squash` → 0777 export root.** Acceptable only because the export is
  peer-only and holds nothing but PV data (see the linked topic), but it is a
  real widening that a reviewer should understand rather than rubber-stamp.
- **Single-writer / locking caveats.** `nfs-subdir` gives each PVC its own
  subdirectory; it is well suited to `ReadWriteOnce`-style single-writer
  workloads. NFS file locking across many concurrent writers is a known rough
  edge and this layer is not intended for high-concurrency shared-write data.
- **NFSv4-single-port is unverified.** The single-2049 firewall assumption has
  not been proven against a node in this build (§4a); the first apply +
  `verify:storage` run confirms it or surfaces the extra ports needed.

### ⟐ Ideal end-state

The end-state is **replicated storage**, so that losing one node does not take
the PV layer with it:

- **Longhorn** — replicated block-storage (CSI) across the nodes, once the nodes
  have enough memory to carry its per-node manager/engine pods without colliding
  with the 8 GB memory pins (scaling design §3.3, §4). Longhorn also brings its
  own snapshot/backup-to-S3 path.
- **or provider block-storage with a provider CSI**, where the infra provider
  offers attachable volumes with API snapshots. Lower in-cluster cost, at the
  price of coupling the storage layer to that provider (a layer-lock, portability
  §2·L2).

Both remove the single-server SPOF that this decision accepts; the choice
between them is a resource-budget-vs-provider-lock trade left open (scaling
design §8, open question 4).

### ⟐ Migration path (NFS → replicated)

The layers are designed to coexist so the move is per-workload, not a big-bang:

1. Stand up the new StorageClass (e.g. `longhorn`) **alongside** `nfs-client`;
   neither is forced default.
2. Migrate PVCs **one workload at a time**: provision a new PVC on the new
   class, copy the data over (or restore from the restic backup into it),
   repoint the workload, verify, then release the old `nfs-client` PVC.
3. Once no workload references `nfs-client`, **phase out NFS**: remove the
   `nfs-storage` Application, the `nfs` role from the server play, the 2049/tcp
   peer rule, and the export path from `backup_extra_paths`.

Because `nfs-client` is not the default, no workload is dragged along
implicitly — each move is a conscious `storageClassName` change, which is
exactly why "not default" was chosen up front.

heading_path: The PersistentVolume layer is a single NFS server, for now
Alternatives considered
text:
The three candidates from the scaling design (§3.3), with why NFS wins **for
now** and why it is not the end-state:

| Candidate | Form | Backup consequence | Resource budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Longhorn** | Replicated block-storage over the nodes (CSI) | PV paths under Longhorn's data-dir → `backup_extra_paths`; also has its own snapshot/backup to S3 | Heavy: replica traffic + per-node manager/engine pods — collides with the 8 GB pins |
| **NFS** (chosen) | One NFS server, `nfs-subdir-external-provisioner` | One export path → `backup_extra_paths` on the NFS host | Low in-cluster, but the NFS server is a new SPOF/layer |
| **Provider block-storage** | Attached volume per node, provider CSI | Volume snapshots via the provider API | Low in-cluster; couples storage to the provider (lock) |

- **Longhorn now** — rejected for this build. It is the ideal end-state
  (replication), but its per-node manager/engine footprint collides with the
  8 GB memory pins; it becomes the right answer once the nodes are larger.
- **Provider block-storage now** — rejected for this build. Low in-cluster cost,
  but it couples the storage layer to a single infra provider, a layer-lock we
  are not ready to take on for a first PV layer.
- **No storage layer (status quo)** — rejected. Leaving the platform on
  `emptyDir`/local-path keeps "the largest missing building block for real
  recoverability" (scaling design §3) unbuilt; a cheap, honestly-bounded NFS
  layer unblocks stateful workloads today while the migration path keeps the
  door open to replication.

heading_path: Alerts leave the cluster via self-hosted ntfy, not ntfy.sh
Context
text:
The alerting chain was plumbed but had no working delivery route: Alertmanager
grouped and deduplicated alerts, but the last hop — getting a notification onto
a phone — was still open (`reference/alert-receiver-draaiboek.md`). Two obvious
external routes were tried against the real nodes on 2026-07-20 and both are
structurally blocked from the netcup VPSes:

- **ntfy.sh is unreachable over IPv4 from both nodes.** A clocked diagnosis
  observed `dial tcp 159.203.148.75:443: connection timed out`; `curl -4` to
  ntfy.sh timed out on both nodes while `curl -6` returned `200` on both, and
  unrelated IPv4 egress was fine (google and github both returned `200`). The
  pods are IPv4-only, so Alertmanager could never reach ntfy.sh — not a config
  bug: the Alertmanager config was correct and live, a test alert arrived in
  Alertmanager, and the notify step failed with a timeout (verified in the
  logs). This is an IPv4/egress fault class, not something the receiver config
  can fix.
- **Outbound SMTP is closed.** Ports 25/465/587 to smtp.gmail.com time out from
  the node — netcup's standard outbound-mail block — so the Gmail e-mail route
  cannot work either without a provider action.

With both external routes blocked at the network layer, the choice was where to
put the receiver: keep depending on an external service that the network cannot
reach, or bring the receiver inside the cluster where the alert already lives.

heading_path: Alerts leave the cluster via self-hosted ntfy, not ntfy.sh
Decision
text:
We run **ntfy self-hosted on the cluster** as a GitOps `Application`, fully
sovereign — no external dependency in the alert-delivery path. Concretely:

- **Locked down by default.** `auth-default-access: deny-all` with declarative
  user/token provisioning — a publish token for Alertmanager and a read token
  for the phone — supplied through the existing Ansible-out-of-SOPS secret route
  (`dec-2026-07-17-app-secrets-ansible-sops`).
- **Alertmanager publishes in-cluster.** It posts to the Service URL
  `http://ntfy.ntfy.svc.cluster.local/soevereinlab-alerts`, which stays entirely
  inside the cluster network and so sidesteps the IPv4/hairpin fault class that
  killed the ntfy.sh route.
- **The phone reads over the public endpoint.** The ntfy app subscribes over
  `https://ntfy.<your-domain>` (existing wildcard DNS, Let's Encrypt
  certificate), with its read token. The concrete host lives in the config
  repo (`gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/ingress.yaml`), not here.

heading_path: Alerts leave the cluster via self-hosted ntfy, not ntfy.sh
Consequences
text:
**What becomes easier:**

- **No external dependency for alert delivery.** The whole path — alert fires,
  Alertmanager posts, ntfy holds it — lives on the cluster, immune to the
  IPv4-egress and SMTP-block fault classes that blocked both external routes.
- **The security no longer rests on a secret topic name.** With `deny-all`,
  publishing and reading both require a token, so the topic name
  `soevereinlab-alerts` can be non-secret — auth carries the protection, not
  obscurity.
- **It reuses a proven, CI-guarded secret route.** The publish/read tokens ride
  the same Ansible-out-of-SOPS path already used for other app secrets
  (`dec-2026-07-17-app-secrets-ansible-sops`), so no new secrets mechanism.

**What becomes harder / the cost we accept:**

- **We own the server now.** Running ntfy ourselves means we patch and update
  it: the image is version-pinned and digest-pinned, and bumping it is our job,
  not a hosted provider's.
- **The auth database is derived state, deliberately.** Users and tokens are
  re-provisioned from config/env on every start, so the auth DB is disposable:
  it lives on an `emptyDir`, with **no PVC and no sqlite-on-NFS**. This keeps a
  fragile file database off shared storage at the cost of nothing durable — the
  source of truth is the SOPS-encrypted config, not the running DB.

heading_path: Alerts leave the cluster via self-hosted ntfy, not ntfy.sh
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Keep using ntfy.sh.** Rejected: structurally unreachable over IPv4 from the
  nodes (measured 2026-07-20). Making it work would mean enabling IPv6 for the
  pods or an egress fix — an infra intervention outside this decision's scope,
  and one that would still leave delivery depending on an external service.
- **A transactional mail API over HTTPS** (bypassing the SMTP block). Rejected:
  it routes around the port block but introduces an external — typically
  non-EU — dependency in the delivery path, which runs against the sovereignty
  goal that motivates the whole platform.
- **A netcup ticket to unblock SMTP, then Gmail.** Rejected for now: the lead
  time is uncertain and it makes delivery depend on a provider action. The
  e-mail channel is parked, not killed — it remains a possible second channel
  later and is explicitly **not part of this decision**.

heading_path: Alerts leave the cluster via self-hosted ntfy, not ntfy.sh
Revisit when
text:
- ntfy needs durable state for a real reason (persistent message history,
  attachments) — then the emptyDir/no-PVC choice reopens against whatever
  storage layer exists by then.
- The e-mail channel is wanted after all (netcup unblocks SMTP, or a sovereign
  mail route appears) — add it as a second Alertmanager receiver alongside ntfy,
  don't replace it.
- Pods gain IPv6 or egress changes for other reasons — the in-cluster Service
  URL still stays the right call, but the constraint that forced it is gone.

heading_path: A behaviour claim is checked against the object itself; inherited repo prose is not a source
Context
text:
The execution-harness truth discipline (marketplace repo,
`docs/plans/2026-07-15-execution-harness.md` §4a) already required every
factual claim in a comment, doc or commit message to be sourced or observed in
the same session. The plan-f T4 post-step audit
(`docs/plans/audits/plan-f-taak-4.md`, finding O-1) exposed a gap in that rule:
an executor wrote a behaviour claim about a specific ConfigMap mount ("kubelet
refreshes those files") into a README as the rationale for a design decision.
The only source was a pre-existing, unverified script comment in the same
repository — and the object's own manifest contradicted the claim: the
deployment mounted the ConfigMap with `subPath:`, which per the Kubernetes
documentation never receives updates, in a file the same commit explicitly
declared untouched. The false claim landed in four places (README twice,
commit message, kustomization comment) and survived the executor's §4a
self-check, because "I read it in the repo" satisfied the letter of the rule.

heading_path: A behaviour claim is checked against the object itself; inherited repo prose is not a source
Decision
text:
Harness §4a gains clause 5. A behaviour claim about a specific object is
checked against that object's own manifest or code in the same session — a
general rule about its kind does not suffice, because one field in the object
can switch the rule off. Repeating a claim found in repo prose (script
comment, README, commit message) in a new document is re-asserting it under
your own name; passing it on is allowed only with attribution ("according to
the audit", "the script comment says"). One exception: claims injected by a
task-brief count as sourced for the executor, because the brief writer carried
the §4a duty when writing the brief (harness §3; the task-brief skill now
states that burden explicitly).

heading_path: A behaviour claim is checked against the object itself; inherited repo prose is not a source
Consequences
text:
Audits can now rule any unattributed repeated claim as the writer's own
untrue statement — no more laundering an inherited guess into authoritative
fact. Writers must open the object they describe before claiming its
behaviour, which costs a read but is exactly the read that would have caught
O-1. Brief writers carry a heavier, explicit sourcing burden, since executors
may treat brief-injected claims as sourced. The clause is codified in the
marketplace repo (harness §4a.5 plus the task-brief skill,
execution-harness plugin 0.2.0, marketplace !46, merge commit `500d76c`).

heading_path: A behaviour claim is checked against the object itself; inherited repo prose is not a source
Alternatives considered
text:
- **Two separate clauses (object-check and inherited-rationale)** — rejected:
  the audit showed they are two faces of the same failure (a general-kind rule
  quoted from repo prose, never checked against the object), and one clause
  keeps the rule readable.
- **A blanket "never repeat repo prose"** — rejected as unfollowable: it would
  also ban attributed citations and the context injection of task-briefs,
  which the harness (§2/§3) requires executors to rely on instead of exploring
  the repos.
- **Independent re-verification of every quoted claim** — rejected: it pushes
  executors into the repo-wide exploration the harness exists to prevent;
  attribution keeps the assertion honest at a fraction of the token cost.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
text:
Alertmanager groepeert en dedupliceert alerts en stuurt ze naar een **receiver**.
Dit draaiboek beschrijft welke receiver we draaien, waar je hem aanpast, en hoe
je bewijst dat een alert écht aankomt.

> **Historie.** Tot 2026-07-21 stond hier een keuzemenu (ntfy.sh, e-mail, chat,
> generieke webhook) met de aantekening "niet getest". Die situatie is
> achterhaald: de publieke `ntfy.sh` bleek **structureel onbereikbaar over IPv4**
> vanaf de netcup-nodes en uitgaande **SMTP is door netcup geblokkeerd**, dus
> zowel de ntfy.sh- als de e-mailroute vielen af op netwerkniveau. De meting en
> de afweging staan in
> [dec-2026-07-21-self-hosted-ntfy](../decisions/dec-2026-07-21-self-hosted-ntfy.md).
> Het "geen secret nodig, kies een niet te raden topicnaam"-advies uit die versie
> geldt **niet meer**: onze ntfy staat op `deny-all`, dus auth is verplicht en de
> topicnaam is bewust gewoon leesbaar.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
De keten zoals hij nu loopt
text:
| Schakel | Wat | Waar |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prometheus evalueert de regels | `gitops/platform/monitoring/` |
| 2 | Alertmanager groepeert (`group_wait: 30s`) en routeert naar receiver `ntfy` | `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml` |
| 3 | Webhook-`POST` naar de **in-cluster** ntfy Service, met Bearer-token | idem |
| 4 | ntfy houdt het bericht vast (`cache-duration: 12h`) | `gitops/apps/ntfy/` |
| 5 | Telefoon leest het over de publieke ingress, met het read-token | `gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/ingress.yaml` |

Alles onder 3–5 staat uitgelegd in [topic-ntfy](../topics/topic-ntfy.md) — elke
vlag die we zetten en waarom.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
Waar je het aanpast
text:
Twee plekken, beide GitOps (merge → Argo synct; geen `kubectl` nodig):

- **De receiver-kant:** `gitops/platform/monitoring/app.yaml`, het blok
  `alertmanager.config`. Dit is de kant die je aanraakt als je routeert,
  groepeert of van receiver wisselt.
- **De ntfy-server zelf:** `gitops/apps/ntfy/` (ConfigMap, Deployment, Service,
  Ingress). Dit is de kant die je aanraakt voor auth, ACL's of de versie-pin.

De huidige receiver-config, letterlijk:

```yaml
route:
  group_by: ['namespace', 'alertname']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 12h
  receiver: 'ntfy'
  routes:
    - receiver: 'null'
      matchers:
        - alertname = "Watchdog"
receivers:
  - name: 'null'
  - name: 'ntfy'
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://ntfy.ntfy.svc.cluster.local/soevereinlab-alerts'
        send_resolved: true
        http_config:
          authorization:
            type: Bearer
            credentials_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/ntfy-webhook-token/token
```

Drie dingen die geen toeval zijn:

- **De URL is de in-cluster Service, niet de publieke hostnaam.** Publiceren naar
  `https://ntfy.<your-domain>` zou het cluster verlaten en over IPv4 terug moeten
  hairpinnen — precies de faalklasse die de ntfy.sh-route sloopte. In-cluster
  verkeer raakt de egress-route van de node nooit.
- **Het token komt uit een bestand, niet uit de values.** `credentials_file`
  wijst naar het pad waar de prometheus-operator een Secret mount:
  `/etc/alertmanager/secrets/<secretnaam>/<key>`, aangestuurd door
  `alertmanagerSpec.secrets: [ntfy-webhook-token]`. Een inline `credentials`
  zou het token in git zetten. De waarde zelf komt via de SOPS→Ansible-route
  ([topic-sops](../topics/topic-sops.md),
  `dec-2026-07-17-app-secrets-ansible-sops`).
- **`send_resolved: true`.** Zonder dit kan een alert alleen aankomen, nooit
  dichtgaan, en moet de lezer raden of het incident nog loopt.
- **De `Watchdog` blijft op `null`.** Dat is een hartslag van ~30s die per
  definitie altijd vuurt; hem doorlaten betekent elke 30 seconden een melding.
  Dat hij vuurt wordt bewezen door `verify:observability`, niet door je telefoon.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
Auth: deny-all met een ACL per gebruiker
text:
De ntfy-server draait `auth-default-access: deny-all`. Iedereen die niet in de
ACL staat — inclusief anoniem — mag niets, lezen noch publiceren. Daarbovenop
staat een ACL die de twee richtingen scheidt:

```yaml
auth-access:
  - "alertmanager:soevereinlab-alerts:wo"
  - "phone:soevereinlab-alerts:ro"
```

`wo` = alleen schrijven, `ro` = alleen lezen. Alertmanager kan dus niet meelezen
en de telefoon kan geen alerts vervalsen. Gevolg voor dit draaiboek: **de
topicnaam draagt geen beveiliging meer** en mag gewoon leesbaar zijn — het token
doet het werk. Gebruikers, hashes en tokens komen als env
(`NTFY_AUTH_USERS`/`NTFY_AUTH_TOKENS`) uit Secret `ntfy-auth`; geen enkele
waarde hoort in deze repo of in een chat.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
Een toestel abonneren
text:
De publieke kant is `https://ntfy.<your-domain>` (host in
`gitops/apps/ntfy/manifests/ingress.yaml`, Let's Encrypt-certificaat via
cert-manager). In de ntfy-app op het toestel:

1. *Abonnement toevoegen* → **een andere server gebruiken** → die server-URL.
2. Topic: `soevereinlab-alerts`.
3. Inloggegevens **verplicht** — de server is deny-all, er is geen anonieme
   route. Gebruik de `phone`-gebruiker of diens read-token; de waarden staan in
   `ansible/vars/secrets.sops.yaml` in `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` en typ je met de
   hand op het toestel over.

Dat het abonnement read-only is, merk je aan de knop "testmelding versturen" in
de app: die geeft een permissiefout. Dat is correct gedrag, geen kapot
abonnement.

> **Aandachtspunt (geen secretwaarde nodig om te snappen).**
> `NTFY_AUTH_USERS` maakt `alertmanager` en `phone` vandaag aan met **dezelfde
> wachtwoord-hash**. De tokens verschillen en de ACL is netjes gesplitst, maar
> wie het telefoonwachtwoord kent kan ook inloggen als `alertmanager` en op het
> topic publiceren. **Aanbevolen verbetering: een eigen hash voor `phone`.**
> Zolang dat niet gebeurd is, behandel je het telefoonwachtwoord met dezelfde
> zorg als het publish-token.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
De berichtgrootte: wat je op je telefoon ziet is afgekapt
text:
We sturen **de rauwe Alertmanager-webhook-JSON** als berichttekst — de bewuste
keuze "begin ruw, verfijn later". ntfy's standaard maximale berichtgrootte is
**~4096 bytes**, en een echte alertgroep met labels en annotations gaat daar
overheen. De melding wordt dan afgekapt.

**Consequentie voor wie de melding leest:** behandel een ntfy-melding als het
signaal *dat* er iets vuurt, niet als de volledige inhoud. Bij een groep van
meerdere alerts kan de alertnaam die je zoekt buiten de afkapgrens vallen, dus
zoek de details op in Alertmanager/Prometheus en niet in de notificatie. Eén
enkele alert past ruim; het is de groep die je bijt.

**Opvolgstap (nog niet gedaan):** templating. ntfy heeft een ingebouwde
`alertmanager`-template, aan te spreken als `?template=alertmanager` of via een
`X-Template`-header, die de firing/resolved-payload zelf tot een nette titel en
korte body formatteert. Dat vervangt de JSON-dump door iets leesbaars en maakt
de afkapgrens irrelevant. Zie ook [topic-ntfy](../topics/topic-ntfy.md).

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
Bewijzen dat het aankomt
text:
Drie niveaus, van goedkoop naar echt:

1. **`verify:ntfy:on-demand` (CI, leest alleen, geen `apply`).** Draait
   `scripts/verify-ntfy.sh` en bewijst per run: `/v1/health` meldt healthy; een
   **onauthenticated** poll van het topic krijgt `403` (deny-all staat er nog);
   een publish met het echte write-token krijgt `200` en hetzelfde bericht komt
   terug met het **read**-token (de round-trip én de rolsplitsing); een
   verzonnen token krijgt `401`; en Alertmanager hangt aantoonbaar aan de
   in-cluster ntfy. Dit is de check die het draaiboek waarmaakt — bewust
   **niet** `allow_failure`, want een stilweg weggevallen deny-all leest als
   "Healthy".
   *Wat het niet bewijst:* de laatste hop naar het toestel.
2. **Handmatige testalert.** Zie
   [rb-2026-07-27-ntfy-alert-e2e-bewijs](../runbooks/rb-2026-07-27-ntfy-alert-e2e-bewijs.md)
   — het volledige, geklokte recept. Kern: `POST` naar Alertmanager's
   `/api/v2/alerts` **via de ClusterIP, niet via de API-service-proxy** (die
   draagt geen `Content-Type` en levert `415`), daarna kijken naar je telefoon.
3. **De Watchdog.** Vuurt continu, maar routeert bewust naar `null`; hem
   tijdelijk omleiden is een alternatief end-to-end-bewijs, met als nadeel dat
   je hem daarna moet terugzetten. De testalert uit (2) is schoner.

**Geklokt bewijs 2026-07-27:** synthetische alert `NtfyE2ETest` afgevuurd om
18:48:37Z, firing-melding op het toestel om 18:49Z (binnen `group_wait` 30s),
resolved-melding om 18:54Z (`resolve_timeout` 5m — Alertmanagers standaard, wij
zetten hem niet — in combinatie met `send_resolved: true`). Daarmee is het
plan-D-restpunt "ntfy-end-to-end-bewijs" gesloten.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
Als je ooit van receiver wisselt of er één bij zet
text:
Alertmanager kan meerdere receivers; ntfy hoeft niet weg om er één bij te
zetten. Waar de andere routes stonden, staat nu wat we ervan weten:

- **E-mail (SMTP) — geparkeerd, niet dood.** netcup blokkeert uitgaand
  25/465/587 vanaf de nodes, dus dit werkt pas na een provider-actie. Daarna:
  `email_configs` met `auth_password_file` en een Secret via
  `alertmanagerSpec.secrets`, hetzelfde mount-patroon als het ntfy-token
  hierboven. Toevoegen **naast** ntfy, niet in plaats van.
- **Chat (Slack/Teams) of een generieke webhook.** Zelfde vorm als de
  ntfy-receiver: de URL of het token is het geheim, dus `api_url_file` /
  `credentials_file` plus een Secret-mount — nooit inline in de values.
- **Terug naar een gehoste dienst.** Alleen zinvol als de IPv4-egressbeperking
  van de nodes verdwijnt; anders herhaal je de faalklasse uit de decision.

Bij elke wissel: werk deze pagina, [topic-ntfy](../topics/topic-ntfy.md) en
[topic-prometheusrule-alerting](../topics/topic-prometheusrule-alerting.md) bij
in dezelfde MR, en laat `verify-ntfy.sh` meebewegen — een verificatie die de
oude receiver test is erger dan geen verificatie.

heading_path: Alert receiver draaiboek — self-hosted ntfy als ontvanger
Openstaande opvolgpunten
text:
- **Templating** in plaats van rauwe JSON (zie de berichtgrootte-sectie).
- **Eigen wachtwoord-hash voor `phone`** (zie het aandachtspunt hierboven).
- **Alertruis van de k3s control-plane — opgelost, controleer het effect.**
  `KubeControllerManagerDown`, `KubeSchedulerDown` en `KubeProxyDown` vuurden
  vanaf 2026-07-17 onafgebroken en werden elke 12u (`repeat_interval`) opnieuw
  naar dit kanaal gestuurd: op k3s draaien die drie ín het k3s-proces en binden
  hun metrics op loopback, dus de chart kan ze niet scrapen zoals hij aanneemt.
  De chart-values zetten ze nu uit; dat is gemerged in
  `soevereinlab-mini-cloud` op 2026-07-27 (ná de meting hieronder, wat aan die
  meting niets verandert) en de monitoring-`Application` synct automatisch.
  **Waarom het hier staat:** een kanaal dat vanaf dag één drie permanente
  criticals stuurt, leert de ontvanger wegkijken — de duurste storing van een
  alertkanaal is niet stilte maar ruis. Controleer bij de eerstvolgende
  gelegenheid dat de drie inderdaad weg zijn van het toestel.

heading_path: Command cookbook — verified recipes for recurring operations
text:
**What:** copy-paste-ready command patterns for the operations agents perform
over and over (MRs, GitLab API, SSH, Windows workstation quirks). Each recipe
states where it was proven. **Copy from here instead of composing from
memory** — the recurring class of review findings "command subtly wrong"
